records.title: News marketing and the promise of insider access
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: In the opening post of a two-part argument, Rosen questions news subscription imagery that promises readers greater access to an inner circle.
records.quote:
I have been looking at the imagery here. There's a tell.

It's not the paywall, almost everyone has a paywall. Every newsroom boasts of their "exclusives"— exclusive or not. Different levels of pay-dom are common too.

"Even more inside." Hmm. That's supposed to be funny, I think. But is it?

1 of 2

records.title: Two meanings of journalism's inner circle
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Continuing his post about news subscription imagery, Rosen distinguishes reporting that makes readers feel present from a paid promise of knowledge withheld from others.
records.quote:
"Join us in the inner circle" is read in two ways.

One is "reporting so good it feels like you're there, in person." Exciting! And worth the money, right?

"Join the inner circle" also says: "You have the money. Now you get to know things unavailable to others." Awesome, right?

That's the tell.

records.title: Commercialization, gatekeepers, and internet distribution
records.author: Jay Rosen

records.quote: It's been a gradual commercialization since the 1960s. The media became widely profitable and influential, in large part because the media companies could control distribution. That's why we called them gate keepers— for a while. Then the internet solved the distribution part on differerent terms.

You may know that I try to show newsrooms that they have an alternative to the horse race model in election coverage: "The citizens agenda."

It's the campaign season and I am starting to get examples sent to me.

Roanoke: roanoke.com/news/local/g...

Cascadia: www.cascadiadaily.com/2026/jul/16/...

If you're interested in the Citzens Agenda model with a Rosen twist try my Internet Archive

pressthink.org/j/rosen-arch...

Put 'citizens agenda' into the search button and see what you get. You can pick 'Newest First' or 'Oldest.' I recommend Newest.

Here's one I knew nothing about until today.

"The Alaska Beacon, Alaska Public Media, KTOO and the Anchorage Daily News worked together this year and have created a voter guide to help Alaskans make informed choices when they vote..."

alaskabeacon.com/2026/08/03/g...

Advice for newsrooms about the citizens agenda model:

The agenda is a high quality product. Or should be if done well.

After asking everyone you can, "what do you want the candidates to be taking about as they compere for votes?" test it, groom it, collect your thoughts, and PUBLISH THE AGENDA.

records.title: Subscribers buy a product. Members join the cause.
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: PressThink essay in which Rosen draws a distinction at the heart of journalism's funding debate: subscribers buy a product, members join the cause -- one a transaction, the other a commitment. Drawing on his 2017-2021 Membership Puzzle Project and Talking Points Memo's membership drive, he contrasts subscription models (Wall Street Journal, Financial Times, New York Times's "journalism worth paying for") with membership models such as the Salt Lake Tribune's decision to drop its paywall and treat trustworthy journalism as a right, not a luxury. He argues membership is about solidarity with a cause -- increasingly, chronicling an authoritarian crisis -- and predicts that donating one's knowledge and civic skills will become common practice in journalism.
records.quote: Subscribers buy a product. Members join the cause. One is a transaction, the other a kind of commitment.

records.title: For Jay Rosen, American Press Needs to Become More Pro-Democracy
records.author: Pau Torres Pages
records.summary: Interview with Jay Rosen for NYU's Journal of Political Inquiry, conducted by Pau Torres Pages. Rosen argues this is the worst time for American journalism because it is the worst time for American democracy, and presses his case that the American press must become more explicitly pro-democracy -- distilled in his slogan "not the odds but the stakes." He diagnoses the collapse of the Washington Post under Jeff Bezos, proposes a Washington Post Foundation/trust to insulate it from owners, assesses the defunding of public media and the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, and questions Bari Weiss's ideologically driven leadership of CBS. He closes that the powerful will always find ways to be informed; the open question is whether publics, in the plural, will remain so.
records.quote: The rich and powerful people will find ways to be informed. The question is whether publics, in plural, will continue to be informed.

records.title: Jay Rosen on the digital revolution that wasn't
records.author: Emily Bell and Heather Chaplin
records.summary: In CJR's Kicker podcast (Journalism 2050 series), Emily Bell and Heather Chaplin interview Rosen about the digital revolution that didn't deliver on its promises. He reflects on his 2006 essay 'The People Formerly Known as the Audience' and how what was initially understood as a technology of liberation became a mechanism of control and surveillance. The Financial Times data shows social media has become 'less social' -- the people formerly known as the audience are once again the audience.
records.quote: What was initially understood to be a technology of liberation became, increasingly, a mechanism of control: a means of surveilling the public, selling ads, and generating enormous profits for a small number of companies.

records.title: A new fellowship is all about putting the news in news creator
records.author: Neel Dhanesha
records.summary: The Columbia Journalism School is launching the News Creator Fellowship, a year-long program designed to support independent journalists and content creators producing original news outside traditional media. The fellowship will provide a $75,000 stipend, access to university resources, mentorship, workshops, workspace, and collaboration opportunities. The program aims to support individuals from diverse backgrounds producing news content on various platforms and who demonstrate a commitment to public service and pushing the boundaries of news. Applications for the inaugural cohort, starting in September 2026, are open now.

records.title: Public journalism redux: Post-academia, Jay Rosen returns to where he started
records.author: Dan Kennedy
records.summary: Dan Kennedy profiles Rosen's post-retirement career move as president of News Creator Corps, a new organization that works with content creators to adopt journalism tools without giving up their independence. Kennedy traces Rosen's career from public journalism and Assignment Zero through his media criticism, noting this new role represents a return to Rosen's original mission of involving the public more directly in journalism.
records.quote: Are there partnerships to be had between newsrooms and creators? Yes, there are partnerships to be had. Can the creator class replace the profession? I say no, it cannot, and should not. But there's an ideal mix between the two that has yet to be found.

records.title: News Consumers are Content Creators in an AI-Driven World
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: The lines between news consumers and content creators are fading because of artificial intelligence. This shift began with the rise of the internet, social media, and smartphones, leading to participatory journalism and citizen reporting. AI tools now amplify this trend, providing automated content generation, media editing, and personalized curation, along with potential for fact-checking. Consumers are also curators and gatekeepers, influencing the visibility of information through their interactions. This new reality brings responsibilities, including combating misinformation, understanding AI's role, and promoting media literacy. The future of news involves active consumer participation, offering opportunities for a diverse information landscape alongside challenges in maintaining accuracy.
records.quote: Journalism — the practice of it — belongs not only to the people who call themselves journalists, but to everyone who does civic work with its tools.

records.title: Q&A with Jay Rosen: How Trump nullifies reality
records.author: Mark Jacob
records.summary: Mark Jacob interviews the recently-retired Rosen about his concept of 'verification in reverse' -- taking established facts and introducing doubt to power political movements. records.quote: If verification is nailing down truth claims with facts, data, documents, video, and testimony, verification in reverse means taking facts that have been nailed down and introducing doubt about them.

records.title: Denialism as an Area of Study
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A 4-post Bluesky thread by Jay Rosen. Thread depth: 3 levels.
records.quote: If I were entering political science today, I would make denialism my area of study.

posts.content: If I were entering political science today, I would make denialism my area of study.

In grad school I took a class about memory. On the first day the professor taught us that memory is associative. This made sense to me. Then week after weak we read articles about experiments in memory that used random digits and nonsense syllables. This did not make sense to me. And so... 1/3

One day I raised my hand. "I don't get it," I said. "The first thing you taught us was that memory is associative. But every week we read these studies that make it impossible to associate because they're based on experiments using random digits and nonsense syllables..."  2/3

"It seems like a mismatch," i said. "The research we're studying tries to eliminate the big thing we really know about memory."

My professor paused for moment. 

"Yes," he said. "That's a problem in the field." 

Then he moved on to another subject. This experience had a huge effect on me.  

3/3

records.title: Reflections on 39 Years at NYU: A Retirement Thread
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A 33-post Bluesky thread by Jay Rosen. Thread depth: 32 levels.
records.quote: After 39 years at NYU, Jay Rosen reflects on a career spent arguing that journalism could be different — more democratic, more honest about its assumptions, and more accountable to the people it claims to serve.

posts.content:
As we say on the internet, "some personal news."

After 39 years on the job I am retiring as an NYU professor.

In this thread I will take a few moments to reflect on my academic career.

Spoiler alert: I am not leaving the field, or the fight for a public service press. 1/

If you don't like threads, here is the essay version at my site, PressThink. 2/ 

pressthink.org

NYU has been my home for most of my academic life, starting in 1980, when I moved to New York to enroll as a grad student in NYU’s Media Ecology program, so I could study with the great media critic, Neil Postman.

Just being around him was an education. archive.pressthink.org/2003/10/07/p... 3/

Postman was then writing his best book, "Amusing Ourselves to Death," which argues that everything is becoming entertainment— schooling, parenting, politics, journalism.

"Orwell feared that the truth would be concealed from us. Huxley feared the truth would be drowned in a sea of irrelevance." 4/

My dissertation was the history of an idea — the idea of a public informed by the press. Where does that notion originate? How viable is it, really? What will it take to make it come true?

A key character in my thesis was Walter Lippmann and his brilliant book, "Public Opinion." (1922)

In May of 1986, I received my doctorate, turned 30, and got my job as a junior professor in NYU’s journalism program, which was part of the arts and sciences, not a separate school with its own dean and budget. 6/

"Part of the arts and sciences..." That may seem like a small detail. It was not. It meant that historians, scientists, mathematicians and literature professors might be on the committee that passed judgment on your tenure case— not just journalists and media types. 7/

The faculty position I was hired into was designed for a researcher in the field of “mass communication,” a social scientist who might publish their findings about media effects in a scholarly journal meant for other scholars.

 That was not what I had in mind. 8/

I was moved by a single sentence from sociologist Raymond Williams. “There are in fact no masses; there are only ways of seeing people as masses.” (!958)

I agreed, and wanted to extend what Williams was saying there. Masses were fine for The Media. Journalists had to speak to a public. 9/

Just as there were no masses, only ways of seeing people as masses, there is no public until we start treating people as a public. And if we fail to do that, support for public service journalism is likely to fade over time. 10/
Treating people as a public — and what does that require? — became the foundation for all of my press criticism, and my classroom teaching. 11/

I feel extremely fortunate to have received tenure from NYU in 1993. I submitted a mix of 40 or so articles and book reviews that went in different directions, from op ed to scholarly quarterly. In the more demanding environment that young academics face today, I'm not sure I would have made it. 12/

In 1989 I gave my first talk to a conference of journalists: the Associated Press Managing Editors. It had one idea. If people don’t participate in civic life, that’s bad for democracy— and bad for journalism. 13/

Ten years later I published my book on this idea: What Are Journalists For? (1999, Yale University Press) It argued for a less distant, less detached press, and told the story of the civic journalism movement, a pre-internet attempt to warn journalists that they were dangerously disconnected. 14/

You can imagine the responses it got from conservatives in the profession (conservative about journalism, I mean.) I put all their criticisms into the book, in the belief that you can learn a lot about journalists from the way they explain and defend their work— or decline to do so. 15/

Which is an idea I put into practice four years later when I started my blog, PressThink. (As in group think, but for journalists.)  Here I took advantage of the way the internet had eroded the gatekeepers' hold on public debate. 16/

Some journalists may remember Jim Romenesko’s MediaNews. It was a daily blog about the industry, widely read by people in the newsroom from summer intern to executive producer. I was able to reach them with my rethink just by convincing Romenesko to link to me. Which he did. Consistently. 17/

That was the great thing about blogging: it leveled the playing field, not entirely, but a lot. Which was super important to me because I was criticizing the practices of the press without any deep experience in journalism.

(I had a bit. Read about that here. 18/ pressthink.org/2010/09/why-...

At Jim Romenesko’s news-about-the-news site, PressThink was put on the same plane as newspapers and networks. This became the foundation of my online audience. That audience grew much larger with the arrival of Twitter, which I joined in 2008 after much badgering from my colleague Jeff Jarvis. 19/

In 2008 I took that a step further, teaming up with Arianna Huffington as co-publisher to launch "Off the Bus," an adventure in what we called "pro-am journalism." 20/

www.cjr.org/feature/get_...

Off the Bus had a simple design. Any reader of the Huffington Post — then at its height — should be able participate in the site's election coverage. Got it? 

Go. 

21/

As Amanda Michel, the project's director put it, "we instructed our citizen journalists to steer clear of the horse race and the top-down coverage that dominates the mainstream press." 

Again, this was 2008.  22/

Blogging went into decline because Twitter was faster and more convenient, so I had to learn the art of the thread, as we have here, and of another practice: repeating my key ideas and invented terms of art until they clicked with readers and writers— and became part of the discourse. 23/

“The view from nowhere” and my focus on the “savvy style” in political journalism both spread in this fashion, as did this mantra during the 2024 campaign: “Not the odds, but the stakes.” 24/

www.cnn.com/2023/11/15/m...

In 2009 I started a graduate program at NYU called Studio 20, a reference to our offices at 20 Cooper Square in Manhattan. Its focus was on “digital first” journalism and other forms of innovation in the newsroom. 25/

The idea was to leverage my online audience and persuade editors and producers to give Studio 20 temporary custody of right-sized, real world problems in digital adaptation, which we would then tackle as a team. 26/

In this approach, students learn by puzzling out a problem that’s 100% real. Editors win by tasking sharp grad students, and getting creative solutions back. Instructors in the program had to figure out what to teach that would be of use to problem-solving and forward-looking students. 27/

Derick Dirmaier, head of product at Talking Points Memo, and Elizabeth Spiers, cofounder of Gawker and formerly the editor in chief of The New York Observer, perfected their Studio 20 courses that way. 28/

The Economist, The Guardian, the Boston Globe, ProPublica, Wall Street Journal, The City: NYC, and the New York Times (when it was thinking local...) These were some of the newsrooms that lent us their "good problems." 29/

Here is an early — and fun — product made by Studio 20.). It's a news song. www.youtube.com/watch?v=timf...

30/

So I leave NYU after 45 years. Six as a grad student, 39 as a member of the Journalism faculty, including five as chair. 

But I won’t be exiting from journalism... 31/

I am shifting to consulting work (I have a couple of clients) and I am open to other opportunities as they may come along: from board membership to speaker at your retreat. 

You can reach me here: rosen.jay at gmail dot com 32/
Farewell, my dear syllabus. [From one of my recent classes.]

posts.content: This is a sentiment common among the people who follow me here at bsky. My view: I do not agree we are "better off" with a dying Washington Post. We are worse off. Like many of you — and many Post subscribers — I was livid at Jeff Bezos for his disastrous sell outs. But we need a strong Post. 1/3

Bezos has lost his way. Current leadership does not inspire confidence, starting with publisher and CEO Will Lewis. The talent drain is making a fair statement. But there are many highly skilled and totally devoted professionals still there. They believe strongly in accountability journalism... 2/3

To lose the Post — and its legacy —  would be terrible for us, just as the loss of an independent Justice Department is terrible for our democracy. It's hard to create these institutions, harder to keep them. They need to be criticized. To cheer for their demise is unwise. 

I still subscribe. 3/3

"When in doubt, draw a distinction." 🧵

In grad school one of my professors told me that. Some of the best advice I have ever received.

This is a thread about the key distinctions I use in my work.

I had a version of it posted at the other joint, which I revised a bit to make this one.

Ready? 1/

posts.content:
"When in doubt, draw a distinction." 🧵

In grad school one of my professors told me that. Some of the best advice I have ever received.

This is a thread about the key distinctions I use in my work.

I had a version of it posted at the other joint, which I revised a bit to make this one.

Ready? 1/

For distinctions to do their work, the terms have to be sufficiently close that prying them apart clears space for thought.

If I write, "bending is not the same as breaking," well, who said it was? 

That one is going nowhere. But "naked is not the same as nude..." is an idea with legs.  😎 2/

These notes about some of the distinctions I draw in order to do my work were written under the influence of two masters of the form: the French critic Roland Barthes, and the political philosopher Hannah Arendt, known for her striking distinctions— such as labor vs. work. (Google it maybe.) 3/

For those who don't know me, I'm a journalism professor and press critic who writes about the media and politics, and journalism's struggle for survival in a digital world. 

I have a PhD in media studies, and 35 years experience in puzzling through problems in press behavor. 4/

Here we go with some key distinctions I use to do my work. 

First: An audience is not a public.

"Audience" is people attending to a common object, typically a performance or spectacle.

A public (to me) is people with a variety of interests who dwell in the same space and share common problems. 5/

Audience vs. public, continued.

When people share common problems but don't realize it, they are an "inchoate" public. (John Dewey.)

One reason the presidential debates are (or used to be) such a big deal is that they are one of the few occasions when the audience is the public and vice versa. 6/

Key distinction number two: journalism vs. the media (vs. the press...)

I think of the media as the attention business, an industry whose product is audiences.

Journalism is a social practice, the purpose of which is to keep publics informed and hold power to account.

However— 7/

Most (but not all) journalists are employees of the media, and thus part of the attention business. This creates endless problems and compromises, which I hear about nonstop.

The press — to my way of thinking — is the institution that endures over time as journalists come in and out of it. 8/

Media, journalism, and the press are not interchangeable terms. Yet they are bound up with one another.

Media is the attention industry
Journalism is a social practice
The press is a key institution in a democracy

Journalists who work in the media carry forward "the press." 9/

My third key distinction: truth-seeking vs. refuge-seeking behavior in journalism.

Truth-seeking needs no definition. It is finding out what actually happened— and letting us know.

Refuge-seeking is telling the story in a way that protects against anticipated attacks... 

10/

My favorite description of refuge-seeking behavior in journalism comes from a former reporter for the Washington Post, Paul Taylor, in his 1990 book about election coverage. I have quoted it many times. 11/

Truth-seeking is what journalists see themselves as always doing. "The best available version of the truth."

Refuge-seeking includes such common practices as false balance, "both sides do it," steering the story "down the middle," and the depiction of "dueling realities" in a divided nation. 12/

What is "political" need not be politicized. This is a point I make again and again in my press criticism. 

When TV journalists with Sunday morning shows push back against major party candiates who are floating poisonous charges without evidence, that is a political act. 13/

But — and here comes my distinction — if journalists let an ideology distort their reporting so as not to injure a cause they manifestly believe in, then their work has been unduly politicized.

Journalism is political. It can also be politicized. That's different. 14/ pressthink.org/2020/05/you-...

The great sociologist C. Wright Mills would distinguish between "troubles" and "issues."

My paraphrase: Troubles are the things people are actively worried about in their lives. 

Mills: “An issue is a public matter: some value cherished by publics is felt to be threatened.” 15/

Troubles are a category of experience. Issues emerge from the political system.

Why does this matter? Well, when people's troubles don't connect to what are called the issues, or when issues don't speak to real life troubles, democracy — and journalism — are working poorly indeed. 16/

If issues as framed don't bear on common troubles, then focusing on "the issues" — as against the horse race — may not be the answer it seems to be.

Also: Great journalism puts a spotlight on troubles and turns them into issues, which is exactly what the movie, "Spotlight" is about. 17/

In grad school I learned to distinguish between "ritual" and "transmission" views of human communication, a distinction introduced by James W. Carey. 

"Transmission" means the movement of messages across space. 

In rituals we produce a shared world and affirm common values. 18/

When your cable news anchor says of an upcoming press conference, "we'll bring it to you live," that's clearly transmission.

Ritual: When we gather at a memorial service to mourn the dead and co-produce loving memories. 19/

What can a media critic do with it? 

When what you're watching on CNN seems to have no value as information — and from it you are learning nothing — you can try to switch frames to see if the news makes better sense as ritual: in production of a shared world. (Which is not always a good thing.) 20/

"I expect what I may not predict."

Twelve years ago, I wrote that my work as a press critic is "primarily about about the legitimation of the modern press: the various justifications for it, and how they match up with actual practice— or don’t." 21/

During Trump's second impeachment I wrote:

I try to distinguish between what I expect (setting a bar) and what I predict (estimating a likelihood.)

Thus, I expect Republican Senators to convict. But I do not predict it will happen.

Expect implies accountability. Predict trades in probability. 22/

Follow me on this one: Subscription and membership are not the same thing.

Subscribers buy a product. Members join a cause.

The distinction matters because around the world readers are being asked to pay more of the costs for quality journalism. 23/ pressthink.org/2020/09/note...

When you cannot receive the product unless you pay your share of the costs, that’s subscription.

Membership does not imply a paywall. People who have joined the cause — and donate to it — often want the journalism to be available to those who are not members. Which is how public radio operates. 24/

To wrap up, some key distinctions I use to do my work:

Public vs. audience
Journalism vs. the media
Truth-seeking vs. refuge-seeking
Political vs. politicized
Issues vs. troubles
Ritual vs. transmission
Expect vs. predict
Subscription vs. membership

"When in doubt, draw a distinction." 25/

A reader reminds me that "when in doubt, draw a distinction" is sometimes written as, "when you come to a contradiction make a distinction."

Meaning, a good distinction can get you out of a jam in your logic.

records.title: Jay Rosen and Taylor Owen: Can journalism survive Trump? Can democracy?
records.author: Jay Rosen and Taylor Owen
records.summary: This podcast discussion between Jay Rosen and Taylor Owen explores the decline of trust in journalism and the challenges facing the profession in the face of political polarization and the rise of misinformation.  They discuss the shift from traditional journalism's 'view from nowhere' to a more subjective approach, the impact of 'savvy journalism' focusing on political gamesmanship, and the phenomenon of 'verification in reverse' used by figures like Donald Trump to undermine established facts.  The conversation highlights the need for a new approach to journalism that prioritizes transparency, accountability, and a commitment to democracy while acknowledging the inherent limitations and evolving nature of the media landscape.
records.quote: Journalism is a social practice – reporting the news – and Jay believes it will never die, because it’s necessary to modern civilization.

records.title: Thinking about the people formerly known as the audience
records.author: Dick Tofel
records.summary: The concept of the audience has evolved due to the internet, transforming passive recipients of news into active participants. The author reflects on this shift, highlighting how individuals now contribute to the conversation through comments, social media, and sharing information. While acknowledging the challenges of managing online engagement, such as dealing with negativity and misinformation, the core idea remains: the traditional passive audience is obsolete. News organizations and journalists must adapt by engaging with and involving individuals in the ongoing journalistic process, recognizing them as potential interlocutors.
records.quote: The question is, how do we get the story, and the facts, and the truth not just reported, but believed?
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Inclusive journalism and the 2024 US elections: Tracking the coverage
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This essay, published in TIME shortly before the 2024 election, urges political reporters to shift their focus from speculative worst-case scenarios and the “horse race” aspects of campaign coverage to a focus on the factual consequences of candidates' actions and policies.  Rosen argues that excessive attention to threats and promises, rather than verifiable facts and their impact, fuels cynicism, breeds anticipatory obedience, and ultimately aids those in power.  Rosen advocates for a reporting approach that prioritizes verifiable effects of policies over speculation and premonition, urging journalists to hold power accountable for what is actually done rather than what is said.
records.quote: It’s hard to argue with Rosen, especially in an election year when the stakes seem so high vis a vis fundamental issues such as democracy and civil rights in the US, the role of the US in the world, wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, climate change, immigration, and more.

posts.content:
In a sense, says Michael J. Socolow, "journalism didn’t fail us — we failed journalism." www.niemanlab.org/2024/11/what... 

One thing I am going to do in the months ahead is wrestle with that problem: what should journalists do when the facts don't matter?

I failed to include this. Socolow is @michaelsocolow.bsky.social 

The problem he's onto here is a lot harder than it may appear. He's not dispensing with journalism's many fall downs. He's pointing to all the times when journalists do their jobs well and yet... the facts don't matter. What then?
When journalists find the facts, tell them well, and still: the facts don't matter... that's part of an even larger problem that for now exceeds my horizon. As I put it on November 5:

records.title: A Second Academic Exodus From X?
records.author: Josh Moody
records.summary: Josh Moody reports on a second wave of academics leaving X/Twitter after the 2024 presidential election. High-profile professors cite platform toxicity, disinformation, and Elon Musk's open support for Donald Trump as reasons for departing. Some see this as the end of Academic Twitter, while others debate whether ceding the platform serves anyone's interests.
records.quote: Twitter has become a plaything of a plutocrat man-child who relishes in trolling the vulnerable and spreading disinformation.

records.title: 36 thoughts on the 2024 campaign
records.author: Brian Beutler; Jay Rosen
records.summary: Brian Beutler's election-day assessment of the 2024 presidential campaign, published as a numbered list of reflections. References Jay Rosen's 'not the odds but the stakes' framework as a test for the national press corps. Discusses press coverage failures, the fascism discourse, and what a Harris win or Trump win would mean for democracy. Partially paywalled.
records.quote: When the critic Jay Rosen coined the phrase 'not the odds, but the stakes' early this cycle, he meant it as a test for the national press corps, working on behalf of the electorate, not a call for activists or voters to take the election seriously.

records.title: A media critic urged 'not the odds, but the stakes.' Did it work?
records.author: Margaret Sullivan
records.summary: Margaret Sullivan interviews Jay Rosen on the eve of the 2024 election about whether his influential phrase 'not the odds, but the stakes' changed campaign coverage. Rosen says it may have reminded journalists of what they already know but didn't fundamentally change the dynamic of horse-race coverage, which remains 'too easy, too available.' Sullivan argues Rosen's influence was greater than he admits, noting that many outlets organized coverage under 'stakes' framing.
records.quote: But the horse race is too easy, too available -- it has all these advantages.

The author contends that building trust requires sharing perspectives and biases upfront, rather than pretending to be neutral.

records.title: Reporters speak at Deerfield Academy on the landscape of political journalism
records.author: Chris Larabee
records.summary: A panel featuring Wall Street Journal's Annie Linskey, Politico's Meridith McGraw, and NYU professor Jay Rosen discussed the role of the press in shaping American elections at Deerfield Academy. The conversation covered journalistic bias, the pursuit of truth amidst misinformation, and the evolving dynamics of information flow. Panelists addressed concerns about echo chambers and the increasing tendency of audiences to seek information that confirms pre-existing beliefs, as well as the impact of AI and deepfakes on political journalism.
records.quote: "I think that is one of the biggest changes that I’ve seen in my 20 years in journalism, is this idea that readers and people who consume the news are becoming more and more interested in learning facts and narratives that support something they already believe and they’re becoming increasingly resistant to stories that challenge their existing beliefs," Linskey said.

records.title: Smartoctober: Constructive campaign coverage
records.author: Em Kuntze; Stefan ten Teije
records.summary: Em Kuntze and Stefan ten Teije connect Rosen’s “not the odds, but the stakes” frame to constructive campaign coverage. The article argues that horse-race polling should give way to coverage that asks what communities need, what politicians would do, and how newsrooms can measure constructive impact.
records.quote: So when Jay Rosen is asked how elections should be covered, his consistent response is that the focus should be on “not the odds, but the stakes.”

posts.content:
CNN’s Abby Phillip last night: “[W]hen there is asymmetrical lying, there will be asymmetrical fact checking.”

Yes, it's aspiration only, but it's also the right principle. Now the practices have to catch up. (Short thread.)

Hmmmm.

The New York Times media reporter says there was a shift "for an evening, at least — in the balance of power between Mr. Trump and the many journalists who have struggled, or stopped trying, to construct factual guardrails around [his] baseless claims." www.nytimes.com/2024/09/11/b... 2/

More on the (slight) advance in fact checking that multiple journalists are observing upon this morning. 

I know you will be skeptical, or even derisive. But I'm bringing it to you anyway because there is a shift in expectations.

From CJR's Jon Allsop cjr.org/the_media_to... 3/

Here it is again, from Oliver Darcy's newsletter.

The big baby step in fact checking the debates.

Note this part: "ABC News' repeated fact-checking of Trump stood in contrast to the approach CNN took when it moderated the debate with President Joe Biden in late June." 4/

You don't have to commit to fact-checking everything. It's bad form to say you will fact check nothing. You can predict and prepare for most of his lies.

That's the logic of the step that was taken in fact checking debates.

Preceded by this statement from ABC. www.nytimes.com/2024/09/08/b... 5/
Correct: 6/

posts.content:
Some good news. A consortium of Colorado newsrooms — many of which compete with each other — are teaming up to switch their election coverage over to the "citizens agenda" model, according to Colorado Public Radio. www.cpr.org/2024/04/02/v...

I will share more about this when I get more details.

Wondering what the "citizens agenda" model is? Here's my post about key steps and its life and times. pressthink.org/2018/11/elec...

Here's an announcement from Vermont public radio and TV. It says they will be using a citizens agenda approach as well. www.vermontpublic.org/local-news/2...

Poster:

Lots more details coming in now. The collaboration announced today in Colorado is without precedent in the history of the citizens agenda approach to campaign coverage, which goes back to 1990-92.

Read this thread from the organizer, The Colorado News Collaborative. twitter.com/colabnewsco/...

I have shared the shocking (in a good way) announcement that 30+ Colorado newsrooms will colaborate in their election coverage by adopting a "citizens agenda" approach, rather than the horse race.

Here's one of them, Colorado Newsline, telling readers about it. coloradonewsline.com/2024/04/04/c...

records.title: The political economy of normalization
records.author: Brian Beutler; Jay Rosen
records.summary: An analysis of how mainstream institutions (news outlets, think tanks, universities) rehabilitate enemies of democracy through the revolving door, using the Ronna Romney McDaniel/NBC News hiring as the central case. Argues that 'normal' has multiple meanings and that the solution is to 'abnormalize' MAGA rather than asking institutions not to normalize it. References Jay Rosen's analysis of what service McDaniel could provide NBC regarding Trump's threats.
records.quote: As Jay Rosen has suggested, one service Romney McDaniel may actually have been able to provide was to offer executives, 'guidance on how seriously they should take his threats to NBC.'

records.title: Jay Rosen in Oz: On Horserace Journalism and the 2024 Election
records.author: Joel Mears
records.summary: So-called “horse-race” reporting—sound bite-driven, he-said-she-said, stat-obsessed, poll-heavy, strategy-focused—is a major draw whichever end of the equator you’re on. Rosen, scathing as ever about the state of modern electoral coverage, has been on TV, behind podiums, and in meeting rooms discussing “horse-race journalism,” which he defined in an interview on the Australian Broadcasting Corporation’s (ABC) Lateline as “a reusable model for how to do campaign coverage in which you focus on who’s going to win rather than what the country needs to settle by electing a prime minister.” “But the biggest advantage of horse-race journalism is that it permits reporters and pundits to ‘play up their detachment,’” Rosen has written.
records.quote: Media focus on polls and predictions undermines democratic discourse.

records.title: NBC's "Pivot" Headline and Horse Race Journalism
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A 10-post Bluesky thread by Jay Rosen. Thread depth: 9 levels.
records.quote:
This was the headline at NBC News: 

"Fewer grievances, more policy: Trump aides and allies push for a post-South Carolina 'pivot.'"

By Matt Dixon, Kristen Welker, Jonathan Allen, Vaughn Hillyard, Garrett Haake and Carol E. Lee.

www.nbcnews.com/politics/don...

I have comments. 

[Thread: 1 of 10]

posts.content:
This was the headline at NBC News: 

"Fewer grievances, more policy: Trump aides and allies push for a post-South Carolina 'pivot.'"

By Matt Dixon, Kristen Welker, Jonathan Allen, Vaughn Hillyard, Garrett Haake and Carol E. Lee.

www.nbcnews.com/politics/don...

I have comments. 

[Thread: 1 of 10]

As your public editor for today, I have a few questions.

You're all experienced professionals so I assume you have good reasons for every call that was made here. I just want know what those reasons are. 

Ready?

2/

* Why did it take six people to make this? 

* Trump’s staff want him to pivot to the general election and rely less on personal grievances. Is there any reason to think that he is capable of — or perhaps newly interested in — a reduction in personal invective? Has he changed?

3/

* If our answer is YES, Trump has changed and he no longer thinks that grievance politics can get him there, then where in our report do we show that? 

* If our answer is NO, he's the same guy, then why are six NBC journalists helping to broadcast the pained wishes of his staff and supporters? 

4/

* Advisers will often try to send a message to the candidate through the media, but is that something we should be involved in? 

* And even if this is a good use of our platform, why do we grant them anonymity— as if they have some huge scoop for us, and face danger if found out? 

5/

* Why is “more policy” the big headline here when by my count that word — policy — comes up exactly once in the reported piece, and it’s a voter talking. 

* Again I ask: any evidence that Trump is interested in — and capable of — a shift to “policy” as the centerpiece of his campaign? 

6/

* In the modern era, or in the memory of anyone at NBC News, has there ever been a president less likely — and less qualified — to make the pivot to “more policy” of which our own headline confidently speaks? 

This bothers me, as your public editor.

* Did anyone wonder, as I have wondered, whether the depiction of “policy” — as possibly the next phase of the Trump campaign was more a wish of our own: to be perceived as serious people engaged in something more edifying than listless horse race coverage and vapid “strategy” talk? 

8/

* One more thing on "policy” as what Trump advisers say they want to feature going forward. Are we really talking to readers, viewers, and voters with that claim? Or are we competing with our peers in journalism upon the dubious and mucked up terrain of the micro-scoop? 

9/

* Treating "fewer grievances, more policy" as a plausible next step for the campaign of Donald Trump is more than a stretch. It conflicts with everything we know about the guy.

10/

records.title: Explaining the News Industry Downturn
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A 14-post Bluesky thread by Jay Rosen. Thread depth: 13 levels.
records.quote:
Last week CNN asked me how I explain the downturn in the news industry: big layoffs, scant investment, no recovery in sight. 

A list of factors is not an explanation, I said. But that is what I have. 

So here's my thread. None of it should be news to people in the business. 0/

posts.content:
Last week CNN asked me how I explain the downturn in the news industry: big layoffs, scant investment, no recovery in sight. 

A list of factors is not an explanation, I said. But that is what I have. 

So here's my thread. None of it should be news to people in the business. 0/

Factors converging on the news industry to hollow it out, weaken the product, scare investors, and threaten jobs: 

1/ With a few exceptions, the search for a stable business model has been unsuccessful, in part because the problem changes faster than R & D in the news business.

2/ The rich guy rescue plan rarely works. The rescuer typically underestimates how hard it is to find money in news and keep quality reasonably high. When that is made clear, rich guy's commitment starts faltering. And the hedge funds lie in wait. See San-Diego Union Tribune.
3/ The ad industry doesn't need the news industry when there are so many other ways to purchase attention, and so many better ways to target users.

4/ The internet is rewiring not only the media sector (as with streaming) but the public itself, which is breaking up, or being broken, into multiple — some say parallel — realities.

As you can tell from my halting attempt to describe it, we do not have a good language for this shift.

5/ The news industry is still struggling to re-establish a direct connection with readers (through newsletters and podcasts, for example...) after social media captured a lot of that territory for itself.
6/ After a period in the 2010s when it appeared that they did, the big tech platforms today clearly don't care much about news delivery or quality, and yet they have greatly disrupted these things.

7/ Local news is the hardest hit, and local is where people form an initial relationship with journalists and journalism— or don't. TV viewers still develop bonds with local anchors. But TV newsrooms lean heavily on the local newspaper's reporting, and that is where the crisis is.
8/ Journalists have to take it upon themselves to treat sustainability as their problem, but this is not what they signed up for. They signed up to do great stories.
9/ Philanthropy has taken its time to grasp what is happening, and government funding is (in my view) as much a threat as it is a solution.

10/ To say that trust in the news media has declined is correct, but too vague. The reality is that destroying confidence in the practice and products of journalism is a potent and successful political strategy, as with Steve Bannon's "flood the zone."

Final note: Decades ago, the leadership class in American journalism accepted the argument that real pluralism had to come to their newsrooms, or the journalism would suffer. Or at least, this is what they said to themselves... 11/

But the bosses also said this: We can have a diverse and multi-colored newsroom, and maintain the view from nowhere. 

See the contradiction? Under-represented journalists are to simultaneously supply a missing perspective and suppress it— in order to prove their objectivity. 12/

I mention this for a simple reason: Some of the wounds are self-inflicted.

records.quote:
CNN's Kaitlan Collins broke into Trump's post-appeals court press conference for what she called "fact checks and reality statements."

That phrase, "reality statements," which barely qualifies as Eng

posts.content:
CNN's Kaitlan Collins broke into Trump's post-appeals court press conference for what she called "fact checks and reality statements."

That phrase, "reality statements," which barely qualifies as English, shows how the limits of language get exposed when propaganda reaches its saturation point. 1/

Now some of you are likely thinking, "Lying is lying. Just say he lies. Problem solved!"

But a wholly propagandistic campaign cuts deeper than that. Things can happen to truth that are worse than lying. For example, losing all sense of the distinction between false and true. Flooding the zone. 2/

So I'm not here to ridicule Kaitlan's awkward phrase: "reality statements." To me it's a sign of how far we've already traveled into truthlessness— because of him. 

It's beyond lying now. The sights are set on human communication itself. That's what she was breaking in for. 3/

records.summary: A year-end compilation episode where On The Media revisits 2023 political coverage to extract lessons for the 2024 election year. The episode includes excerpts from multiple guests, with Rosen's contribution drawn from the CNN impossible dilemma segment. It covers the threat to democracy, media accountability, and how journalism must adapt for an election cycle featuring Trump as a candidate.
records.quote: When covering an election featuring Trump, journalism faces an impossible dilemma: treating the threat to democracy as a normal campaign issue normalizes the abnormal, yet framing it otherwise risks appearing partisan.

records.title: On the Washington Post's Jim Jordan Profile
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A 7-post Bluesky thread by Jay Rosen. Thread depth: 6 levels.
records.quote:
I read every word of this long (VERY long) profile of Jim Jordan by the Washington Post. "Relentless Wrestler" is the title. [gift link] 

As the pages wore on, their central conceit began to seem thinner and thinner, which is what led to this short thread. 1/

posts.content:
I read every word of this long (VERY long) profile of Jim Jordan by the Washington Post. "Relentless Wrestler" is the title. [gift link] 

As the pages wore on, their central conceit began to seem thinner and thinner, which is what led to this short thread. 1/

By conceit I mean a device for organizing the profile that lifts it beyond a series of anecdotes, and "to be sure" paragraphs.

Here the device is unmistakable: Jordan today is the same guy he was as a championship wrestler: relentless, disciplined, "old school"— and a winner. 2/

There's a LOT about the sport of wrestling in the article, which probably made sense to the authors on two levels: wrestling shaped Jim Jordan into the "fighter" he is today, and it's where the skeletons in his closet are— meaning his nearness to a sexual abuse scandal at Ohio State. 3/

Told through the wrestling lens, the Jim Jordan story provides instant balance: there are reasons to admire his almost fanatic commitment to wrestling, and reasons to doubt his word about the sexual abuse. 

This must have appealed to the Post when it looked like he would become the next Speaker. 4/

But the more I thought about it, the less adequate the sports lens felt. 

Wrestling is sublimated violence. What makes it acceptable and athletic — rather than barbaric and dangerous — are the tight rules that govern behavior on the mat, plus the extremely close eye of the referee. 5/

And what is Jim Jordan (the "firebrand," as journalists call him) known for in his political career?

Is it sticking to the rules of the game? Honor in ritualized combat? Respect for the keepers of order? Champion law giver? 

Admired for his excellence, or despised for his ruthlessness? 6/

The more you interrogate it, the less apt "relentless wrestler" becomes. Jordan is no college champion extending his quest for excellence and talent for discipline to the next level of achievement. 

He's a student of what he can get away with, betting that there are no refs. 7/

records.title: "Not the Odds, But the Stakes": Election Coverage in 2024
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A 9-post Bluesky thread by Jay Rosen. Thread depth: 8 levels.
records.quote:
"Not the odds, but the stakes." 

That's been my shorthand for the principle that could most improve election coverage in 2024. Not "who's going to win?" but the consequences for our democracy. Not the odds but the stakes. 

Today something happened with this idea. THREAD. 1/

posts.content:
"Not the odds, but the stakes." 

That's been my shorthand for the principle that could most improve election coverage in 2024. Not "who's going to win?" but the consequences for our democracy. Not the odds but the stakes. 

Today something happened with this idea. THREAD. 1/

"We’re demoting the horse race and elevating constituent interests." 

That's the headline on today's announcement from the editor of Colorado Newsline, Quentin Young. 

coloradonewsline.com/2023/10/12/w...

His newsroom is officially putting "not the odds, but the stakes" into practice. 2/

"High-value election coverage revolves around families, individuals and every affected resident," Quentin Young writes.

"Low-value election coverage clings to the question of who’s going to win." 

And just like that, the horse race is not abandoned, but demoted— as it should be. 3/

"Horse race coverage prioritizes those in power, not the people the powerful are supposed to serve. " 

In explaining why today he demoted the horse race model, Colorado Newsline editor Quentin Young acknowledged that his newsroom had participated like any other in that ritual. 4/

Colorado Newsline is a nonprofit, nonpartisan, and independent newsroom of modest size, focused on politics and policy in the state Capital.

It is part of a larger nonprofit, States Newsroom, statesnewsroom.com which arose to fill the gap left by shrinking local newspapers. 5/

Why am I going on about this announcement in Denver today?

Because it's something any newsroom can do tomorrow, from NBC News to The Current in Lafayette, Louisiana:

Demote the horse race, and use the savings to put voters and communities at the center of your coverage. 6/

Here's one suggestion for what can replace the race once you demote it. For years I have been writing about the citizens agenda model. It puts a key question at the center: "what do you want the candidates to be talking about as they compete for votes?" pressthink.org/2019/06/key-... 7/

A small but important step in American journalism was taken today in Denver. An editor promised readers that treating elections as sport had met its demise.

coloradonewsline.com/2023/10/12/w... 

Colorado Newsline will, I predict, still be standing tomorrow. Which newsroom will be next? 8/

If you're a news executive in charge of election coverage at your shop, and you think you might want to take the plunge that Colorado Newsline took, feel free to shoot me an email. Address is on my Twitter profile and my NYU bio. 

Suggested subject line: demoting the horse race. Funders welcome.

records.title: Media Critics Agree: Stop Interviewing the Bad People!
records.author: Matt Welch
records.summary: The article discusses the debate within the media regarding whether to interview Donald Trump. Critics argue that interviewing him legitimizes his actions and spreads misinformation, while others contend that avoiding him deprives the public of crucial information and strengthens his position. The author ultimately argues against deplatforming Trump, emphasizing the importance of journalistic perseverance and the potential for impactful reporting even when dealing with difficult figures.
records.quote: It may seem counterintuitive that protecting democracy requires refusing to talk with a primary-frontrunning former president who more than 74 million Americans voted for in 2020.

records.summary: A 9-post Bluesky thread by Jay Rosen. Thread depth: 8 levels.
records.quote: Thread: I said I would try to keep an open mind as I watched Meet the Press last Sunday to see how NBC handled its interview with Trump and the debut of a new host. After viewing the show, reading NBC's fact check, and monitoring the program's Twitter feed, I am left with these impressions. 1/

posts.content: Thread: I said I would try to keep an open mind as I watched Meet the Press last Sunday to see how NBC handled its interview with Trump and the debut of a new host. After viewing the show, reading NBC's fact check, and monitoring the program's Twitter feed, I am left with these impressions. 1/

NBC chose a "zero innovations" model for how to conduct and present a Trump interview at this stage in his degradation. Everything was predictable, nothing was surprising, and new host Kristen Welker did nothing to justify going to the well again with another Trump Q & A. 2/

On the show, Welker raised the criticism she knew NBC would get for doing this, and asked Peter Baker to respond. He said it's unthinkable that we journalists would stop asking questions of a major party candidate, even though it's true that Trump lies a lot and and constructs his own reality. 3/

Baker said this was a "hard problem" for people in his profession, but what can we do? Which is what I mean by a "zero innovations" model, in which you simply ignore the fact that interviewing Trump with traditional tools for traditional reasons does not work. No accountability moment ever comes. 4/

Trump enjoys being the unreliable narrator of his own deeds and intentions. So if Welker gets him to say, "Yes, I will testify to that!" (as she did) the informational gain is zero even though she did her job by "pinning him down." 

The transcript is full of meaningless victories like that. 5/

These problems are old news and well known to anyone who pays attention. What I learned by bringing an open mind to Meet the Press Sunday was... nothing, really. But let me tell you why I watched the interview. 

It's not true that the news system never learns from its dealings with Trump. 6/

We have a recent counter example. After CNN's debacle in staging a "town hall" with Trump, no one else has tried to do it. The risk is too high. It's become common wisdom that you need to tape and edit him. Even Fox does it. 

Okay, it's not a momentous change, but it does show a bit of learning. 7/

I doubt we will ever know (same company) but I would love to hear what Rachel Maddow thought about NBC's interview with Trump.

She is the one who said on air: “There’s a cost to us as a news organization of knowingly broadcasting untrue things.”

NBC willingly paid that cost with this interview. 8/

In a scathing review of NBC's interview, Oliver Darcy highlights a failure that escaped broad notice in the reactions after: a failure to protect your talent and set them up to succeed. 9/ view.newsletters.cnn.com/messages/169...

records.title: Note to repliers...
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A Mastodon post by Jay Rosen from 2023-08-28.
records.quote:
Note to repliers. I"m not trying to suss out what McCarthy is up to. It's pretty obvious. 
My concern is with the journalists at CNN, and what they do in response to this kind of maneuver. 
Do they make a strategy story from it? Is that the right frame?
Or is the news the outlandish idea of impeachment in the abstract, with evidence to come later in the process? 
First the action, then the cause of action, is pretty Alice in Wonderland of them. To me that's the news.

records.title: CNN headline today:...
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A Mastodon post by Jay Rosen from 2023-08-28.
records.quote:
CNN headline today:
"McCarthy starts to plot Biden impeachment strategy while GOP skeptics remain."
What the GROUNDS for impeachment might be is addressed in paragraph nine. CNN thus buries the lede of a more striking story: a vibes-based approach, where you establish first the feeling, "we wanna impeach," relegating the small matter of "impeachment for what?" to later stages.
That's news! Instead CNN frames for us another strategy story.
https://www.cnn.com/2023/08/28/politics/mccarthy-biden-impeachment-strategy/index.html
#journalism #uspol #science

records.title: "Not the odds, but the stakes...
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A Mastodon post by Jay Rosen from 2023-07-17.
records.quote:
"Not the odds, but the stakes."
That's my shortand for the organizing principle we most need from journalists covering the 2024 election. Not who has what chances of winning, but the consequences for our democracy. Not the odds, but the stakes.

records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A Mastodon post by Jay Rosen from 2023-06-19.
records.quote:
@JaneGray 
Not totally sure what you are referencing there. 
Might have been Brandolini's law, also known as the bullshit asymmetry principle, which is an internet adage coined in 2013. It emphasizes the effort of debunking misinformation, in comparison to the relative ease of creating it in the first place. The law states the following:
"The amount of energy needed to refute bullshit is an order of magnitude bigger than that needed to produce it."
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandolini%27s_law

records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A Mastodon post by Jay Rosen from 2023-06-10.
records.quote:
As a guest for public radio's 'On the Media' this week, I tried to explain how the propaganda method known as "flooding the zone with shit" is still bedeviling Anerican newsrooms. 
I also respond to Anderson Cooper's "get out of your silo" lecture after CNN's town hall debacle with Trump. 
It's a 12 minute listen: https://www.wnycstudios.org/podcasts/otm/segments/cnn-impossible-dilemma-on-the-media
And if you do listen, let me know what you thought. Thanks.
#uspol #propaganda #journalism #science

records.title: CNN's impossible dilemma
records.author: Brooke Gladstone; Jay Rosen
records.summary: Following CNN CEO Chris Licht's firing, Rosen and Gladstone discuss the impossible dilemma CNN faces: the network's Trump town hall was a disaster that demonstrated the failure of conventional formats, yet the 'business as usual' approach Licht promised advertisers was itself the problem. Rosen argues that journalism still needs an emergency mode and that the firehose of falsehood continues to overwhelm traditional coverage methods.
records.quote: Journalism still needs an emergency mode, because the firehose of falsehood continues to overwhelm traditional coverage methods.

records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A Mastodon post by Jay Rosen from 2023-05-29.
records.quote:
It's wired in, it's blatant, and it's old news, but to me it remains pretty remarkable that the establishment press in the U.S. uses the term "conservative" to mean any action the extreme right wing favors. 
The more extreme the act, the more "conservative" are the actors!
Thus, the Freedom Caucus in the House — the members of which are the most ready to let the U.S. default on its debt — are routinely described as the most conservative faction in the government. 
#uspol #science #journalism

My shorthand for the approach we most need in election coverage is this:
"Not the odds, but the stakes."
How does this work in practice? Margaret Sullivan answers that in The Guardian today. "Now’s the time to think about just how bad a DeSantis presidency would be." 
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2023/may/25/ron-desantis-florida-record-presidential-campaign?CMP=Share_iOSApp_Other
Not how DeSantis plans to outwit Trump and then succeed in "the general" (itself an insidery phrase...) but what life would be like if he took power.
Not the odds, but the stakes.
#uspol #journalism

records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A Mastodon post by Jay Rosen from 2023-05-15.
records.quote:
I have a new approach when I am asked to go on TV, which happens once in a while. Usually it's MSNBC, sometimes CNN under the old regime. 
My new goal is to introduce a term or concept that has not been heard before on network television. 
A few weeks ago it was "verification in reverse" on Maddow. 
On May 11 (The 11th Hour) it was "not the odds, but the stakes," which I had pre-tested in Twitter and Mastodon. 
Let me know if it worked: https://www.msnbc.com/11th-hour/watch/fallout-from-trump-town-hall-174063173939

records.title: Fallout from Trump town hall: Jay Rosen on the tightrope news outlets face
records.author: Stephanie Ruhle; Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen returns to The 11th Hour to analyze the fallout from CNN's Trump town hall, which was widely criticized for giving Trump an unchallenged platform. He discusses the structural dilemma news organizations face when covering Trump: traditional formats like town halls and debates are exploited by a figure who operates outside normal political norms, yet ignoring him is not an option either.

records.title: "Not the odds, but the stakes...
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A Mastodon post by Jay Rosen from 2023-05-09.
records.quote:
"Not the odds, but the stakes." 
That's my shorthand for the organizing principle we most need in news coverage of the 2024 campaign. Not who has what chances of winning, but the consequences for American democracy. Not the odds, but the stakes.
You may find me repeating this principle.
You may also find me linking to writers who help explain it. Today it's Perry Bacon, Jr. "How the media can cover Trump better this time." 
[Gift link] http://wapo.st/3MayqOY 
#journalism #uspol #science

records.title: A fuller description of 'verification in reverse...
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A Mastodon post by Jay Rosen from 2023-04-25.
records.quote:
A fuller description of 'verification in reverse.' 
To verify is to take a truth claim and nail it down with facts, data, documents, expertise.
“Verification in reverse” is when you take what has been nailed down and publicly doubt it. This creates friction, controversy, excitement, story. You can tap that energy to power a political movement. This is how Trump’s candidacy got started. He became a birther. Then he did it again with COVID-19 and again with Stop the Steal.
 
#uspol #journalism

records.title: How 'verification in reverse' powers the conservative media bubble and right-wing politics
records.author: Rachel Maddow
records.summary: Jay Rosen discusses the concept of "verification in reverse," where established truths are questioned and denied to create energy and power for political movements, particularly within the conservative media landscape. He argues this approach, exemplified by figures like Trump and events like "Stop the Steal," fuels political asymmetry and challenges the traditional understanding of shared facts between parties. Rosen acknowledges the uncertain future of this dynamic, questioning whether it will lead to a crash or continue to shape American politics.
records.quote: That's what "Stop the Steal" was all about. It's taking something that's been established as true, denying it, and the power of that denial moves your movement closer.

records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A Mastodon post by Jay Rosen from 2023-03-23.
records.quote:
One day it may dawn on them: sounding neutral can conflict with the greater imperative of accuracy. 
The New York Times today:
"Unease about the banking system’s stability and a stalemate over raising the debt limit are engulfing the capital simultaneously, ratcheting up an already high level of financial anxiety."
Is "stalemate over raising the debt limit" an accurate description? To me it feels more neutral, but reads as less truthful than, say, "a threat to sow chaos."
#uspol #journalism

Not the odds, but the stakes.

"Can Mr. Trump show enough restraint to persuade moderate Republicans and independent swing voters to choose him over President Biden in 2024?" https://www.nytimes.com/2023/03/21/us/politics/trump-2024-campaign-indictment.html

records.title: NYU journalism professor Jay Rosen: Fox is "the commercial wing of the MAGA movement that has overtaken the Republican party" | Media Matters for America
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Jay Rosen, in an interview on MSNBC, argues that Fox News is not a news organization but rather the commercial wing of the MAGA movement, producing "resentment news." He explains that the Dominion court documents reveal how Fox News's power to manipulate its audience through resentment backfired when some Fox employees reported truthfully, causing an internal crisis. This crisis, Rosen contends, demonstrates that Fox News prioritizes its political agenda over journalistic integrity.
records.quote: If responsible journalism by a handful of Fox people resulted in a company crisis, that means the company is not a news company – because giving truthful news actually was a big problem.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

People are asking me this today. I don't think any of them are going to like the answer.

Liberal politicians think that's not a good look.

records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A Mastodon post by Jay Rosen from 2023-02-20.
records.quote:
Though it is styled as one, Fox is not a news organization. And it's not opinion, either. It is something else: Power formation by means of resentment news. 
But the formula doesn't always work. The crowd seethes back when the machine miscalculates, generating its own kind of power. 
Reactionary is the right term for it. 13/

records.title: Dominion's filings describe a time when the audience took charge of the Fox resentment machine...
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A Mastodon post by Jay Rosen from 2023-02-20.
records.quote:
Dominion's filings describe a time when the audience took charge of the Fox resentment machine. 
Power traded hands for a moment. Viewer backlash from the Fox newsroom's correct call in Arizona felt ruinous to the people at the top of the network. 
Stars with their own shows and executives nominally in charge of Fox saw how weak their positions were.
Read Brian Stelter in the Atlantic about this: https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/archive/2023/02/fox-news-dominion-voting-lawsuit-2020-election-conspiracy/673111/
10/

records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A Mastodon post by Jay Rosen from 2023-02-20.
records.quote:
By "machine" I mean to evoke both the steady manufacture of politicized grievance for fun and profit, and the kind of machine through which Richard Daley rose to power in the mid-twentieth century. A machine in the sense of the Cook County Democratic Machine.
Again: that's not a news organization. 9/

records.title: When I use the term "Fox," I mean the commercial arm of a political movement that has taken control ...
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A Mastodon post by Jay Rosen from 2023-02-20.
records.quote:
When I use the term "Fox," I mean the commercial arm of a political movement that has taken control of the Republican Party.
The product is resentment news. By which I mean: Current ways to resent. New people to resent. "Here's something they call Critical Race Theory. You should resent it."
Success in a market like that makes for political power. That's the Fox I know. A kind of machine. 8/

records.title: If Fox is not a news organization — to me it's not — and it is not "opinion," either (because the Do...
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A Mastodon post by Jay Rosen from 2023-02-20.
records.quote:
If Fox is not a news organization — to me it's not — and it is not "opinion," either (because the Dominion filing shows the hosts are frightened to share their opinions) then what is it, exactly?
Some common answers I receive: 
It's entertainment, a lot like professional wrestling.
It's propaganda; what else do you need to know?
No, Jay, it's just ratings.
7/

records.title: "Sidney Powell is lying," said Tucker Carlson to his producer...
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A Mastodon post by Jay Rosen from 2023-02-20.
records.quote:
"Sidney Powell is lying," said Tucker Carlson to his producer.
"Sidney Powell is a bit nuts," said Laura Ingraham to her colleagues. 
But they did not share this view with their audience. 
Defenders of Fox get a lot mileage out of describing its evening line-up as the "opinion side" of the operation. 
But that's not accurate either. About Sidney Powell the prime time stars withheld their opinions. Meanwhile the bookers at Fox placed her on show after show. 6/
See: https://www.npr.org/2023/02/20/1158223099/fox-news-dominion-wackadoodle-election-fraud-claim

https://twitter.com/jacquiheinrich/status/1327354119439470592?s=46&t=nr4aN_Oyhjkkw-TifvNatA 
It is a very careful, limited statement. Mild pushback. But Tucker Carlson felt panic over it, and demanded her head.

records.title: The Dominion suit establishes that Fox stars (like Tucker Carlson) and executives (like CEO Suzanne ...
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A Mastodon post by Jay Rosen from 2023-02-20.
records.quote:
The Dominion suit establishes that Fox stars (like Tucker Carlson) and executives (like CEO Suzanne Scott) were fearful and enraged when some of their own people blundered into delivering a true and accurate report about the 2020 election.
Think about that for a moment. When its own talent reported the facts truthfully, the result was an atmosphere of crisis in the company. 
This is one way we know that Fox is not specifically a news organization.
There are others... 2/

records.title: THREAD...

records.quote:
THREAD
The latest filing by Dominion Voting Systems in its defamation suit against Fox nails something critics have long argued for.
Fox is not a news organization. It's something else. 
But what is this other thing? In this thread, I will try to answer that.
Next slide, please. 1/

records.title: What we now call "normalizing" originates in a conflict within the journalist's code...
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A Mastodon post by Jay Rosen from 2023-02-05.
records.quote:
What we now call "normalizing" originates in a conflict within the journalist's code.
One part tells journalists to highlight the shocking, the unexpected, the ruptured pattern, the broken norm.
"Man bites dog" is a phrase for it.
But another part of the code says: stay current. Don't come off as naive or slow to adapt.
"The new normal" is a phrase for that.
Over time the second command tends to succeed the first. And when that happens we call it "normalization."
#journalism #uspolitics

records.title: The market has failed...
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A Mastodon post by Jay Rosen from 2023-01-25.
records.quote:
The market has failed. Philanthropy can't do it. The public good that is local news needs another support system. Now there's an alliance calling for public policy solutions. Rebuild Local News it is called. Their ideas: 
* A tax credit for consumers to subscribe to or donate to local news
* A tax credit for small businesses to advertise in local news
* A tax credit for local news organizations to hire and retain local journalists
https://www.cjr.org/opinion/how-public-policy-can-help-save-local-news.php
#journalism #localjournalism

records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A Mastodon post by Jay Rosen from 2023-01-07.
records.quote:
Did you watch the "Kevin McCarthy's tormentors" this week?
I did. During which I kept thinking of this piece published in the Washington Post in 2012 by Norm Ornstein and Tom Mann.
https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/lets-just-say-it-the-republicans-are-the-problem/2012/04/27/gIQAxCVUlT_story.html
It's difficult to describe how utterly establishment Mann and Ornstein were at the time. One was at Brookings, the other at American Enterprise Institute.
They saw what was happening: The GOP's attack on all institutions. The press didn't want to know. Now it does.
#journalism #uspolitics

records.summary: A Mastodon post by Jay Rosen from 2023-01-04.
records.quote:
Semafor said today that "a critical mass of conservatives do not trust McCarthy to lead them..."
Conservatives. Is that what they are?
John Boehner's description of the same crowd in his memoir:
"What they're really interested in is chaos... They want to throw sand in the gears of the hated federal government until it fails."
Are the sowers of chaos properly called "conservatives?"
Is MAGA conservative?
Why do #journalists with a commitment to accuracy maintain this fiction?
#uspolitics

The panel, titled "Why News Matters: Exploring Journalism Solutions," features Craig Newmark, Vivian Schiller, and Jay Rosen.  The conversation explores the challenges facing local news, the role of technology in supporting journalism, and the impact of political polarization on the media landscape.  Participants reflect on past experiences and brainstorm potential solutions for improving the state of journalism.

This one includes a fascinating fact. Walker and his wife wanted to spend "significant time in heavily Democratic areas to woo Black voters."
Staff tried to clue them in: sorry, that's not where your support is. His wife "even suggested her husband should be winning as much as 50 percent of the Black vote in Georgia!"
Delusion on this scale is almost poignant. They had no clue how he was being used.
#USpolitics

records.summary: A Mastodon post by Jay Rosen from 2022-12-03.
records.quote:
Politico put it this way: 
"The former president and the person that polls show is still the most likely GOP presidential nominee in 2024, today on Truth Social called for the suspension of the Constitution."
This poses a problem for journalists who would cover the 2024 election. By what logic can that coverage proceed?
Neutrality makes sense only within a constitutional order that his candidacy is trying to upend. "Just report the news" pretends this will be a normal campaign.
#journalism

records.summary: A Mastodon post by Jay Rosen from 2022-11-30.
records.quote:
One of the leading newsrooms in trust-through-transparency is @ProPublica
Here, they publish a review of criticisms they got after publishing a story on the lab leak hypothesis in debate over the origins of COVID-19.
https://www.propublica.org/article/editors-note-a-review-of-criticisms-of-a-propublica-vanity-fair-story-on-a-covid-origins-report 
This is quite different from the "we stand by our story" routine.
In fact, they DO stand by their story in this case, but they also take criticisms seriously and respond in detail, which is sound practice.
#journalism #lableak #propublica #transparency

I said skeptical of, not expert in.
When the big publishers of news have been approached for things like this before, they have been reluctant to cannibalize their subscription business. But a system that does not include the big publishers (NYT, WP, WSJl) is not likely to be a difference maker. 
However, I'm not dismissing Post.news. Not saying it can't or won't work. I signed up and I am trying to use the platform so I can understand what's special about it.

records.title: Here in the attachment is the founder of Post...
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A Mastodon post by Jay Rosen from 2022-11-28.
records.quote:
Here in the attachment is the founder of Post.news, Noam Bardin, explaining what led him to the conclusion that something new was needed.
His main point is this: "We need other models and we can’t have a world of just advertising or subscription." 
I agree with him on that. But his alternative begins with micropayments for news publishers. There I am highly skpetical. 
For more about what Post.news intends, click this link: https://www.niemanlab.org/2022/11/post-the-latest-twitter-alternative-is-betting-big-on-micropayments-for-news/
#journalism #micropayments #freepress

See the attachment for Josh Marshall's apt description of "both sides" journalism. 
As I've said before, "both sides" is not primarily a truth-seeking practice, but a refuge-seeking one. 
"Press bias avoidance" as Josh calls it, is not about depicting what happened. Not in the main, I mean. Rather it's a pre-response by journalists to criticisms they have anticipated or internalized.
@joshtpm
#journalism #bothsides #journalists #mediabias

@maria 
I very much agree that one of journalism's problems is losing touch with and failing to ID as fellow citizens.
But to write "all journalism is citizen journalism" is just a way of saying, "don't use that term, it's useless."
Or: "this combination of words lacks meaning."

I don't agree with any of that. 
There's still a need to talk about journalistic acts performed by people who do not primarily identify as journalists.

I never properly introduced myself when I joined Oct. 29.
I have been teaching #journalism at NYU since 1986. I have a PhD in media studies. My masters thesis was on McLuhan. My PhD thesis was about the concept of "the public." 
I write a lot about press coverage of politics, and try to puzzle out what journalists as a group are thinking, which is why my site is called pressthink.org 
I've been online since 1996. Been blogging since 2003. On Twitter since 2008. 
Thanks for making Mastodon.

records.title: Jack Shafer at Politico:...
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A Mastodon post by Jay Rosen from 2022-11-21.
records.quote:
Jack Shafer at Politico: 
"The over-reliance on predictive journalism does a disservice to everybody."
https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2022/11/20/pundits-blew-midterm-results-00069539
One thing he misses: The press organizes election coverage around "who's gonna win?" for many reasons. It's easy. It's portable. It sells. But it's also that "who's gonna win?" feels to them like a non-ideological question. 
That makes it "safe" for journalists to dive in, even though the predictions themselves are risky— and often end in ridicule.
#journalism
