records.title: "She Said" eludes clichés...
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A Mastodon post by Jay Rosen from 2022-11-20.
records.quote:
"She Said" eludes clichés. Crusty old city editor, for one. Newspaper movies (and documentaries) often find irresistible repeated shots of the big printing presses as copies of the paper roll out.
Here that's all gone away. An editor pushes the "publish" button, and the word goes forth about Harvey Weinstein. It is the high point of the film. 3/
#journalism #journalists

records.title: Quoting Elon Musk:...
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A Mastodon post by Jay Rosen from 2022-11-19.
records.quote:
Quoting Elon Musk: 
"As Twitter pursues the goal of elevating citizen journalism, media elite will try everything to stop that from happening." 
My definition of citizen journalism— 14 years ago: 
"When the people formerly known as the audience employ the press tools they have in their possession to inform one another, that’s citizen journalism." 
http://archive.pressthink.org/2008/07/14/a_most_useful_d.html
I still like that definition.
But: that citizen journalism can or should replace the professional kind is a crazy claim.

records.title: One thing I teach my journalism students: It used to be that when you finish your story, you were "d...
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A Mastodon post by Jay Rosen from 2022-11-06.
records.quote:
One thing I teach my journalism students: It used to be that when you finish your story, you were "done." You could go on to the next assignment. 
It doesn't work that way anymore. Now when a work of journalism is published, the people who published it — including the author — have to get it to the people who need it, or want it, or who delight in it once they discover it.
I try not to call this "promotion," although it is that. It's really a second creative act: the post... and the thread.

records.title: Why aren’t mainstream journalists sounding the alarm about the threat to democracy?
records.author: Dan Froomkin
records.summary: The article explores why mainstream political journalists aren't aggressively addressing the threat to democracy.  It posits several theories, including the possibility that journalists are not truly alarmed by the threat or are unable to grasp its significance due to a lack of understanding of democracy's fragility, a lack of diversity in newsrooms, and a reliance on outdated journalistic norms of 'balance' that fail to adequately address a fundamentally asymmetric threat. The author highlights a Twitter discussion with prominent journalists and academics who agree that the issue is less about capability and more about will, perspective, and the profession's outdated practices.
records.quote: This is why Black journalists and the traditions of the Black press are so critical. We know that democracy has been and is always contested and fragile, and at times missing altogether.

records.title: Journalist have to be more agile in their news reporting! - Professor Jay Rosen on Democracy-ish
records.author: Democracy-ish
records.summary: This article analyzes the current state of political journalism, particularly in the context of Donald Trump and the Republican party. It discusses the challenges journalists face in reporting on anti-democratic candidates who perpetuate lies and undermine the electoral system. The piece also explores the conflict within newsrooms between older journalists clinging to traditional practices and a new, more diverse generation that questions objectivity and demands a more agile approach to covering abnormal times.

records.title: Jay Rosen on the mess at CNN and the perils of "both sides" journalism
records.author: Aaron Rupar; Thor Benson
records.summary: Thor Benson interviews Jay Rosen for Public Notice about CNN's purge of Trump critics under new management, the perils of 'both sides' journalism, and why the decades-long campaign to convince journalists of 'liberal bias' ranks among the most successful propaganda campaigns in post-war America. Rosen advocates for pro-democracy journalism and suggests reframing political coverage as a three-way fight: MAGA, the Republican Party, and Democrats.
records.quote: The decades-long campaign to persuade journalists that they are filled with liberal bias was one of the most successful propaganda campaigns in post-War America.

records.title: Beyond the ‘Democracy Desk’: Why U.S. newsrooms need to become explicitly pro-democracy
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: The U.S. is experiencing democratic backsliding, weakening the informal systems that underpin democracy. The American press needs to become more explicitly pro-democracy, rather than treating it as an assumed background condition. This requires experimentation and a willingness to show what's at stake in the battle for American democracy, despite concerns about being perceived as partisan.
records.quote: Democratic backsliding, which is the tendency for a democratic system to decay, presents huge problems for journalists as they try to inform the American public.
concepts: Not the odds but the stakes

records.title: He used to edit political stories at the Chicago Tribune. Now he says the press is failing our democracy. - PressThink
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This is an interview with Mark Jacob, a retired journalist, who reflects on his experience in political journalism and critiques the "he said/she said" approach to news reporting. Jacob argues that this approach, prioritizing equal representation of both sides regardless of truthfulness, has been exploited by propagandists and has ultimately failed to serve democracy. He details how this approach, while intended to appear fair and objective, unintentionally enabled the spread of misinformation and undermined the power of fact-checking. He also discusses the various motivations behind this flawed approach, including commercial pressures, the pursuit of attention, and the fear of upsetting powerful figures or the public.
records.quote: “I didn’t think I was helping either party,” you wrote. “I thought I was helping the readers. I was wrong.”

records.title: Again and Again
records.author: Brooke Gladstone; Jay Rosen
records.summary: On the Media episode anchored in the aftermath of the Buffalo mass shooting. Rosen restates the emergency-mode argument and reframes horse-race coverage as a portable lens that fails the moment democracy disintegrates. The Republican Party's continued investment in Trump's lies, Rosen argues, is itself a civic emergency that newsrooms keep failing to confront.
records.quote: We live in a two party system and one of the two parties is anti-democratic. That is a civic emergency.

records.title: Andrew Tyndall comments on CBS News hiring Trump’s former chief of staff Mick Mulvaney as a news analyst and paid contributor
records.author: Andrew Tyndall
records.summary: Andrew Tyndall analyzes the controversy surrounding CBS News's hiring of Mick Mulvaney, Donald Trump's former chief of staff, as a paid contributor. The analysis includes excerpts from a broadcast discussing the hiring, which was quickly reversed after internal criticism. The main reasons for the controversy were the impression that CBS was actively recruiting former Trump officials and Mulvaney's strong opinions on current national security issues. The author also notes that the hiring gave the impression of a move to bring more conservative voices to the network.
records.quote: It is to pay him to be on our side of the line, the journalist’s side, when he has not yet accounted for his actions when he was on the other side, the politician’s side.

records.title: Answers to Craig's Questions - PressThink
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen presents a conversation between Rosen and Craig Newmark about lessons learned from the 2016 election regarding the trustworthiness of the press. Key takeaways include the press's flawed predictions, disconnect from large portions of the country, vulnerability to demagoguery, and challenges in dealing with disinformation and the erosion of truth in the Trump era. The conversation highlights shifts in journalistic practices, such as explicitly calling out lies and acknowledging the right-wing media's role in shaping reality, but also acknowledges ongoing challenges like the inability to effectively counter open corruption.

records.title: The savvy turn in political journalism - PressThink
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen examines the "savvy style" in American journalism, a tendency to prioritize political strategy and insider knowledge over factual accuracy and accountability. Rosen contrasts this approach with a "citizens agenda" model, exemplified by the Charlotte Observer's efforts to focus on voters' concerns. He argues that the savvy style, which accepts political maneuvering as a given, often prevents journalists from probing the justifications for actions and policies, as illustrated by the lack of scrutiny given to Republican opposition to voting rights legislation. Rosen concludes that the savvy temptation remains strong in American journalism, hindering effective public engagement.

records.title: After six years of asking, NPR interviewed Trump. A journalist for VICE asked me how it went.
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Donald Trump was interviewed by NPR's Steve Inskeep, marking the first time in six years, and after Trump directly contacted Inskeep. Rosen, listening to the interview, found it interesting, commending Inskeep's handling of questions, including Trump's continued false claims about the 2020 election. A journalist from VICE then contacted Rosen for their thoughts on the interview, and Rosen conveyed their positive assessment, emphasizing the importance of NPR securing the interview despite Trump's false statements. The discussion also touched on the complexities of real-time fact-checking during interviews. Overall, Rosen considered the interview significant and valuable for hearing from different perspectives and challenging those in positions of power.
records.quote: The goal should not be to get him to admit that he is wrong. He will never do that. The goal should be to show the audience how he operates. He is a master of deflection, distraction, and deception. Journalists need to be masters of exposure.

records.title: Professor Jay Rosen on 'pro-democracy' agenda for media
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Jay Rosen discusses the challenges facing political journalism in an era where one of the two major political parties is exhibiting anti-democratic tendencies. He argues that traditional journalistic practices are inadequate when dealing with a party that rejects common facts and undermines democratic norms. Rosen suggests that news organizations should explicitly state their commitment to democracy, truth, science, evidence, and voting, and then revise their practices accordingly. He also advocates for a 'citizens' agenda' approach, focusing on voter priorities and using an 'urgency index' to assess the state of democratic backsliding.
records.quote: We are pro-democracy, pro-truth, pro-science, pro-evidence, pro-voting.

records.title: Jay Rosen says news outlets should be 'pro-democracy'
records.author: Ramishah Maruf
records.summary: A CNN article summarizing Rosen's appearance on Reliable Sources, where he argues news outlets should openly identify as pro-democracy. He contends that major news organizations should be pro-truth, pro-science, pro-evidence, and pro-voting, and that taking these positions does not compromise journalistic integrity but rather defends the conditions that make journalism possible.
records.quote: Major news organizations should be pro-truth, pro-science, pro-evidence, and pro-voting, because taking these positions does not compromise journalistic integrity but rather defends the conditions that make journalism possible.

records.title: Transcript: Nicole Hemmer Interviews Jay Rosen for ‘The Ezra Klein Show’ - The New York Times
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This transcript of an interview on "The Ezra Klein Show" features Jay Rosen discussing the shortcomings of mainstream media coverage, particularly concerning complex legislation like the Build Back Better bill. Rosen critiques the focus on incremental updates and "inside game" reporting, arguing that this prioritizes daily content production over genuine public understanding. He highlights the lack of an "architecture of understanding" in news coverage, leading to an overemphasis on strategy, speculation, and drama, rather than informing the public. The interview also touches upon the problematic use of terms like "moderate" and "centrist" in political journalism, and the challenges faced by the news industry in the digital age.
records.quote: I think transparency will ultimately triumph over viewlessness, but we don’t know if American democracy will survive until then.

records.title: It's Time for the Media to Choose: Neutrality or Democracy?

The conflict with honest journalism is structural, not merely partisan.
records.quote: Making it harder to vote, and harder to understand what the party is really about — these are two parts of the same project.

records.title: The "here's where we're coming from" statement in journalism - PressThink
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: The article discusses the shift from the traditional "view from nowhere" objectivity in journalism to a transparency-based approach where journalists disclose their perspectives and biases. It highlights examples like Casey Newton's newsletter Platformer and ProPublica, emphasizing the importance of journalists being upfront about their values and intentions to build trust with their audience. The piece also stresses the need for news organizations to adopt a broader transparency system, including disclosing ownership, funding, and decision-making processes.
records.quote: "Transparency is the new objectivity."

records.title: Disinfo Discussions: The Role of News Media with Jay Rosen
records.author: Aspen Digital
records.summary: Aspen Digital executive director Vivian Schiller interviews Jay Rosen about the “view from nowhere,” both-sides reporting, Donald Trump’s exploitation of traditional newsworthiness, the truth-sandwich approach to false claims, and why the press must become more openly pro-democracy.
records.quote: we need a much more aggressively pro-democracy press than we have now

records.title: The 'troubled' relationship media and big tech have with democracy
records.author: Paul Blanchard
records.summary: UK-based Media Masters interviews Rosen at length. He argues the United States lives in a two-party system where one party is anti-democratic and the other is unsure that is a problem; attacks Fox News for deliberately and cynically provoking rage and loyalty; and condemns Facebook as ungovernable and a danger to democracy around the world.
records.quote: We live in a two-party system... one of the two is anti-democratic, and the other is not sure that's a problem.

records.title: Jay Rosen on right-wing TV drifting 'further from the real,' and how journalists should 'rethink and rebuild' to cover it
records.author: Brian Stelter
records.summary: CNN's Reliable Sources podcast hosts Rosen for a 44-minute discussion of the devolution of Fox News, the difficulty of describing a shifted political universe in the United States, and why journalists should rethink and rebuild to cover it.
records.quote: Rosen on Reliable Sources discussing the devolution of Fox News and the difficulty of describing a shifted political universe in the United States.

records.title: How to cover the ongoing siege on democracy
records.author: Brooke Gladstone; Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen and Gladstone discuss how to cover democracy under sustained attack. Rosen introduces the truth sandwich method for reporting on misinformation, advocates for dedicated democracy beats at news organizations, and praises WITF's 'never forget' policy of contextualizing every GOP election story with the party's anti-democratic actions. He argues the civic emergency did not end with Trump leaving office.
records.quote: The civic emergency did not end with Trump leaving office, and journalism needs dedicated democracy beats and consistent contextualization of anti-democratic actions to cover a sustained siege on democratic norms.

records.title: Jay Rosen looks at what happened to journalism norms during the Trump years
records.author: Eric Black
records.summary: Eric Black reviews and extensively excerpts a Rosen PressThink post examining the collapse of journalism norms during the Trump years. Rosen argues that norms like objectivity, balance, and the church-state separation between news and opinion were already weakening before Trump, but his presidency exposed them as unable to handle a political figure who systematically exploited them. The article includes reader comments debating Rosen's analysis.
records.quote: Norms like objectivity and balance were already weakening before Trump, but his presidency exposed them as unable to handle a political figure who systematically exploited them.

records.title: Lucid Interview: Jay Rosen
records.author: Ruth Ben-Ghiat
records.summary: Ruth Ben-Ghiat interviews Rosen about the press's struggles during the Trump administration. Rosen explains how presidential conventions became invisible assumptions that Trump exploited, discusses the dangers of expecting the press to function as political opposition, and identifies his central concern: that one of two major parties is anti-democratic and the political press doesn't know what to do about it.
records.quote: What I'm most concerned about right now is that we have a two-party system and one of the two parties is anti-democratic. And we don't have a political press that knows what to do about that.

records.title: A current list of my top problems in pressthink, May 2021 - PressThink
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: The article discusses the challenges faced by journalism in the current political climate, particularly with the rise of an anti-democratic Republican party that relies on counter-majoritarian and counter-factual narratives. It examines the inadequacy of the 'both sides' model of news coverage and the difficulty of determining newsworthiness in an era of disinformation. Rosen grapples with the dilemma of platforming harmful viewpoints while also needing to inform the public.
records.quote: As I wrote five years ago, asymmetry between the major parties fries the circuits of the mainstream press.

records.title: If you're worried that journalists have learned nothing from the Trump years.
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen discusses encouraging developments suggesting some journalists understand the need for change after the Trump presidency, the Stop the Steal movement, and the January 6th insurrection. It highlights examples such as WITF's policy of contextualizing future actions of officials who spread election fraud lies, the Cleveland Plain Dealer's refusal to amplify baseless claims, and ProPublica's creation of a democracy beat and Votebeat's efforts to build capacity within the American press to cover voting restrictions.
records.quote: "Journalists should have a bias. A bias towards democracy."

records.title: TNR Live: Politics and the Media
records.author: The New Republic
records.summary: This is a discussion about media coverage of politics, particularly regarding Donald Trump, and lessons learned from the past five years. Participants discuss the press's struggle to deal with falsehoods, the importance of challenging amplification, and the need to stand against 'the big lie.' The January 6th events are highlighted as a critical moment of transition, revealing a moral vacuum. The conversation also touches on conservative media's manipulation of mainstream media, and the persistence of accepting Republican ideas about 'real Americans.' The lack of progress in addressing race and racism in newsroom leadership is also discussed.

records.title: Prof. Jay Rosen was a guest on On The Media this week in a segment titled, "What The Press Have And Should Have Learned From The Trump Era." Also included in the same discussion was Yamiche Alcindor, NYU alum and White House correspondent for PBS NewsHour. - NYU Journalism
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Jay Rosen discusses with Brooke Gladstone and Bob Garfield how the press has learned it is a subject in the story, especially during the Trump era, and argues that it must prioritize democracy over objectivity. He notes the emergence of a 'democracy beat' but criticizes the persistence of 'both-sidesism.' Rosen suggests the press should be more transparent and serve as a 'cheerleader' for the democratic process itself, holding power accountable for its commitment to democratic norms and values.
records.quote: I think the press has learned that it is a subject in the story. It is a participant in the drama. It is one of the institutions that is under attack.

records.title: What the press have and should have learned from the Trump era
records.author: Brooke Gladstone; Jay Rosen
records.summary: Two days after Biden's inauguration, Gladstone assembles journalists including Yamiche Alcindor, Jay Rosen, Karen Attiah, David Leonhardt, and Masha Gessen to reflect on Trump-era lessons. Rosen advocates for pro-democracy, pro-voting, pro-truth journalism -- arguing that the press must take a stand for democratic values rather than hiding behind false neutrality. He pushes for journalism that openly supports the conditions that make journalism possible.
records.quote: The press must openly support the conditions that make journalism possible — pro-democracy, pro-voting, pro-truth — rather than hiding behind false neutrality.

records.title: Two paths forward for the American press
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: The article discusses the future of the American press after Donald Trump's presidency. It contrasts two potential paths: a restoration of order and a return to normalcy, or a democratic breakthrough in journalism. Rosen critiques the media's longing for symmetry and 'both sides' narratives, even when facts don't warrant it, and highlights the importance of defending democracy and truth, as demonstrated by some journalists during the 2020 election.
records.quote: This time, journalism was prepared.

records.title: America’s Press and the Asymmetric War for Truth
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.pub: The New York Review of Books
records.summary: The Republican Party is increasingly becoming a minority party that relies on counterfactual narratives to maintain power. This creates a structural conflict with honest journalism, as the GOP must fight with fictions to appeal to its dwindling base. The Democratic Party is evolving into a coalition representing 'literally everyone else'.
records.quote: The Democrats’ coalition of transformation is now larger—even much larger—than the Republicans’ coalition of restoration.

records.title: The coming confrontation between the American press and the Republican Party
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen argues that the Republican Party's increasingly counter-majoritarian stance necessitates a conflict with honest journalism. The GOP's reliance on fictions, such as widespread voter fraud, clashes with reality-based reporting. Rosen criticizes mainstream media's tendency towards "he said/she said" journalism and "balanced treatment of unbalanced phenomena," arguing that this refuge-seeking behavior protects journalists from criticism rather than serving the public. He contends that the right-wing's creation of its own media ecosystem has shifted the dynamics, rendering traditional journalistic practices insufficient to address the asymmetrical political landscape.
records.quote: Sometimes I worry that my squeamishness about making sharp judgments, pro or con, makes me unfit for the slam-bang world of daily journalism. Other times I conclude that it makes me ideally suited for newspapering– certainly for the rigors and conventions of modern ‘objective’ journalism. For I can dispose of my dilemmas by writing stories straight down the middle.

records.title: To protect democracy, journalists need to learn to think like hackers and spies
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen develops his threat modeling proposal for newsrooms, consulting former Facebook CSO Joshua Geltzer and national security expert Alex Stamos. Explains how threat modeling works in practice: identifying adversaries, mapping attack surfaces, running red team exercises, and creating a Threat Urgency Index. Argues newsrooms need these tools because traditional campaign coverage cannot address threats to democracy itself.
records.quote: To be a safeguard of democracy you cannot just react to what explodes into the news from now until 20 January. You have to zoom forward in imagination, glimpse danger, and then work your way back to decisions made today and tomorrow.

records.title: Trump exploited a broken press. Here’s how to fix it.
records.author: Sean Illing
records.summary: The article discusses how Trump and his allies use the strategy of "flooding the zone with shit" to overwhelm the media and public with falsehoods, making it difficult for journalists to effectively counter the misinformation. Jay Rosen argues that the traditional journalistic code is inadequate to deal with this strategy, and the press needs to adapt by abandoning the "savvy style" and owning their agenda to effectively combat disinformation and protect democratic values.
records.quote: Trump has hacked the newsworthiness code by being newsworthy in the traditional sense every day, many times a day.

records.title: Four radical ways the media can protect US democracy from Trump
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen proposes four concrete recommendations for how the media should shift to 'emergency mode' in covering Trump: (1) stop covering live speeches/rallies, (2) suspend normal relations with the White House, (3) add an amplification check to every presidential quote, and (4) shift focus from what Trump says to what his government does. Then escalates to 'active threat' measures: create threat modeling teams, a live Threat Urgency Index, pressure officials to go on record, and track solutions instead of the horse race.
records.quote: When the powers of the federal government are turned against the reliability of the vote itself, we have crossed an invisible boundary that separates a bitterly fought election from an enterprise-threatening event.

records.title: Journalists should be in 'emergency' mode
records.author: Brooke Gladstone; Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen argues that journalism needs to switch to an emergency setting for covering the Trump era. Recorded during the 2020 dueling town halls, the conversation covers the citizen's agenda model, the firehose of falsehood, the limits of the view from nowhere, and why normal political coverage routines are inadequate for an abnormal presidency. Rosen urges journalists to recognize the civic emergency and adapt accordingly.
records.quote: Normal political coverage routines are inadequate for an abnormal presidency — journalism must switch to an emergency setting that recognizes the civic stakes of covering a firehose of falsehood.

records.title: Don't let Trump be the protagonist of the pandemic (and four other ways the media can improve how it covers the coronavirus)
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Five proposals for improving pandemic coverage: (1) End duplication through newsroom consortiums publishing simultaneously, (2) Create an Urgency Index ranking what the public should be most worried about, (3) Treat confusion as a governing style rather than isolated incidents, (4) Dislodge Trump from the 'protagonist' role in the COVID story, and (5) Track your own coverage metrics. Includes the viral 'plan is to have no plan' passage. Originally from PressThink.
records.quote: The plan is to have no plan, to let daily deaths between one and three thousand become a normal thing, and then to create massive confusion about who is responsible.

records.title: In the 2020 US election, journalists need an agenda: defending democracy
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen argues that journalists covering the 2020 election need their own agenda to avoid being swept up in Trump's. He distinguishes between the 'properly political' and the 'overly politicised' in journalism, then proposes four specific agendas: a citizens agenda (asking voters what matters), fighting authoritarianism, evidence-based political debate, and pro-participation coverage. Originally published on PressThink.
records.quote: You cannot keep from getting swept up in Donald Trump's agenda without a firm grasp on your own.

records.title: You might not like it, but it's smart politics.
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: The article discusses how the press, particularly the political press corps, became overly focused on "savviness" and understanding politics as a strategic game played by insiders. This focus made them ill-equipped to cover the rise of Donald Trump and the challenges he posed to American democracy. Rosen argues for a shift in political journalism, emphasizing the defense of democracy, symmetrical accounts of asymmetrical realities, and a rejection of the "politics as strategic game" frame.
records.quote: In politics, our journalists believe, it is better to be savvy than it is to be honest or correct on the facts.

records.title: What newsrooms can learn from threat modeling at Facebook
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen interviews Alex Stamos, former Facebook CSO, about how newsrooms could adapt corporate threat modeling for election coverage. Stamos explains threat modeling, threat ideation, red teaming, and tabletop exercises in detail, then applies each to a journalism context. They discuss how the 2016 GRU hack-and-leak campaign manipulated the press, how to prepare for similar 2020 attacks, and why newsrooms need internal guidelines for handling manipulated information. Published on The Verge.
records.quote: For journalists, I think you have to accept that somebody will try to manipulate you, perhaps in an organized and professional fashion.

records.title: The Membership Guide: Handbook
records.author: Ariel Zirulnick, Emily Goligoski, Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen defines membership in journalism as a social contract between a news organization and its members. It emphasizes the importance of memberful routines, a membership strategy, and a membership program. It distinguishes membership from subscription, donation, and crowdfunding models, highlighting the unique value proposition and expectations associated with each. The article draws on research from diverse member-driven movements to offer insights into successful membership programs, including the importance of listening to members, connecting to a larger purpose, offering flexible participation, and growing at a human scale.
records.quote: Membership is a social contract between a news organization and its members in which members give their time, money, energy, expertise, and connections to support a cause that they believe in.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.author: Arthur L. Carter Journalism Institute
records.summary: Jay Rosen discusses the media's coverage of the jobs crisis, arguing that it's being treated as a political story rather than a national crisis. He suggests that the press is too focused on objectivity, the horse race in Washington, and is disconnected from the public's experience of unemployment. Rosen advocates for more stories about the real-life impact of unemployment and a shift towards public journalism that helps citizens solve problems.

records.title: Jay Rosen Presents “The Citizens Agenda”
records.author: Bridget Thoreson
records.summary: Jay Rosen, a journalism professor, presented the idea of a "Citizens Agenda" to improve how journalists and news organizations serve the public. He suggests that instead of prioritizing politicians and political strategy, news outlets should identify and report on the issues that the public deems most important.
records.quote: We’re not going to start with the candidates and their fundraising and their poll numbers and their attacks on each other. We’re going to start with the voters and what they want this election to be about.

records.title: What I learned by watching the American press try to cover Donald Trump
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Jay Rosen reflects on his observations of the American press's coverage of Donald Trump's presidency.  He argues that the press's practices rest on assumptions about presidential behavior that don't apply to Trump, leading to a normalization of his actions rather than a critical examination.  He introduces the concept of 'verification in reverse,' where publicly doubted claims are used to generate controversy and power political movements.  He also notes the effectiveness of strategies like 'flooding the zone' (or the Russian equivalent, 'firehose of falsehoods') in undermining trust in journalism by overwhelming the truth with misinformation.
records.quote: I wouldn't say any American news organization has gotten it right.

records.title: Jay Rosen and Nicholas Johnson on What the Media Can Do About Disinformation
records.author: Amy Westervelt
records.summary: Jay Rosen's call to focus on the stakes of the 2024 election, rather than the odds, critiques the dominance of "horse race journalism" in mainstream US media.  This focus overshadows crucial issues and diverse perspectives, while the rise of partisan media and misinformation further complicates the landscape.  The article highlights the need for more inclusive and issue-oriented coverage, contrasting the prevalent focus on campaign strategy and polling with examples of impactful investigative and local reporting.
records.quote: This season we've traced the creation of Big Oil's big propaganda machine. In this episode, the season finale, we look at what can be done about it now that it has delivered us into an era of disinformation.

records.title: NYU Professor Jay Rosen Tears Chuck Todd Over Trump Lies
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Jay Rosen critiques Chuck Todd's Rolling Stone interview, where Todd admits naiveté regarding Republican misinformation under the Trump administration. Rosen argues this isn't naiveté but professional malpractice, highlighting Todd's influential position and responsibility to understand political dynamics. Rosen contends Todd's failure stems from willful blindness and a lack of imagination, not a lack of knowledge.
records.quote: It’s not naive of him. It’s malpractice. Chuck Todd’s entire brand is based on the claim that he understands politics.

records.title: Bad headline, small changes at the New York Times - PressThink
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the internal tensions at the New York Times regarding its coverage of Donald Trump. Rosen, a self-described Times loyalist, highlights the growing disconnect between the paper's editorial decisions and the expectations of its core readership, particularly concerning the portrayal of Trump's racism and the handling of the 2016 election coverage. The article notes a generational divide within the Times newsroom, with younger journalists advocating for a more aggressive stance against Trump, while older journalists prefer a more traditional approach. The absence of a public editor is criticized, and Rosen questions the paper's ability to adapt to the changing media landscape and its evolving relationship with its audience.
records.quote: What frustrates them is that the country’s core institutions are under assault by a radical ethnonationalist minority and the sense of crisis is not being conveyed.
