records.title: The Correspondent's editor-in-chief talks about what U.S. expansion means and doesn't
records.author: Laura Hazard Owen
records.summary: Nieman Lab interviews The Correspondent's editor-in-chief Rob Wijnberg about the confusion surrounding their U.S. expansion. After raising $2.5 million with ambassadors including Rosen and Nate Silver, the site announced it would remain headquartered in Amsterdam rather than opening a U.S. newsroom. Rosen acknowledged the confusion was the company's fault due to earlier messaging, while Wijnberg defended their global-first approach.
records.quote: I think it's understandable why people had the impression that there would be a U.S. headquarters, because some of the signaling that The Correspondent did was suggesting that. So that's not anyone's fault but The Correspondent's.

records.title: How journalists and the public shape our democracy: From social media and 'fake news' to reporting 'just the facts'
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen discusses the role of journalists in a democracy, emphasizing the pursuit of truth and ethical considerations. It highlights four principles of ethical journalism: seeking truth and reporting it accurately and fairly, minimizing harm, acting independently, and being accountable and transparent. The article also addresses the distinction between news and opinion within news organizations and provides tips for identifying "fake news," including checking sources, attribution, and using fact-checking websites. Finally, it emphasizes the public's role in verifying information and combating misinformation.
records.quote: This first principle of journalism-its disinterested pursuit of truth-is ultimately what sets journalism apart from other forms of communication.

records.title: Has Trump Changed the Media?
records.author: Andrea Mitchell Center for the Study of Democracy
records.pub: Andrea Mitchell Center for the Study of Democracy
records.summary: Jay Rosen discusses the press coverage of Donald Trump, grading their performance in different areas. He gives an A for investigating Trump due to parallel investigations and familiarity with corruption scandals. He gives a C for preventing Trump from setting the agenda, highlighting the press's tendency to report what the president says as news. He gives a D for innovating on the fly during what he considers a civic emergency, noting a lack of novel practices in presidential news coverage. He gives an F for reflecting on the 2016 election debacle and an incomplete grade for addressing the fact that a third of the electorate relies on Trump as their primary source of information.
records.quote: what the president says and what the president does is news by definition

records.title: Jay Rosen at IRE discussing the importance of crowdsourcing
records.author: Andrea Mitchell Center for the Study of Democracy
records.pub: Andrea Mitchell Center for the Study of Democracy
records.summary: The article discusses the importance of crowdsourcing for journalists, emphasizing that readers often possess knowledge that journalists do not. It highlights that engaging with the audience improves trust in journalism and provides a different perspective on the profession. The piece also suggests various tools for crowdsourcing, including Google Documents, Survey Monkey, blogging, email lists, Twitter, and Facebook groups, stressing that these are affordable and easily accessible.
records.quote: my readers know more than I do
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Trump's attacks on journalists could incite violence, study warns
records.author: Cristiano Lima
records.summary: A report from the Committee to Protect Journalists warns that President Trump's attacks on the media mirror authoritarian regimes and could provoke violence against journalists. The report, titled “The Enemy Within: Trump’s War on the Press,” highlights Trump's repeated use of the term "fake news" and labeling some journalists as "enemies of the people," along with government attempts to control information access. The study suggests his rhetoric, which includes aggressive verbal assaults at rallies and on social media, endangers journalists and undermines the credibility of the U.S. press internationally. The report concludes by emphasizing the importance of defending the media from rhetoric that undermines its crucial role.
records.quote: When the president of the United States targets journalists, he empowers others to do the same.

records.title: NYU's Jay Rosen says 2020's political journalism will be even worse than 2016's
records.author: Peter Kafka
records.summary: Two years after the first Recode Media appearance (RECORD-00784/00785), Rosen returns to Peter Kafka's podcast to forecast the 2020 cycle. He argues the horse-race frame is structurally incapable of covering an anti-democratic candidate and warns that the press has not absorbed the lessons of 2016.
records.quote: Rosen returns to Peter Kafka's Recode Media to argue that political journalism in 2020 will be even worse than in 2016 if newsrooms keep treating the Trump presidency as politics-as-usual.

records.title: Radical Rethink: 2014 Journalism Ethics Conference
records.author: UW School of Journalism & Mass Communication
records.pub: UW School of Journalism & Mass Communication
records.summary: This transcript captures the closing session of a conference focusing on national security and the press. A non-journalist speaker, Gabe, argues that the media, while often responsible, has exhibited instances of irresponsible reporting post-9/11, citing examples from The New York Times's coverage of counterterrorism programs and NSA activities.  He contends that the government holds excessive secrets, many innocuous, and that while the press plays a vital role in uncovering wrongdoing, its actions haven't always been responsible.
records.quote: I think he's assessment that the media has been overwhelmingly responsible in carrying out that function I think it has been responsible in many cases but I think there are also in the post 9/11 era cases where it's been you know radically irresponsible

records.title: Stand Up! with Pete Dominick: Episode 861 - Journalism Professor Jay Rosen
records.author: Pete Dominick
records.summary: Rosen appears on Pete Dominick's podcast to discuss journalism, media criticism, and the state of public conversation in America. The wide-ranging interview covers Rosen's key ideas about press reform and the challenges facing journalism.
records.quote: Journalism's capacity for self-reform—rethinking how the press relates to its audience and to power—is central to restoring public trust in American media.

records.title: Creating a Space for Ad-Free Journalism with The Correspondent
records.author: Trevor Noah
records.summary: This transcript discusses The Correspondent, a successful member-funded, ad-free news site from the Netherlands, and its plans to expand to English-language publishing.  The discussion highlights the site's unique principles: rejecting advertising, corporate sponsors, and clickbait; focusing on in-depth reporting; and emphasizing solutions-oriented journalism.  The conversation also touches upon the challenges of unbiased news coverage, particularly in the context of the Trump administration's manipulation of the press briefing room, and advocates for transparency in journalism by openly stating the journalist's perspective.
records.quote: No reporting about problems unless you also report about what we can do about it, what you can do about it, what we as a society can do about it.

records.title: Jay Rosen pitches the English-language Correspondent on The Daily Show
records.author: Joshua Benton
records.summary: The decline in trust in journalism is discussed, highlighting the closure of numerous local news outlets and the rise of alternative, less reliable information sources such as social media influencers.  The article points to the role of social media in crippling journalism's business model and fostering misinformation, but also suggests that journalists share some responsibility for the current 'post-truth' environment.  Jay Rosen's perspective on the issue is mentioned, emphasizing the need for further discussion, particularly given the upcoming Canadian election.
records.quote: If The Correspondent wanted to see an immediate tsunami of financial support after the segment aired last night, it might be a little disappointed.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Speaking the hard truth to journalism (Center for Media at Risk podcast)
records.author: Center for Media at Risk
records.summary: The Center for Media at Risk podcast features Rosen discussing the hard truths facing journalism, including the profession's reluctance to acknowledge its own role in the current crisis and the structural challenges that make reform so difficult.
records.quote: Journalism is reluctant to acknowledge its own role in the current crisis, and that reluctance is itself one of the structural challenges that makes reform so difficult.

records.title: Letter to My Network: Join The Correspondent - PressThink
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Jay Rosen, a prominent press critic, urges his readers to support The Correspondent, a member-funded, ad-free news site. He highlights its innovative principles, such as no ads, no clickbait, and a participatory model where members are active contributors. Rosen argues that this model offers a superior alternative to traditional journalism's reliance on advertising and its inherent biases, advocating for a more transparent, inclusive, and constructive approach to news.
records.quote: If you have ever wondered what I would recommend to public-spirited people who want a better press, this is it.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: A roundup of trends that are changing journalism
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A syllabus-style overview of 21 trends reshaping journalism, developed for Rosen's NYU 'digital thinking' class. Covers social media as distribution, mobile shift, new business models (data, events, native ads, nonprofit, crowdfunding), analytics, product focus, UX design, data journalism, structured data, personalization, transparency, open journalism, automation, agile newsrooms, personal franchise model, niche journalism, explainer journalism, news as service, curation, fact-checking, and platform power. Originally from PressThink, republished on IJNet.
records.quote: Twenty-one interlocking trends — from social media distribution and mobile shift to fact-checking, automation, and platform power — are collectively reshaping what journalism is and how it operates.

records.title: The public service veto: How The Correspondent protects itself from profit maximization
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: As Trust Advisor to The Correspondent, Rosen explains the legal structure that prevents the member-funded news site from being sold to a profit-maximizing company. He details how a Dutch foundation, SDM, holds a 'priority share' that acts as a public service veto over changes to the site's founding principles, including its 5% profit cap and ad-free model.
records.quote: Turning away from their founding principles is not a power the directors of the company have, which is the genius of the priority share design.

records.title: What The Correspondent will add to the American press
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen explains his decision to work with De Correspondent on its English-language expansion, describing it as a response to the deep structural problems in American journalism exposed by 2016. He details the site's seven key features -- no ads, member-funded, no meter, escape from the news cycle, revised editorial contracts, knowledge exchange with readers, and no 'view from nowhere' -- arguing the model reconfigures how a public stands toward journalists.
records.quote: By kicking the advertisers out of bed, by pushing the distinction between subscription and membership to the key point of sustainability, by exiting from the hamster wheel of clickbait and 24-hour news... De Correspondent went beyond tinkering with a broken business model. It reconfigured how a public stands toward the makers of journalism.

records.title: Twitter CEO Jack Dorsey interviewed by NYU professor Jay Rosen; podcast, transcript | Vox
records.author: Jay Rosen, Jack Dorsey
records.summary: This is a transcript of an interview between Twitter CEO Jack Dorsey and Jay Rosen, a professor of journalism at NYU. The conversation covers a range of topics related to Twitter's functionality, algorithm, and perceived bias. Dorsey discusses his efforts to improve the platform, including a listening tour, and acknowledges the challenges posed by bad-faith actors and the difficulty of creating a perfectly unbiased system. Rosen's perspective as a long-time Twitter user and media scholar informs the discussion, touching upon issues of algorithmic transparency and the impact of Twitter's design on public discourse.
records.quote: Dorsey says “we have definitely been gamed” by bad-faith

records.title: Center for Media at Risk Launch Symposium, Panel 4: Journalism
records.author: Annenberg School for Communication
records.summary: This transcript captures a panel discussion focusing on journalism and journalists at risk.  The moderator introduces four panelists: Arzu Geybulla, a freelance writer from Azerbaijan; Parker Higgins, director of special projects at the Freedom of the Press Foundation; Jay Rosen, a journalism professor at NYU; and Sylvia Weisbord, a professor at George Washington University.  Geybulla's opening remarks illustrate the state of journalism in Azerbaijan through the lens of the April 11th presidential elections, highlighting the lack of independent elections and the dynastic nature of the country's leadership.
records.quote: Azerbaijan hasn't really had independent elections since 1993

records.title: Why Trump Is Winning and the Press Is Losing
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.pub: The New York Review of Books
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the organized campaign to discredit the American press, spearheaded by the Republican coalition and amplified by Donald Trump. Jay Rosen details how this campaign operates on three segments of the electorate: core supporters, committed opponents, and those neither strongly supporting nor opposing Trump. The campaign's success is attributed to factors such as the rejection of independent news sources, the failure of Republican elites to push back, and the challenges posed by social media platforms. The text highlights the risks to journalism, including the erosion of trust in facts, the ineffectiveness of fact-checking, and the potential loss of institutional footing.
records.quote: The real opposition is the media. And the way to deal with them is to flood the zone with shit.

records.title: Center for Media at Risk launch symposium
records.author: Various
records.summary: Event page for the Center for Media at Risk launch symposium at the University of Pennsylvania's Annenberg School, featuring a panel with Amy Siskind, Jay Rosen, and Leah Wright Rigueur discussing threats to journalism and democracy.
records.quote: Threats to press freedom and threats to democracy are inseparable—when independent journalism is under pressure, the public's capacity for self-governance is compromised with it.

records.title: Optimizing journalism for trust
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen argues that news organizations should be optimized for trust rather than clicks or scoops, proposing that trust must be designed into journalism. He unpacks what 'optimizing for trust' means in practice, from transparent data policies to showing your work, and explains why he is helping De Correspondent expand to English-language publishing.
records.quote: The problem is how to combine high standards of verification with a bold and creative vision that optimizes for trust, and finds support among readers, viewers, listeners. It's not how to stay in business, it's how to stay in journalism.

records.title: Journalism’s perfect storm? Confronting rising global threats from “f*ke news” to censorship, surveillance, and the killing of journalists with impunity
records.author: Bob Garfield, Brooke Gladstone
records.summary: This panel discussion at the International Journalism Festival will address the converging threats to journalism, including the killing of journalists, imprisonment of media workers, internet shutdowns, the spread of fake news, mass surveillance, platform-driven economic challenges, declining public trust, state-sponsored harassment, and layoffs in traditional newsrooms. Experts will analyze these threats and explore collaborative solutions.
records.quote: The killing of journalists with impunity, the indiscriminate jailing of media workers and bloggers, internet shutdowns, the ‘fake news’ crisis, mass surveillance and targeted interception, the platforms strangling digital profitability, erosion of trust in news, State-sponsored harassment of journalists, continuing mass layoffs in traditional newsrooms… these threats to journalism are converging to create what could be described as journalism’s ‘perfect storm’.

records.title: Jay Rosen (ONA17 speaker profile)
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Speaker profile page for Rosen at the 2017 Online News Association conference, where he participated in discussions about digital journalism, press criticism, and the future of news in the Trump era.
records.quote: In the Trump era, digital journalism faces not just technological disruption but a political environment actively hostile to the press's legitimacy and democratic function.

records.title: Normalizing Trump: An incredibly brief explainer - PressThink
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Journalists covering Trump face a conflict: their ethical code demands reporting on his actions and words, but his incompetence, untrustworthiness, and lack of policy knowledge render much of their work absurd and painful. This leads to "normalization", where journalists downplay or reinterpret his behavior to maintain respect for the presidency and their profession.
records.quote: What they have to report brings ruin to what they have to respect.

records.title: What are journalists for in the age of Trump?
records.author: Tracey Taylor
records.summary: A brief write-up of a conversation between Jay Rosen and journalist Kathy Kiely at the Uncharted Festival of Ideas in Berkeley about the right frame for interpreting press coverage during the Trump presidency. The article accompanies an audio recording of their discussion about journalism's role and responsibilities.
records.quote: The unprecedented presidency of Donald Trump has graphically exposed journalism's weaknesses.

records.title: DATELINE-SAIGON Panel: Jay Rosen on the distinctions between “journalism” and “the media
records.author: ProPublica
records.summary: Jay Rosen discusses the distinctions between “journalism” and “the media.” Rosen explains the important distinction between journalism as a craft or calling and "the media" as an industrial complex focused on monetizing attention. He notes that while journalists often have to work for media companies, their principles can conflict with the commercial requirements of their employers. This tension, he argues, results in a "hybrid product" and that the public's perception of commercial interests overriding journalistic truths is a primary reason for declining trust in the news media.
records.quote: When people perceive commercial imperatives overcoming journalistic truths, they're not wrong.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Is trust-based journalism the future? Jay Rosen thinks so
records.author: Dan Kennedy
records.summary: Dan Kennedy at GBH profiles Rosen's argument that trust-based journalism represents the future of the industry. The piece discusses Rosen's work with De Correspondent and his broader thesis that news organizations must design their operations around earning and maintaining public trust.
records.quote: News organizations must design their entire operations around earning and maintaining public trust, not simply producing content, a thesis Rosen developed through his work with De Correspondent.

records.title: Jay Rosen: This is what a news organization built on reader trust looks like
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen explains why De Correspondent, a Dutch member-funded news site, represents what a trust-optimized news organization looks like. He describes its ad-free model, freedom from the 24-hour news cycle, writer-centered structure, and journalist-as-discussion-leader approach, then announces the Membership Puzzle Project and his role as ambassador for The Correspondent's U.S. expansion.
records.quote: Trump is manufacturing mistrust at a faster rate than journalists can adapt their methods for inspiring public confidence in what they do.

records.title: NYU to launch Membership Puzzle Project
records.author: Knight Foundation
records.summary: Knight Foundation announces $515,000 in funding from Knight, First Look Media, and Democracy Fund for the Membership Puzzle Project at NYU, led by Rosen, working with Dutch news startup De Correspondent. The project aims to bring De Correspondent's membership model to the United States and research how membership can advance sustainability and trust in journalism.
records.quote: The Membership Puzzle Project aims to bring De Correspondent's reader-funded model to the United States and research how membership can advance both sustainability and trust in journalism.

records.title: NYU Journalism launches Membership Puzzle Project led by Prof. Jay Rosen
records.author: NYU Journalism
records.summary: NYU Journalism announces the launch of the Membership Puzzle Project, a research initiative led by Rosen to study how membership models can sustain journalism and build trust. The project, funded by Knight Foundation and others, will research membership-driven news organizations worldwide.
records.quote: The Membership Puzzle Project set out to study how membership models can sustain journalism and build trust between news organizations and the public they serve.

records.title: After the Agora: Jay Rosen: Rebuilding trust in media
records.author: Texas A&M University
records.summary: Texas A&M University announces Rosen's lecture in its 'After the Agora' series, where he discusses rebuilding trust in media and the challenges facing the public sphere in the digital age.
records.quote: Rebuilding trust in media requires confronting the deeper challenges facing the public sphere in a digital age that has fractured the shared spaces where democratic discourse once took place.

records.title: Jay Rosen on the hazards of journalism-as-usual under the Trump administration
records.author: Benjamin Mullin
records.summary: Rosen discusses with Poynter's Benjamin Mullin the collapsing notion of the White House spokesperson, how to cover Trump's tweets, why news organizations should send the interns to the briefing room, and journalism's tendency to stay the same. He argues that routines from previous administrations no longer apply and that the White House Correspondents' Dinner should become an unconference about covering the Trump White House.
records.quote: There's a tendency from top to bottom in the press culture to say, 'what we have works.' We can keep using the routines that we used for the previous administration. And every day, I think more evidence comes in to suggest actually none of that is useful.

records.title: Full transcript: Jay Rosen on Recode Media
records.author: Peter Kafka
records.summary: Extended transcript of Rosen's interview with Peter Kafka covering the press under Trump. Rosen discusses threat modeling for press freedom, the weakening of reality as a constraint in politics, why journalists should stop interviewing Kellyanne Conway without journalistic rationale, and the lessons of David Fahrenthold's transparent reporting methods.
records.quote: We have taught our audiences that there is no such thing as a fact-check.

records.title: Maximize trust: Jay Rosen on covering the Trump administration
records.author: Vermont Public Radio staff
records.summary: Vermont Public Radio interviews Rosen about his advice for journalists covering the Trump administration. Rosen argues that maximizing trust, not just producing scoops, should be the press's primary strategic goal when facing a president who actively works to discredit journalism.
records.quote: When facing a president who actively works to discredit the press, maximizing public trust—not chasing scoops—should be journalism's primary strategic goal.

records.title: Jay Rosen addresses journalism's changing landscape
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Saint Michael's College reports on Rosen's lecture about journalism's changing landscape, titled 'What We Need From Journalists Now That Trump Has Been Elected,' delivered to the college community.
records.quote: What journalists need to provide now that Trump has been elected is a clearer account of what they stand for and what kind of information the public actually requires from them.

records.title: New reality (On the Media episode)
records.author: Brooke Gladstone and Bob Garfield
records.summary: A full On the Media episode featuring Rosen on Trump-era journalism, exploring how the new political reality requires the press to fundamentally rethink its assumptions, practices, and relationship with a president who actively works to undermine factual discourse.
records.quote: The new political reality requires the press to fundamentally rethink its assumptions and practices when covering a president who actively works to undermine factual discourse.

records.title: How the press can save itself in the age of Trump (Recode Media podcast)
records.author: Peter Kafka
records.summary: Rosen discusses with Peter Kafka how the press can survive and remain effective in the Trump era. He outlines strategies including threat modeling, shifting from the view from nowhere, and learning from David Fahrenthold's transparent reporting methods.
records.quote: The press can survive the Trump era by abandoning the view from nowhere, doing explicit threat modeling, and adopting the kind of transparent, show-your-work reporting that David Fahrenthold pioneered.

records.title: Journalists should stop interviewing Kellyanne Conway (Recode Media clip)
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A clip from the Recode Media podcast where Rosen argues that journalists should stop interviewing Kellyanne Conway because the journalistic rationale for booking her has evaporated -- she doesn't reliably represent Trump's positions and her interviews leave viewers more confused than before.
records.quote: Journalists should stop booking Kellyanne Conway because the original rationale has collapsed — she no longer reliably represents Trump's positions, and her interviews leave viewers more confused than before.

records.title: Why the view from nowhere is a harmful myth
records.author: Brooke Gladstone
records.summary: On the Media features Rosen explaining why 'the view from nowhere' -- journalism's claim to a God's-eye objectivity -- is a harmful myth that undermines trust and prevents reporters from telling audiences what they actually know to be true.
records.quote: The 'view from nowhere' — journalism's claim to a God's-eye objectivity — is a harmful myth that undermines trust and prevents reporters from telling audiences what they actually know to be true.

records.title: NYU and De Correspondent launch new laboratory for community supported investigative news
records.author: Josh Stearns
records.summary: Josh Stearns reports on the launch of the Membership Puzzle Project, a joint initiative between NYU and De Correspondent led by Rosen, which serves as a research laboratory for studying how community-supported models can sustain investigative journalism.
records.quote: The Membership Puzzle Project is a research laboratory studying how community-supported models can sustain investigative journalism — asking what it takes for news organizations to earn, and keep, the public's trust and financial support.

records.title: Jay Rosen on the view from nowhere
records.author: Stowe Boyd
records.summary: Stowe Boyd discusses and amplifies Rosen's concept of 'the view from nowhere,' explaining how journalism's claim to objectivity masks real ideological choices and why this matters more than ever in the Trump era.
records.quote: Journalism's pose of objectivity — what Rosen calls 'the view from nowhere' — doesn't eliminate ideological choices; it just makes them invisible, substituting the appearance of neutrality for the harder work of truth-telling.

records.title: Prospects for the American press under Trump, part two - PressThink
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the crisis in American political journalism following the election of Donald Trump. Rosen argues that the existing model of political reporting is inadequate and proposes several measures to improve the situation, including uncoupling the news agenda from Trump's Twitter feed, adopting an 'outside-in' reporting pattern, increasing unpredictability in coverage, and learning from the example of David Fahrenthold's investigative reporting. Rosen emphasizes the need for journalists to think politically about their profession, broaden their audience engagement, and build trust with a more diverse public.
records.quote: Learn from Fahrenthold! I can’t make it any clearer than that.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Winter is coming: prospects for the American press under Trump - PressThink
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen details a multifaceted crisis facing the American press, encompassing economic instability, declining public trust, a broken political journalism model, organized efforts to discredit mainstream media, the rise of 'verification in reverse,' and the influence of entertainment values. Rosen argues that these interconnected factors create a severe threat to the free press and its role as a check on power, exacerbated by Trump's presidency and the amplification of false narratives through social media. While acknowledging some positive signs, the overall tone is deeply pessimistic regarding the future of journalism.
records.quote: "Over the years, we’ve effectively brainwashed the core of our audience to distrust anything that they disagree with… Because the gatekeepers have lost all credibility in the minds of consumers, I don’t see how you reverse it."

records.title: The thin legitimacy of social media as a news source
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: In PBS NewsHour's Brief But Spectacular series, Rosen discusses the 'thin legitimacy' of Facebook as a news platform, distinguishing between thin and thick legitimacy in how platforms relate to users. He argues that choosing serious journalism is connected to the choice to continue being a democracy.
records.quote: I think it's really important for people to understand that we're not going to have serious journalism unless you choose it. Choosing serious journalism is related to an even more serious choice we have, which is choosing to continue to be a democracy.

records.title: Brief but Spectacular: Jay Rosen on the state of journalism in the age of Facebook
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Full transcript of Rosen's PBS Brief But Spectacular segment. He discusses how making media has become easier while getting people to read serious journalism has become harder. He introduces the concepts of 'thin legitimacy' (Facebook's terms of service) versus 'thick legitimacy' (genuine trust), and argues that choosing serious journalism is connected to choosing democracy.
records.quote: I think it's really important for people to understand that we're not going to have serious journalism unless you choose it. Choosing serious journalism is related to an even more serious choice we have, which is choosing to continue to be a democracy. Democracy is not a spectator sport. It's a participant thing.

records.title: Journalism: Where we went wrong and what we can do about it
records.author: Newmark JSchool
records.pub: Craig Newmark Graduate School of Journalism
records.summary: This text is an announcement of a post-election panel discussion featuring experts from various media outlets and academic backgrounds.  The panel will analyze shortcomings in election reporting and explore potential improvements to journalism, particularly political journalism, and new approaches to covering pivotal moments in American politics.
records.quote: Part 1 of 2 from our special post-election panel examining where reporting of the long election cycle fell short.

records.title: Media critic Jay Rosen on 2016 campaign coverage and the rise of Trump: "That's the way authoritarian societies work"
records.author: Paul Rosenberg
records.summary: Paul Rosenberg interviews Jay Rosen about his six-point framework for what the campaign press should not be neutral toward: participation, verification, deliberation, accountability, transparency (against opacity), and demagoguery. Rosen argues these values are already latent in journalism and need to be made explicit in an era of authoritarian politics.
records.quote: An opaque society that remains opaque -- opaque power holders, opaque institutions -- kills the desire for news at its root. Because why would you need constant news reports if there's nothing to be understood? That's the way authoritarian societies work.

records.title: Newspapers shouldn't apologize for telling the truth about Donald Trump
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: The article discusses a Florida newspaper's apology for being too critical of Donald Trump and uses this as a springboard to explore the challenges journalists face in maintaining objectivity while covering a figure who openly disregards political norms. It highlights the tension between seeking truth and avoiding criticism, arguing that the era of doing both is over, particularly when covering figures like Trump.
records.quote: Yes, I am seeking truth. But I’m also seeking refuge.

records.title: Asymmetry between the major parties fries the circuits of the mainstream press - PressThink
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the challenges faced by mainstream political journalism during the 2016 US presidential election campaign, particularly in covering Donald Trump. Rosen argues that the traditional journalistic framework, based on the assumption of symmetry between the two major parties, is inadequate for understanding Trump's unconventional candidacy and the resulting asymmetric polarization. He proposes three key propositions: 1) Political journalism relies on a shared mental picture of politics that assumes similar actors with 'warring philosophies'; 2) This symmetry is disrupted by the Republican Party's extreme stance and Trump's disregard for facts and norms; and 3) The media's failure to adapt to this asymmetry resembles 'technical debt', leading to a distorted representation of reality.
records.quote: A balanced treatment of an unbalanced phenomenon distorts reality.

records.title: Civic journalism, engaged journalism: Tracing the connections
records.author: Geneva Overholser
records.summary: Geneva Overholser traces the connections between the 1990s civic journalism movement and the 2010s engaged journalism practices for the Democracy Fund. She argues that while civic journalism was resisted by newsrooms in the 1990s (only 7% of AP managing editors strongly agreed with it), its core principle of richer conversation with audiences has come into widespread practice. The piece positions engaged journalism as a 'much-evolved descendant' of civic journalism.
records.quote: Within the two decades between then and now, the most basic principle of civic journalism has come into widespread usage. Virtually every newsroom has a richer conversation with its readers, viewers, listeners. In this way, civic journalism prevailed after all.
concepts: people formerly known as the audience

records.title: Donald Trump is crashing the system. Journalists need to build a new one.
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen argues that Trump's candidacy upends the assumptions underlying campaign journalism -- from the seriousness of policy proposals to the shaming effect of fact-checking. He urges journalists to recognize that normal rules don't apply and to develop novel, less predictable responses to an 'unbound' candidate who exploits and crashes the conventions of political reporting.
records.quote: Trump is crashing the system -- violating norms and assumptions that were previously taken for granted because so far, everyone who had reached the point of consideration had obeyed them.

records.title: Jay Rosen's NYU students dig deeper into disruption of news business
records.author: Various
records.summary: MediaShift reports on Studio 20 students at NYU, under Rosen's direction, researching the disruption of the news business. The piece highlights student projects examining new models for journalism sustainability and innovation.
records.quote: Studio 20 students at NYU are researching the disruption of the news business by examining new models for journalism sustainability, treating the crisis not as a problem to lament but as a design challenge to solve.

records.title: Jay Rosen, Public Radio's Loyal Critic
records.author: Current
records.summary: Jay Rosen is criticized for alleging timidity and false balance in public media journalism, but his main criticism is lazy reporting. The comments were made at a live recording of "The Pub" at Mercer University’s Center for Collaborative Journalism.
records.quote: New York University journalism professor Jay Rosen is hardly the only critic alleging timidity and false balance on the part of public media journalists.

records.title: Too Much Of Podcasting Is In New York
records.author: Current
records.summary: Jay Rosen is criticized for alleging timidity and false balance on the part of public media journalists, but his most cutting criticism is that of lazy reporting. He was the main attraction at a live recording of "The Pub" at Mercer University’s Center for Collaborative Journalism.
records.quote: New York University journalism professor Jay Rosen is hardly the only critic alleging timidity and false balance on the part of public media journalists.

records.title: The Pub #62: Jay Rosen on his love-hate relationship with public media
records.author: Adam Ragusea
records.summary: Current's The Pub podcast features Rosen discussing his complicated relationship with public media. He is famous for applying 'the view from nowhere' to NPR's impartial journalism but calls himself 'a total fan of public radio' and a 'loyal critic.' He criticizes NPR reporters for covering controversies without trying to discover which side is right, which he says is different from arbitrating who is right.
records.quote: I understand that people who work in the system get frustrated with me and think I don't know what I'm talking about, and a lot of times I don't. I'm just a listener who's pissed off.

records.title: The Many Ways Journalists Are Complicit in Political Polarization
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen argues that journalists are not the sole cause of political polarization but are active participants in it, especially when they distance themselves from conflicts their own conventions help sustain.
records.quote: Roy Blunt (R-MO) and moderator Chuck Todd appear on 'Meet the Press' in Washington, D.C., Sunday, Oct.

records.title: So I will try to explain why the Trump candidacy has been so confounding to our political press. - PressThink
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the changing dynamics of political journalism in the context of the 2016 US presidential election, particularly the impact of Donald Trump's campaign. Rosen argues that the traditional 'laws of political gravity' governing campaign coverage, based on shared assumptions within the political class and media, have broken down. This breakdown is attributed to Trump's disregard for established norms and the media's struggle to adapt, leading to homogeneity in coverage and a lack of clear purpose. Rosen contrasts this with the approach of Jorge Ramos, who demonstrates a clear sense of purpose and audience representation, illustrating an alternative model for political journalism.
records.quote: To put it a little more sharply, power-seeking and truth-seeking are different behaviors, and this is what creates the distinction between politics and journalism.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Tech is eating media
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen responds to John Herrman's essay on how the tech industry is absorbing the press. He argues that tech platforms may end up ingesting journalism without owning the problem of keeping real journalism going, and calls for more companies willing to take on the headache of editorial responsibility.
records.quote: Tech doesn't want the responsibility, solemnity or expense of owning the cranky news divisions that keep the press alive. But it refuses to slow the absorption rate. So it may end up ingesting the press without 'owning' the problem of how to keep real journalism going.

records.title: The Pub #43: Why public media are sponsoring polls, and how a CBC video went viral
records.author: Adam Ragusea
records.summary: The Pub podcast episode opens with Rosen's Twitter critique of WBUR for sponsoring horse-race polls and asks how polling fits with public media's mission. WBUR's Sam Fleming responds to Rosen's argument; the episode also features Marketplace host Kai Ryssdal.
records.quote: Rosen pushed back on public radio horse-race polls in a Twitter exchange with Dan Kennedy. WBUR Managing Director of News and Programming Sam Fleming responds on The Pub.

records.title: Adapting Journalism to the Digital Space
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: NYU's Studio 20: Digital First program prepares the next generation of journalists for the digital age by focusing on practical, project-based learning in collaboration with established media companies and digital startups. The program aims to equip students with skills to innovate in digital newsrooms, bridge business, editorial, tech, and audience challenges, and regain public trust.
records.quote: So what I want you to appreciate is if you can visualize the audience in that fragmented one way disconnected atomized State then you can realize how weird that is It's just a strange interval in human history that people were able to be combined in that way and for example their attention could be aggregated and sold as a commodity strange weird Behavior.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Misinterpreting Williams' misremembering
records.author: The Griffin Daily News
records.summary: Article discusses the Brian Williams controversy over false reporting and mentions Jay Rosen in relation to media credibility issues. The piece appears to reference Rosen's commentary on the Williams situation.
records.quote: The Brian Williams controversy raises deeper questions about media credibility and how news organizations handle false reporting by prominent figures.

records.title: Journalism Professor Rosen on changing nature of news
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Saint Michael's College announces a lecture by Rosen on the changing nature of news, part of the college's ongoing engagement with questions about journalism, democracy, and media evolution.
records.quote: The nature of news is changing in ways that force journalism to reckon with its relationship to democracy and the public it claims to serve.

records.title: Verstehen, was den Journalismus derzeit verändert
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Journalism is undergoing significant changes, and many struggle to understand them, often getting caught between condemning the new digital landscape or clinging to the old ways. The core issue lies in the fact that journalists are products of the changing society they are trying to understand, making it hard for them to objectively assess their own role. To better comprehend these shifts, media houses and journalists must observe society, technology, science, economics, and politics, recognizing patterns and connections rather than judging individual phenomena. Breaking down silos and fostering collaboration among various professionals is crucial to understanding and shaping the future of journalism and remaining relevant in a constantly evolving world.
records.quote: Die neuen Technologien und die neuen Märkte stellen den Journalismus vor fundamentale Herausforderungen.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Comment être au courant de ce qui change le journalisme ?
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: To stay informed about the evolving landscape of journalism, one should utilize various resources. Newsletters like La Matinale du Monde and Le 5 à 7 de l’AFP provide key information. Specialized websites such as Journalisme.com and Arrêt sur images offer in-depth analysis. Books like “Le Journalisme sans journalistes” and “La Fabrication de l’information” offer deeper insights. Blogs and Twitter accounts, including those of Daniel Schneidermann and Slate.fr, provide real-time updates and commentary.
records.quote: Quelles sont vos sources d’information sur l’avenir du journalisme?
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: The Studio 2.0 Program at NYU (directed by Jay Rosen and Clay Shirky) once again presents Open Studio Night!
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Studio 2.0 at NYU, co-directed by Jay Rosen and Clay Shirky, is hosting its second Open Studio Night. The event allows the program's twelve students to showcase their projects focused on the future of news, providing opportunities for interaction, feedback, and discussion. Attendees can learn about emerging trends in journalism. The event will be held on Wednesday, November 19, 2014, at the Studio 2.0 Room in New York, NY, and requires an RSVP. Studio 2.0 emphasizes experimentation and creation, encouraging students to build prototypes and design new services in response to changes in journalism. The program prioritizes invention and creation alongside critical thinking, with a focus on practical application.
records.quote: Come meet the future of journalism and the people making it happen.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: NYU professor Jay Rosen's roadmap for understanding the media landscape
records.author: Bleacher Report staff
records.summary: Bleacher Report covers Rosen's framework for understanding the changing media landscape, likely from a talk or presentation he gave about the forces reshaping news and the digital media environment.
records.quote: Rosen maps the forces reshaping the media landscape, offering a framework for understanding how digital disruption has transformed the relationship between news organizations, journalists, and the publics they once held captive.

records.title: Journalists need a point of view if they want to stay relevant
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen argues that extreme political polarization has made traditional journalistic objectivity obsolete. He contends that newsrooms should hire reporters with transparent points of view, call out falsehoods rather than hiding behind balance, and adopt accountability journalism models like ProPublica's -- or risk sliding into irrelevance.
records.quote: Intellectual honesty is a more reliable basis for trust than a ritualized objectivity. A clear voice is more valuable than a nonpartisan veneer.

records.title: Rosen's Trust Puzzler: What Explains Falling Confidence in the Press? - PressThink
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen explores the declining public trust in news media despite improvements in journalistic professionalism. Rosen presents several competing explanations, including the general decline in trust across institutions, the negative influence of bad actors in media, accusations of liberal bias, strategic manipulation of journalists ('working the refs'), and a potential misalignment between journalistic professionalization and public needs. Rosen concludes that none of these explanations fully capture the complexity of the issue and invites further discussion.
records.quote: So the puzzle is: how do these things fit together? More of a profession, more educated people going into journalism, a more desirable career, greater cultural standing (although never great pay) bigger staffs, more people to do the work … and the result of all that is less trust.

records.title: Open Studio Night, 2013: where our students present their final projects
records.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20
records.summary: These twelve presented their final projects in front of an East Village crowd with friends, family and digital journalism people from the New York media world. Boryana created an engagement strategy for Narratively’s core readership, which could expand their content outside the New York City area. Danielle Powell / Al Jazeera America : The problem: Repurposing TV documentary by putting it online is lame: there has to be a better way!
records.quote: Studio 20 students presented final projects to a New York media audience, tackling problems like audience engagement strategy and the challenge of repurposing TV documentary content for online platforms.

records.title: Real reporting is about revealing truth; not granting 'equal weight' to bogus arguments
records.author: Mike Masnick
records.summary: Mike Masnick uses Jay Rosen’s critique of he-said/she-said reporting to argue that journalism should report what is true rather than give equal weight to weak claims. The article centers on New York Times coverage of plagiarism allegations involving Rick Perlstein and Craig Shirley, and cites Margaret Sullivan’s public-editor response.
records.quote: Journalism should be about reporting what’s true, not just what people say is true.

records.title: When quoting both sides and leaving it there is the riskier call
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen critiques the 'he said, she said' approach in journalism, arguing that in situations where facts are verifiable, presenting both sides equally can be reckless and even misleading.  Rosen uses examples from the New York Times' coverage of plagiarism accusations against a book and the BBC's handling of climate change reporting to illustrate how clinging to false equivalence can confer legitimacy on false claims and distort the truth. Rosen contends that the old standard of 'no position' is increasingly risky and that newsrooms need to evolve beyond this approach.
records.quote: A newsroom that goes with “he said/she said” when a call can be made is engaged in reckless behavior that may easily blow up in its face.

records.title: This is just a stub for a PressThink post
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Jay Rosen plans to expand a post regarding The New York Times' need to explain why it published a front-page story about Russian officials releasing photos of soldiers in Ukraine that later proved false. Rosen's post initially appeared on Facebook and criticizes the newspaper's inadequate correction, specifically pointing out the lack of explanation for the new evidence and the Times' downplaying of its original assertion that Russia released the photos. Rosen contends that this failure hinders readers' ability to assess the images' credibility and suggests the State Department's reliance on the Times compromises the paper's value.
records.quote: The failure of the press to explain to its public the limited role that journalism can play in “solving” big public problems.

records.title: Blogging and the new public intellectual
records.author: Jay Rosen and Megan Garber
records.pub: Hannah Arendt Center at Bard College
records.summary: Rosen and Megan Garber discuss how blogging created a new form of public intellectual engagement, one that bypasses traditional academic and media gatekeepers. Published by the Hannah Arendt Center at Bard College, the piece connects blogging to Arendt's ideas about public life and thinking in the open.
records.quote: Blogging created a new form of public intellectual engagement that bypasses traditional academic and media gatekeepers, connecting the act of thinking in the open to Hannah Arendt's ideas about public life.

records.title: ISOJ 2014/2019 speaker: Jay Rosen
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.pub: ISOJ / Knight Center, University of Texas at Austin
records.summary: Speaker profile for Rosen at the International Symposium on Online Journalism (ISOJ), where he participated in both the 2014 and 2019 editions of the conference discussing online journalism, digital media, and press reform.
records.quote: The ongoing evolution of online journalism demands sustained critical attention to press reform and the democratic responsibilities of digital media institutions.

records.title: Pierre Omidyar plunges first $50m into media venture with Glenn Greenwald
records.author: Ed Pilkington
records.summary: Pierre Omidyar, founder of eBay, is investing $50 million (the first tranche of a $250 million commitment) in a new journalism venture, First Look Media, with Glenn Greenwald. This venture will consist of both a non-profit (501(c)(3)) news organization and a for-profit media technology company. The for-profit entity will support the non-profit's independent journalism. The venture's structure is compared to that of the Guardian Media Group and Bloomberg News, with Jay Rosen, a NYU professor advising the venture, highlighting its innovative funding model.
records.quote: Any profits generated by this company will go towards supporting the independent journalism.

records.title: A First Look at NewCo's structure - PressThink
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Pierre Omidyar's $50 million investment establishes First Look Media, a new media organization comprised of both for-profit and non-profit entities. The non-profit arm will focus on independent, public-interest journalism, while the for-profit arm will develop new media technologies. Profits from the for-profit entity will support the non-profit's journalistic mission, offering a new model for sustainable, independent journalism.
records.quote: First Look Media is made up of several entities, including a company established to develop new media technology and a separate nonprofit journalism organization. The journalism operation, which will be incorporated as a 501(c)(3), will enjoy editorial independence, and any profits eventually earned by the technology company are committed to support First Look’s mission of independent journalism.

records.title: A first look at NewCo's business, journalism structure
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen examines the business and editorial structure of Pierre Omidyar's First Look Media, analyzing its dual structure of a for-profit tech company and a nonprofit journalism organization. The piece, syndicated from PressThink, discusses what Omidyar's venture means for investigative journalism.
records.quote: First Look Media's dual structure—a for-profit tech company housing a nonprofit journalism organization—represents Pierre Omidyar's bet that investigative journalism can be sustained by separating its commercial and editorial functions.

records.title: A News Organization That Rejects the View From Nowhere
records.author: Jay Rosen, Conor Friedersdorf
records.summary: Rosen discusses a new $250 million news organization founded by Pierre Omidyar that will not adhere to traditional journalistic objectivity. The article features an interview with Jay Rosen, a media theorist and critic of the 'View From Nowhere,' who is joining the organization as an advisor. Rosen discusses the challenges and implications of implementing his 'View From Somewhere' theory, which emphasizes transparency about journalists' perspectives and priors, while maintaining high verification standards. The interview explores the tension between individual journalist perspectives, organizational viewpoints, and the need for editorial oversight, touching upon issues of ideological diversity, accountability, and the role of readers.
records.quote: We can insist on the struggle to tell it like it is without also insisting on the View from Nowhere. The two are not connected.

records.title: Studio 20
records.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20
records.summary: ¶ ● (L-R) Students Nuha Abujaber, Jesse Kipp, and Simran Khosla From Amy Webb, Head of Webbmedia Group This past spring, Studio 20 students in their second term partnered with a diverse group of companies for a project focusing on networked reporting. I think it shows the interconnectedness between a lot of companies and makes you realize it’s not just a series of start-ups going through similar cycles; there’s actually many key players and investors who really shape the ecosystem. note: NYU instructor Jonathan Soma will be featured in an upcoming Q&A on this blog soon - stay tuned.)
records.quote: Studio 20 students partnered with a diverse group of companies to explore networked reporting, revealing that the media ecosystem is shaped by many key players and investors whose interconnections run deeper than a series of independent startups cycling through similar phases.

records.title: Open Studio night: Dec. 12, 6 to 8 pm at NYU. Would you like to come?
records.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20
records.summary: And… Josh Benton, director of Harvard’s Nieman Lab, will present his slide show: “The Year in Innovation." Our graduating students present their final projects in innovation, which they have spent six months working on. So please make plans to be there: Thursday, December 12 at NYU Journalism, 20 Cooper Square, New York, NY, 7th floor.
records.quote: NYU Journalism's Studio 20 graduating students present their final innovation projects, with Josh Benton of Harvard's Nieman Lab presenting his slide show on the year's most significant developments in news innovation.

records.title: Jay Rosen, the view from nowhere, and 'arrogance born of monopoly'
records.author: Caroline O'Donovan
records.summary: Nieman Lab highlights Rosen's PressThink blog post using the Old and New Testaments as a framework for discussing the age of mass media. Rosen argues that journalism's 'new testament fundamentalism' -- its rigid objectivity -- was 'arrogance born of monopoly' that is now giving way as journalists begin blogging, using social media, and recognizing that their business model is broken.
records.quote: A kind of new testament fundamentalism common in journalism from the 1970s to the 1990s held form through the early years of blogging in this century. It felt scorn for the more opinionated style and ridiculed its followers as 'echo chambers.' It defined itself as 'the traditional' and dismissed everyone else as marginal. This was arrogance born of monopoly.

records.title: Old testament and new testament journalism - PressThink
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: The article contrasts two forms of journalism, "old testament" and "new testament," characterized by political argument intertwined with information and the separation of facts and values, respectively. It argues that both forms are necessary and that the rise of the internet has allowed the old testament form to gain new life, while weaknesses in new testament traditions have been exposed. Rosen sees a potential reconciliation and détente between the two, acknowledging the virtues and vices of each.
records.quote: Each form can spur the other, keep it honest.

records.title: Studio 20
records.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20
records.summary: Some quotes from the conversation: “I have a habit of creating jobs for myself.” “The best journalists are marketers.” “I get so many ideas on things from Twitter.” “Suggest an alternative and how you’re two steps ahead - that’s golden.” Professor Jay Rosen was interviewed by Callie in 2010. Last night, the tables were turned as Rosen discussed ideas around innovation (and a bit of politics too), with the final takeaway being: Figure out what needs to be done and do it, regardless of whether it fits with the “image” you have of yourself and your position. That, right there, is the encapsulation of what we do at Studio 20.
records.quote: Figure out what needs to be done and do it, regardless of whether it fits with the image you have of yourself and your position.

records.title: The NSA's next move: silencing university professors?
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A Johns Hopkins professor's blog post criticizing the NSA was requested to be taken down by the university's dean, raising concerns about academic freedom. The request, seemingly originating from the university's Applied Physics Laboratory with ties to the NSA, was later retracted after media attention, highlighting the vulnerability of academic freedom to government pressure and the university's initial failure to uphold its principles.
records.quote: The institution failed in the clutch. That it rectified it later in the day is welcome news, but I won't be cheering until we have answers that befit a great institution like Johns Hopkins, where graduate education was founded on these shores.

records.title: The awayness problem
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: An analysis of what Rosen calls "the awayness problem" in journalism — how the press can be physically present yet intellectually absent from the stories it covers. Published in Columbia Journalism Review.
records.quote: The press can be physically present at a story while remaining intellectually absent from it — Rosen's 'awayness problem' names journalism's tendency to cover events without ever grasping what is actually at stake.

records.title: Summer reading 2013: Getting the connections right
records.author: Sarah Darville
records.summary: Nieman Lab excerpts Rosen's 1996 book 'Getting the Connections Right' as part of its Summer Reading series. The excerpt contrasts journalism's obsession with 'getting the separations right' (editorial vs. business, facts vs. values, news vs. opinion) with Rosen's argument that the deeper challenge is getting the connections right -- between journalism and the public, between facts and values, between the editorial product and civic life.
records.quote: Suppose that getting the separations right isn't the central problem. This is what public journalism is saying: getting the connections right is the deeper challenge in journalism right now.

records.title: Defining journalists - and their rights
records.author: The Griffin Daily News
records.summary: Article discusses the definition of journalists and their rights in the context of citizen journalism and blogger protections. Mentions Jay Rosen of NYU's journalism program in the context of discussing citizen journalism and how it relates to traditional journalism.
records.quote: The rise of citizen journalism and bloggers forces a reckoning with who counts as a journalist and what legal protections should follow from that status.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Studio 20 gets an assignment from Quartz News
records.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20
records.summary: ¶ ● Studio 20 gets an assignment from Quartz News These specs were sent by the editors of Quartz to Professor Jay Rosen as part of Studio 20’s networked reporting project in spring 2013. Jay Rosen responded with his presentation, Designs for a Networked Beat , May 13, 2013. The problem: As well as Quartz’s longer-term obsessions, we often obsess on shorter-term stories that turn into big news for a few days or weeks, but that we don’t know in advance are going to become big.
records.quote: Quartz editors identified a key editorial challenge: stories that turn into big news for days or weeks often cannot be identified in advance as significant, making networked beat reporting difficult to plan.

records.title: Studio 20's Networked Reporting Project
records.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20
records.summary: We had six partners: ProPublica, The Wall Street Journal Social Media Desk, Mashable.com’s gaming beat, PandoDaily.com, Fast Company and Quartz News (qz.com). Each came to class and explained  the problems they have making more productive use of a networked approach. The Wall Street Journal Social Media desk A tool for locating likely sources within an established Twitter network.
records.quote: Studio 20's networked reporting project partnered with six news organizations—including ProPublica, The Wall Street Journal Social Media Desk, and Quartz—to explore how journalism can make more productive use of a networked approach.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Press Publish 3: Jay Rosen on the public, how the press thinks, and the production of innocence
records.author: Joshua Benton
records.summary: Joshua Benton interviews Rosen for the Nieman Lab Press Publish podcast, covering his entry into journalism academia, the influence of James Carey and Neil Postman, the Lippmann-Dewey debate, the rise and quasi-fall of civic journalism, why horse race journalism needs improvement, and what Rosen calls 'the production of innocence' -- journalism's way of distancing itself from its own role in political outcomes.
records.quote: Jay has been so valuable to the field -- he's an inside-outside voice pricking journalism when it needs to be pricked. His ideas, once shouted down in newsrooms, have become something closer to received wisdom for many.

records.title: Studio 20
records.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20
records.summary: ¶ ● Studio 20 would like to extend a big thanks to everyone who made it out for last night’s Open Studio presentations and helped make the night a big success! You can find more info on the ten innovative presentations below: Kat Patke: User-to-User Community Building with the Huffington Post Laura Edwins: Decoding User Engagement with the Christian Science Monitor Silva Shih: Data Viz On The Go with Quartz Nadja Popovich: Re-framing elections with the Guardian US Khwezi Magwaza and Patrice Peck: PUSH New Media: Collaborative Innovation (with test partner Ebony.com) Yoo Eun Lee: Video Template with Global Voices Tracy Levy: Online Video: How What Why with Tablet Tando Ntunja: Clients-As-Storytellers/Clients-As-Reporters with Safe Horizons ATP Ana Maria Benedetti: Dreamers Across America with UNIVISION 0 notes
records.quote: Studio 20's Open Studio showcased ten innovative student projects spanning user engagement, data visualization, election framing, and collaborative media partnerships.

records.title: Open Studio Night: An Invitation.
records.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20
records.summary: PUSH worked with Ebony.com as a test client to develop an original man-on-the-street video series, among other creative multimedia projects. The new template will encourage contributors to package existing content (text and images) into video news clips. She has been working on funding, design and community outreach, including advisory sessions with Homicide Watch.
records.quote: Studio 20 projects like PUSH developed original multimedia series for real clients such as Ebony.com, with students working on video production, community outreach, and funding alongside editorial work.

records.title: Lewis Dvorkin fields some good questions from Studio 20
records.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20
records.summary: ¶ ● Lewis Dvorkin fields some good questions from Studio 20 Lewis Dvorkin recently stopped in Studio 20 to talk with first year masters students about innovation in the digital age. “We felt like equals, which is really cool when you’re talking to the head honcho of online media at Forbes,” notes Studio-20er Simran Khosla . Well, it’s far more than making phone calls, writing a story and going home.
records.quote: Journalism today is far more than making phone calls, writing a story and going home.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Ungovernable reality, not Candy Crowley, threatens Obama and Romney
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the dynamics between presidential campaigns, the Commission on Presidential Debates, and journalists moderating debates. It highlights the tension between the desire of campaigns to control the debate format and the journalist's role in pressing for answers and holding candidates accountable. Rosen explores different moderator styles, from the 'Vanishing Moderator' to a more active interlocutor, and argues that the lack of consensus on the ideal approach reflects a deeper question about whether presidential power needs an independent check.
records.quote: The debates in their current form are a temporary alliance among three players: the campaigns of the major-party candidates for president, the Commission on Presidential Debates and the journalists who are chosen to moderate and maintain order.

The article proposes a new journalistic beat focused on wicked problems, suggesting that it should be a network, pattern-based, global, and reliant on diverse perspectives rather than solely on expert opinions. This beat would highlight the process of grappling with these problems, focusing on narratives of getting stuck and getting unstuck, and acknowledging the role of denial in hindering progress.

records.title: Four Types of Scoops

records.summary: Jonathan Stray identifies four ways journalists beat the competition: exclusive leaks from confidential sources, enterprise reporting through public records and legwork, expert interviews, and original analysis. He argues that enterprise reporting — digging through obscure records and finding on-the-record sources — is the most valuable form, yet also the most threatened by the economics of modern journalism.
records.quote: We tend to venerate this kind of scoop, but the journalist is often just a transcription service.

records.title: Verification in reverse': A chat with Jay Rosen
records.author: Scott Rosenberg
records.summary: This article presents a conversation between Scott Rosenberg and Jay Rosen about "verification in reverse," a process where previously established truths are challenged. The discussion centers on a Huffington Post article concerning a letter from NASA retirees criticizing the agency's climate research. Rosen defines verification in reverse and explains how it poses a significant problem for journalists who must balance reporting controversies with upholding factual accuracy. He highlights the conflict between science journalists who consider climate change a settled issue and political journalists who focus on partisan debates, emphasizing the reluctance of many political journalists to confront climate change denialism. Rosen suggests that journalists should not only investigate what happened but also determine whether denialism is involved and treat this as news itself.
records.quote: The phenomenon of “verification in reverse” poses a special problem for journalists. On the one hand, they are supposed to report what people are saying. They are supposed to bring us the news of controversies, protests, disagreements. “Conflict makes news,” and all that. On the other hand, verification is their business. If they cannot support that, they cannot support themselves or their users. They are socially useless, in fact, if they cannot stand up for verification.

records.title: Anatomy of a Facebook Fail (mine)
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen recounts a Facebook mishap involving an event invitation. Intending to invite spouses of friends using the "suggest invitees" feature, they accidentally invited thousands of people, including all their friends and their spouses' friends. This resulted in a flood of notifications and inquiries. Due to the event's public setting, Rosen couldn't uninvite everyone or delete the event initially.  With a friend's help, they changed the privacy settings and deleted the event. Rosen shares lessons learned, including the importance of caution with the "select all" feature, carefully checking privacy settings, acting quickly to address problems, seeking help when needed, and following up with those legitimately invited.  Rosen encourages others to share their social media failures.
records.quote: The great thing about this whole episode is that it has sparked a fascinating conversation among my friends about the new rules of friendship, privacy and etiquette in the age of Facebook.

records.title: A Brief Theory of the Republican Party (2012)
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Before the 1980s, the Republican Party was similar to the Democratic Party. The Great Realignment saw Ronald Reagan build a new coalition consisting of socially conservative Christians, the wealthy, and the Southern working class, united by exploiting social tensions. The Republican Party then shifted its focus from economic to social issues, fostering resentment towards groups considered the "liberal elite." After Reagan, the party found a new unifying force in attacking the government, though this created internal tension regarding popular programs. The Republican Party is now in crisis, divided by its inability to shrink the government while still protecting popular programs. The party's future is uncertain, possibly fracturing or fading away without a new way to unite its factions.
records.quote: The party is going to have to decide whether its future lies with the evangelical Christians of the heartland or with the secular, pro-business voters of the suburbs. It cannot be the party of both Rick Santorum and Mitt Romney. It has to choose.

records.title: Serious Journalism in the Age of Digital Networks
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Journalism is undergoing a significant transformation due to technological advancements, evolving economic models, shifting audience expectations, and open-source culture. These changes present both challenges and opportunities. Serious journalism, upholding principles like transparency, accuracy, and accountability, is crucial, especially in the digital age. This involves curating information, fostering community engagement, and providing tools for civic action. Journalists must collaborate, innovate, and adapt, embracing new technologies and storytelling formats. A strong ethical foundation is essential to navigate the complexities of information in the digital landscape. Journalism students are entering a dynamic field and have the opportunity to shape the future of journalism by embracing new approaches, technologies, and community engagement strategies.
records.quote: Their comparative advantage is no longer in telling us what is happening, because we can learn this from multiple other sources. Rather, their real value-added will be in investigating and explaining why something is happening.

records.title: Why Political Coverage Is Broken
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Political journalism's focus on the "Game Story" hinders understanding of the political world. This story prioritizes politicians' strategies and actions within a competitive game, neglecting policy substance, impact on citizens, and diverse perspectives. Rosen argues this approach, often rooted in objective journalism, results in a detached view that makes politics less accessible and more alienating. The solution proposed is a journalism that interprets political struggles, examines policy impacts, and centers on citizens, ultimately fostering a better understanding of the issues. This shift requires a more engaged journalism that helps citizens understand the world, rather than simply reporting on the political game.
records.quote: If you’re still reporting on the game, you’re still part of the problem. Because the game is not the substance. And the substance is what matters.

records.title: Three different kinds of context were missing
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen identifies three crucial kinds of context often missing in discussions of intellectual history, using Hayek's work as a case study. The first is the specific problem Hayek was addressing, which was how a society of free individuals could achieve optimal resource allocation despite dispersed knowledge. Second, the relevant intellectual tradition, namely the Austrian school, and Hayek's engagement with Mises and subjectivism, is essential. Lastly, the context of the arguments within Hayek's essay "Economics and Knowledge" itself clarifies his focus on coordinating decentralized knowledge through the market process rather than individual plan optimization. Rosen emphasizes that these contextual elements shape the interpretation of Hayek's ideas, differentiating them from the concerns of others like Robbins.
records.quote: When you’re an expert in a field, you forget what it was like to be a novice. You forget that the things that seem obvious to you are not at all obvious to someone who’s just starting out. And so you fail to explain the context of your requests.

records.title: A theme in responses to critics found in the…
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A recurring pattern in responses to criticism involves claiming the critic "just doesn't get it," often employed to avoid directly addressing the substance of the critique. This tactic is frequently used by politicians, pundits, and online commentators. Rosen identifies two potential causes: a simple misunderstanding stemming from differing ideas of clarity, or deliberate vagueness in the initial statement. The latter allows speakers to maintain flexibility, deflecting criticism by claiming misinterpretation or difficulty on the critic's part, enabling them to present ideas without the risk of being clearly contradicted. Rosen observes this trend particularly in online discussions about social media, blogging, and politics, prompting an examination of its frequent use.
records.quote: This way of responding to critics seems to immunize Christianity against any rational criticism. For any objection, no matter how powerful, one can always draw a distinction that the critic has failed to draw.

records.quote: But in the real world, when a man is accused of rape by two different women and he refuses to answer any questions about it, we have a different word for that. And the word is not “smear campaign.” The word is “guilty as hell.”
