records.title: Jay Rosen on why climate science reporting is so bad
records.author: Joe Romm
records.summary: Joe Romm at ThinkProgress reprints Rosen's extended comment explaining why climate science reporting fails. Rosen argues that journalism's commitment to neutrality breaks down when confronting manufactured controversies like climate denial, because the press has no instructions for how to react when 'report both sides' reaches its natural limits. He identifies the problem as structural: the same ideology that protects journalism from government also prevents it from calling out illegitimate debate.
records.quote: Neutrality and objectivity carry no instructions for how to react when they reach their natural limits. And so journalists tend to deny that there are such limits. But with this denial they've violated the code of the truth-teller because these limits are real. See the problem?

records.title: Arming us not with knowledge of, but acquaintance with
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Many high school students lack even a basic understanding of fundamental concepts such as the Constitution, Bill of Rights, and scientific theories, according to the National Assessment of Educational Progress results. A significant percentage of students score below basic in U.S. History, Civics, and Science, indicating a failure to grasp essential knowledge. Rosen believes this lack of education harms both students and the country, hindering informed participation in democracy and the ability to critically evaluate information. Addressing this issue requires a renewed focus on educating youth to ensure a healthy and functional democracy.
records.quote: We are armed not with knowledge of things, but acquaintance with them.

records.title: Jay Rosen's Advice to the Next Generation of Journalists
records.author: Jay Rosen / Studio 20
records.summary: It took a while before those outside of the government began gaining access to information and developed ways to communicate what went on behind closed doors, and when they did, they began changing the culture of news around diplomacy: Let’s jump ahead to Paris in 1919 and the Peace Conference that ended World War I. At  previous international conferences intended to conclude wars and settle  borders, the diplomats would negotiate in secret and emerge weeks later  with a result which was then conveyed to the home countries as a more  or less finished product. Professional journalism,  which dates from the 1920s, has lived its entire life during this phase,  but let me say it again: this is what your generation has a chance to  break free from.
records.quote: At previous international conferences, diplomats negotiated in secret and presented results as finished products; when professional journalism gained access, it began changing the culture of news around diplomacy by communicating what happened behind closed doors.

records.title: The Journalist Formerly Known as The Media (M)
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: The article explores how the definition of "media" is changing and the impact on those who work in journalism. As new forms of information dissemination emerge, like blogging and citizen journalism, Rosen questions the need for a new term to describe journalists who uphold traditional journalistic principles and work within established media institutions. Rosen proposes calling these individuals "traditional journalists" or "professional journalists" to differentiate them within the evolving media landscape and acknowledge their continued significance.
records.quote: The people formerly known as the audience are those who were on the receiving end of a media system that ran one way, in a broadcasting pattern, with high entry fees and a few firms competing to speak loudly while the rest of the population listened in isolation from one another— and who today are not in a situation like that at all.

records.quote: Journalists covering campaigns should start by asking voters what they need to know to cast an informed vote, rather than defaulting to horse-race coverage that serves the profession's interests more than the public's.

records.title: The Citizen’s Agenda in Campaign Coverage: Ten Steps to a Better Narrative
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen proposes a "Citizen's Agenda" approach to campaign coverage, arguing that journalists should prioritize voters' concerns rather than focusing solely on the "horse race." Rosen outlines a ten-step process for creating and implementing this agenda, involving extensive community engagement, feedback loops, and prioritizing voters' questions in campaign reporting. Rosen contends that this approach improves the quality of political discourse and counters the negative aspects of typical election coverage, even acknowledging potential conflict with candidates who might resist this approach.
records.quote: What does the electorate want the candidates to be discussing as they campaign for votes in this year’s election?
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.quote: Rather than relying on daily dispatches that assume no prior knowledge, journalism should maintain persistent, updatable background documents that give ongoing stories the context they need.

records.title: Jay Rosen takes aim at 'horse race journalism'

Rosen advocates for a 'citizens' agenda' approach, where journalists focus on the issues that matter most to the public. He also discusses the role of the internet and social media in news consumption, and the challenges and opportunities they present for traditional media organizations.
records.quote: horse race journalism is sort of a a reusable model for how to do campaign coverage in which you focus on who's going to win rather than um what the country needs to settle by electing a prime minister

records.title: PressThink: The Afghanistan War Logs Released by Wikileaks, the World's First Stateless News Organization
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the Wikileaks release of the Afghanistan war logs, focusing on Wikileaks' strategy of releasing documents to select major newspapers while simultaneously posting them online. Rosen discusses the implications of Wikileaks' stateless nature and its challenge to traditional notions of journalistic verification and the power dynamic between the state, the press, and a new type of non-state media organization. He also explores the potential for large-scale revelations to generate surprisingly muted public reactions, suggesting a cognitive dissonance in how we expect investigative journalism to impact public discourse and policy.
records.quote: We tend to think: big revelations mean big reactions. But if the story is too big and crashes too many illusions, the exact opposite occurs.

records.title: The Ideology of Journalists: A Response to Jay Rosen
records.author: Marc Ambinder
records.summary: This article responds to Jay Rosen's advice for journalists, largely agreeing with his emphasis on transparency and accountability but adding considerations about judgment and the limits of self-disclosure. The author argues that while journalists should strive for transparency and avoid opacity as a tool of power, they must also recognize trade-offs and acknowledge the complexities of personal bias.  The author questions the feasibility and value of extensive personal ideological disclosure, suggesting that a journalist's body of work should speak for itself and that excessive self-reflection can detract from journalistic practice.
records.quote: I don't like people who lie, cheat, or steal, or who dissemble for the sake of acquiring or using power, or who think narrowly about everything rather than broadly; who hold fast to dogma; who are quick to condemn those who refuse to condemn.

records.title: Objectivity as a Form of Persuasion: A Few Notes for Marcus Brauchli
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen argues that journalistic objectivity, as traditionally practiced, is a form of persuasion designed to build trust by appearing unadorned and fact-based.  However, this approach, characterized by phrases like “just the facts,” is inherently flawed because all journalism involves judgment. Rosen proposes shifting away from the "View from Nowhere" toward greater transparency and a plurality of approaches, allowing journalists to express viewpoints while maintaining rigorous reporting standards. This shift is necessary to address declining trust in the press in the era of the internet and audience atomization.
records.quote: Reporting has authority because the reporter did the work.

records.title: What is the actual ideology of our political press?
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen challenges the common perception that the ideology of the US political press is easily definable as either liberal or conservative. Rosen argues that the press's apparent ideology is far more complex, shaped by factors such as journalists' cosmopolitanism, their pursuit of authoritative narratives that disrupt established viewpoints, and their inherent preference for 'good stories' which often highlight negative events. This results in a complex dynamic where journalists, while often personally liberal, generate narratives that are not consistently aligned with either the left or right. Rosen illustrates this complexity through analysis of journalist behaviors and the contrasting interpretations of their work from both sides of the political spectrum.
records.quote: In the sphere of deviance we find “political actors and views which journalists and the political mainstream of society reject as unworthy of being heard.” As in the sphere of consensus, neutrality isn’t the watchword here; journalists maintain order by either keeping the deviant out of the news entirely or identifying it within the news frame as unacceptable, radical, or just plain impossible…

records.title: PressThink: How the Backchannel Has Changed the Game for Conference Panelists
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen discusses the impact of the internet and social media on audience engagement, particularly at conferences.  Rosen, Jay Rosen, introduces the concept of "audience atomization overcome," describing how audiences, once isolated, are now connected horizontally (peer-to-peer) and vertically (to speakers/institutions). This interconnectedness significantly increases the risk for unprepared speakers, raising the bar for presentations. The article then provides ten strategies for avoiding negative feedback in this new context, emphasizing pre-event planning, audience engagement, and incorporating audience feedback during presentations.
records.quote: The people formerly known as the audience, once connected up to big institutions and centers of power, but not across to one another, have overcome their own atomization, which was a normal condition during the age of mass media. With the rise of social media and mobile devices they are now connected horizontally, peer to peer, at the same time as they connect vertically: to the news, the program, the speaker, the spectacle.

records.title: Eight Key Terms For Determining Legitimacy In Journalism
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Legitimacy in journalism hinges on several key terms. Expertise is demonstrated through experience and knowledge. Independence, crucial for separating news from propaganda, requires journalists to avoid being swayed by external agendas. Objectivity involves presenting stories fairly and accurately. Transparency demands that journalists disclose their sources and methods. Accountability requires taking responsibility for errors and upholding ethical standards. Impartiality means treating all parties equally. Serving the public interest, by providing relevant information and promoting informed debate, is essential. Verification, through cross-referencing and fact-checking, is crucial for maintaining credibility, especially in the era of misinformation. These elements work together to ensure news is trustworthy and serves the public good.
records.quote: The primary obligation of a journalist is to the public.

records.title: What to reject when you’re rejecting the wisdom of crowds: tips for debunkers
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: When considering the wisdom of crowds, it's crucial to avoid blanket statements and recognize the nuanced nature of crowd behavior. It's essential to reject the notion that all crowds or their decisions are inherently wise or always wrong. Factors like emotion, misinformation, and groupthink can sway crowds. Individuals shouldn't automatically assume they are correct when disagreeing with a crowd, nor should they always go against the crowd. There are varying types of crowd wisdom, and the ability to discern when a crowd is wise isn't always obvious. Learning from crowds, even "dumb" ones, is possible, and blindly following or rejecting the crowd should be avoided. The key lies in understanding when and what aspects of crowd behavior should be rejected.
records.quote: When you’re thinking about whether to trust a crowd, the question isn’t whether you believe in the wisdom of crowds or not; the question is, are the conditions right for the crowd to be wise?

records.title: Get there by clicking a link and the New York Times paywall disappears
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen expresses dissatisfaction with the New York Times paywall, noting that it is easily bypassed by clicking a link, unlike the Wall Street Journal's paywall. Rosen, while supporting the NYT's right to generate revenue, questions the effectiveness of a paywall that can be circumvented. They suggest the paywall might serve different purposes, such as targeting a specific audience or encouraging subscriptions to RSS feeds, and propose that the NYT clarify its intent. Rosen ultimately believes the NYT should either fix its paywall to prevent access via links or be transparent about its function.

records.title: How to Know If You Are Behaving Ethically as a Journalist: Jay Rosen’s Checklist
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Jay Rosen's checklist offers a framework for ethical journalism, focusing on the impact of actions rather than perfect moral behavior. The checklist, developed for students and newsrooms, comprises eight key components: transparency regarding methods and motives; admitting and correcting mistakes; involving the community in newsgathering; showing empathy and humanity towards subjects; actively listening to audiences and sources; ensuring fairness and proportionality in reporting; practicing humility and self-doubt; and demonstrating courage. These principles aim to guide journalists in adapting their ethical practices amidst changes in the field, encouraging accountability and a rational, transparent approach to reporting.
records.quote: If you were on the receiving end of the story you are reporting and writing, would you feel that you were being treated fairly?
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.summary: Rosen reflects on a conversation about Obama's call for transparency and expresses skepticism about its feasibility given the political system's reliance on secrecy. They are concerned that the same people who initially praised Obama's transparency call are now defending the White House's spin tactics, questioning the Church of the Savvy's stance on the issue. Rosen believes that prioritizing the perceived greater good can erode transparency over time, making them distrustful of any statements made on the topic by this group.
records.quote: I suspect the press embraces savviness because it makes them feel like insiders. The rest of us may believe a candidate when he says he will do something, but they know better. They’ve seen it all before.

records.title: What I Told the Man from Politics Daily
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: The Republican Party in Texas faces internal challenges, despite its history of electoral success. The party struggles with a primary problem, as run-offs often push the party toward extremes, silencing moderate voices. Moderate Republicans sometimes vote in the Democratic primary. However, the party's conservative principles, like low taxes and regulations, remain popular, and the state's growing population brings in new conservative voters. The Republican Party can succeed in Texas by addressing the primary issues and re-integrating moderate viewpoints. The future of the party in Texas is promising, but requires effort.
records.quote: What you are witnessing is the de-bugging of the software that runs in the heads of Washington journalists. The software is called, “the view from nowhere.”

records.title: Sources of subsidy in the production of news: a list
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: The economics of the news business involves various subsidies because news production is often not profitable on its own. Jay Rosen poses the question of what are the main and emerging sources of these subsidies. Examples include unpaid citizen labor, foundation grants, corporate underwriting, government support, losses absorbed by news organizations, profits from related companies, and advertising revenue. Rosen seeks input from readers to compile a comprehensive list of these subsidies, which are essential for the existence of the news system as it is known.
records.quote: By subsidy I mean something that lowers the cost of producing the news, and thus encourages more of it than the market would otherwise support. These are things that make journalism cheaper to do.

records.quote: Rosen argues that 'explainer' journalism represents a new niche on the demand side of news — where the journalist's job is to meet audiences where they are and help them understand complex topics.

records.quote: Rosen and Winer discuss WordPress's growing financial scale and the week in ReadWriteWeb-flagged news experiments.

records.title: Rebooting the News #15
records.author: Jay Rosen; Dave Winer
records.summary: Episode 15. Dave reports back from the Reboot conference in Copenhagen; Jay leads the show-notes write-up. The conversation surveys the European context for the kinds of news experiments Rebooting The News has been chronicling on the US side.
records.quote: Rosen and Winer on the Reboot conference in Copenhagen and the state of online news experimentation in mid-2009.

records.title: Modern media madness: Brooke Gladstone and Jay Rosen on Bill Moyers Journal
records.author: Bill Moyers; Brooke Gladstone; Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen and On The Media host Brooke Gladstone appear together on Bill Moyers Journal to decode media spin and discuss 'modern media madness.' The segment examines how the press covers politics and the ways media narratives are constructed and reinforced.
records.quote: The press constructs and reinforces political narratives through media spin, and journalists need tools to decode how those narratives are built and sustained.

records.title: Rebooting the News #7
records.author: Jay Rosen; Dave Winer
records.summary: Episode 7 of the weekly Rebooting The News podcast, an open conversation between NYU journalism professor Jay Rosen and software developer / blogger Dave Winer about the future of news in the post-print, social-web era. Show notes are minimal; the canonical archive is the rebootnews.wordpress.com post.
records.quote: Weekly 40-plus minute Rebooting The News conversation between Jay Rosen and Dave Winer, recorded April 26, 2009.

records.title: "He Said, She Said" Journalism: Are We Done With That Yet?
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen criticizes he said, she said journalism as a newsroom refuge that avoids judging competing truth claims, using AIG bailout coverage to argue that reporters should move beyond stenographic dispute framing.
records.quote: There I am, sitting at the breakfast table, with my coffee and a copy of the New York Times, in the classic newspaper reading position from before the Web.

records.title: Audience Atomization Overcome: Why the Net Erodes the Authority of the Press
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen uses the spheres of consensus, legitimate debate, and deviance to argue that the internet weakens press authority by letting publics challenge which voices journalists classify as fringe.
records.quote: Take a sheet of paper and make a big circle in the middle.

records.title: Is "He Said, She Said, We're Clueless" Coverage Dying?
records.author: Chris Mooney
records.summary: The author critiques Jay Rosen's optimistic view on the decline of "he said, she said" journalism.  While acknowledging that sophisticated journalists recognize the flaws of false balance, the author argues that economic pressures in the media industry, including job cuts and the loss of specialized journalists, make the lazy shortcut of "he said, she said" reporting even more prevalent. The author concludes that the blogosphere's ability to counteract this trend is limited due to the underlying economic realities of the media business.
records.quote: There's a reason the critique of false "balance" emerged, in significant part, from the science journalism world. In CJR, I was very much channeling the complaints of many evolutionary and climate scientists, who were outraged by media coverage and continually pointed out that since there's no such thing as "balance" in science, reporting about science which employs such a paradigm often gets the story completely wrong.

records.title: PressThink: he said/she said Journalism: Lame Formula in the Land of the Active User
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen critiques the "he said, she said" style of journalism, arguing that it often fails to assess competing truth claims and instead offers a false sense of balance.  Rosen contends that this approach, while seemingly a quick and easy solution to reporting deadlines and the complexity of verifying information, ultimately hinders truth-telling.  The rise of the internet and readily available information sources have made this style of reporting increasingly untenable, as readily available evidence allows for a more nuanced and accurate presentation of facts, moving beyond a simple recitation of opposing viewpoints.
records.quote: “How much more evidence do you need?” is the kind of exasperation a lot of us have felt with what he calls “false balance,” which is another name for the pattern I’m describing.

records.title: "He Said, She Said" Journalism: Are We Done With That Yet?
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen critiques "he said, she said" journalism — the practice of presenting two opposing claims without assessing their truth — arguing that this form of false balance fails the public and should be abandoned.
records.quote: Presenting two opposing claims without assessing their truth is a form of false balance that fails the public and should be abandoned.

records.title: PressThink: Introducing the new Huffington Post Investigative Fund (And My Own Role in It)
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: The Huffington Post launches the Huffington Post Investigative Fund, a non-profit initiative funded by The Huffington Post and The Atlantic Philanthropies, aimed at producing investigative journalism. Jay Rosen, a senior advisor to the project, discusses its goals, including the use of open-source and distributed reporting methods, collaboration between professional and amateur journalists, and the importance of high verification standards. The Fund aims to 'report once, run anywhere,' making its content freely available for republication. The initiative sparks discussions about the future of investigative journalism, particularly its role in smaller communities.
records.quote: The announcement of its birth, along with the $1.75 million starter budget, is really the launch of a new Internet-based news organization with a focus on original reporting.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Flying Seminar on the Future of News
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen curates a collection of essays and blog posts from March 2009, forming a 'flying seminar' on the future of news in the face of the newspaper industry's crisis.  The pieces explore various perspectives, from the sociological implications of the decline of the traditional press (Paul Starr, Yochai Benkler) to the internal struggles of news organizations (Clay Shirky) and the potential of new media ecosystems (Steven Berlin Johnson).  The authors discuss the changing production models of news, the potential for citizen journalism, and the challenges of adapting to a rapidly evolving media landscape.
records.quote: Society doesnt need newspapers. What we need is journalism.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Web site arranges funding for freelancers
records.author: San Francisco Chronicle
records.summary: This article discusses the website Spot.Us and its efforts to provide funding for freelance journalists, mentioning Jay Rosen as a figure involved in citizen journalism and related projects.
records.quote: Spot.Us pioneered a community-funding model for freelance journalism, reflecting Jay Rosen's broader argument that new institutional forms — not just new technologies — are needed to sustain independent reporting.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: It Took 23 Years, But I Finally Got to Give My View of the National Press on National Television
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This post reflects on Jay Rosen's appearance on Bill Moyers Journal, discussing his article "Audience Atomization Overcome" and the lack of coverage in the mainstream press.  Rosen highlights the discrepancy between the blogosphere's reception and the silence from the established political press, emphasizing his unique perspective gained from years of studying the national press. He expresses gratitude to Bill Moyers, PBS, and Glenn Greenwald for their support.
records.quote: I have been studying the national press since I received my PhD in 1986. This is the first time I have been able to unfold my own view of it on national television.

records.title: Glenn Greenwald and Jay Rosen on Bill Moyers Journal
records.author: Bill Moyers; Jay Rosen; Glenn Greenwald
records.summary: Rosen and Glenn Greenwald argue on Bill Moyers Journal that the political press has become an establishment institution with a vested interest in preserving Washington's status quo. Rosen explains that the press cannot consider the possibility that Washington's institutions have failed because the press is one of those institutions. Both guests see the internet as a way to circumvent top-down information exchange and force change.
records.quote: What cannot be considered is that there could be anything radically wrong with Washington. That the entire institution could be broken. That idea doesn't really occur to the press, because they're one of those institutions.

records.title: Write it yourself
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen reflects on the relationship between the presidency and the press, tracing its evolution from Theodore Roosevelt's proactive engagement with the media to George W. Bush's strategic distancing.  Rosen argues that Barack Obama's presidency presents an opportunity to redefine this relationship, advocating for greater transparency and a more direct engagement with the public, moving beyond the traditional model of a single interlocutor (the White House press corps) and the dominance of 'Big Media'.  Rosen emphasizes the need for Obama to actively shape the narrative, urging him to 'write it himself' – to control the information flow and actively engage with a broader, more diverse media landscape.
records.quote: What we should care about is not how many questions the press gets to ask at White House news conferences—a hapless metric—but how open to questions the Obama White House is in all the available ways: old, new and recovered.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Audience Atomization Overcome: Why the Internet Weakens the Authority of the Press
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes Daniel C. Hallin's model of the three spheres of journalism (consensus, legitimate debate, and deviance) to explain how the US political press operates. Hallin's model reveals how journalists implicitly define what constitutes acceptable political discourse, often marginalizing dissenting views and reinforcing existing power structures. The rise of the internet and blogging, however, allows like-minded individuals to connect, challenging the press's ability to control the narrative and define consensus, a phenomenon Rosen summarizes as “audience atomization overcome.”
records.quote: The ability to infect us with notions of what’s realistic is one of the most potent powers press and political elites have.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Why I Write 400 Words a Day and Put Them on Twitter
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen documents Rosen's process of writing a piece about his use of Twitter for the Chronicle of Higher Education.  It details his approach to explaining Twitter to a non-Twitter using audience, outlining the key aspects he plans to cover, and soliciting input from his readers on how they utilize the platform. Rosen frames his Twitter usage as a hand-built tipster network and seeks similar experiences from others to enrich his article.
records.quote: What I have so far: A dummy title. Why I Write 400 Words a Day and Put Them on Twitter. Whether that’s the actual title or not, it’s the question my piece must answer.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Make Something Valuable to Journalism and Give it Away: Stanford Re-Deploys its Journalism Fellows
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen discusses a shift in the Knight Fellowships at Stanford University, moving away from a model of general enrichment for mid-career journalists to one focused on journalistic innovation and entrepreneurship. The change is driven by the instability of the news industry, with newsrooms increasingly unable to absorb returning fellows or value their newly acquired knowledge. The new model emphasizes the creation of tangible, public goods by fellows, mirroring an open-source approach and aiming to increase the fellowship's impact on journalism beyond the individual level.
records.quote: The people who steer the Knight Stanford program decided it had to become more valuable to the social practice of journalism, worldwide. They don’t necessarily know how to do this, but they want to increase the supply of public goods the fellows create as a result of their year at Stanford.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Citizen journalism carries unique pitfalls
records.author: San Francisco Chronicle
records.summary: Article discusses challenges of citizen journalism including the potential for false reporting and verification issues. Mentions that Professor Jay Rosen did not return calls for comment.
records.quote: Citizen journalism carries the real risk of false or unverified reporting, exposing the gap between professional editorial standards and the unfiltered, informal accountability structures of amateur news production.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: The Culture War Option For The Palin Convention
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen argues that John McCain's Palin convention strategy turned toward culture-war politics by creating conflict with journalists and bloggers, blurring press-blogosphere-party boundaries, and betting on backlash.
records.quote: It revives cultural memory: the resentment narrative after Chicago '68 but with the angry left more distributed.

records.title: Hype Busters at Mother Jones Bring the Noise
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen examines Mother Jones's approach to debunking media hype and political spin, analyzing how the magazine's investigative methods contrast with the credulity of mainstream political reporting.
records.quote: Mother Jones's investigative approach stands apart from mainstream political reporting by actively debunking media hype and spin rather than absorbing and amplifying it.

records.title: If Bloggers Had No Ethics Blogging Would Have Failed, But it Didn’t. So Let’s Get a Clue.
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen explores the evolving relationship between bloggers and journalists in the early days of the internet. Rosen argues that the distinctions between traditional journalism and blogging are less about inherent ethics and more about the different structures of closed and open editorial systems. He highlights the differences in production methods, gatekeeping versus filtering, and the nature of trust in each system. Ultimately, he contends that the success of blogging demonstrates that it has developed its own ethics based on the trust built between bloggers and their audiences within the open platform.
records.quote: If “ethics” are the codification in rules of the practices that lead to trust on the platform where the users actually are—which is how I think of them—then journalists have their ethics and bloggers have theirs.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Extreme Makeover: 'Lipstick on a pig'

records.quote: New York University professor Jay Rosen says it doesn't really matter whether the outrage is real or contrived.

records.quote: Short HuffPost morning podcast featuring Jay Rosen on press think and the 2008 campaign.

records.title: A World Made More Opaque: Scott McClellan
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Analysis of former White House press secretary Scott McClellan's memoir and what his account of the Bush administration's media strategy reveals about how the press briefing room was used to obscure rather than illuminate.
records.quote: McClellan's memoir shows how the White House press briefing room — nominally a site of transparency — was systematically used to obscure rather than illuminate the Bush administration's decision-making.

records.title: PressThink: The Palin Convention and the Culture War Option
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: John McCain's selection of Sarah Palin as his running mate is analyzed as a culture war strategy aimed at creating conflict with journalists and bloggers, exploiting the resentment narrative, and focusing on personalities rather than issues.  The strategy hinges on Palin's charisma and the ensuing controversy, leveraging both the intense support from social conservatives and the negative press coverage to generate a wave of attention and fundraising. Rosen notes the risks involved and the uncertainty of the strategy's success.
records.quote: At the center of the strategy is the flashpoint candidacy of Sarah Palin, a charismatic figure around whom the war can be fought to scale, as it were.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Bill Keller: I'm Proud to Stand by This Story
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen examines New York Times executive editor Bill Keller's defense of a contested story, analyzing what "I'm proud to stand by this story" reveals about how editors handle criticism and accountability at major newspapers.
records.quote: When Bill Keller said 'I'm proud to stand by this story,' it revealed how editors at major newspapers use professional pride as a shield against accountability rather than as an engagement with legitimate criticism.

records.title: PressThink: Hype Busting at Mother Jones Goes Bust
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen critiques a Mother Jones feature questioning whether Barack Obama's campaign rhetoric exaggerated its historical significance. Rosen challenges the feature's premise, arguing that there's no direct quote or evidence supporting the claim that Obama compared his campaign to past progressive movements. Rosen details their correspondence with Mother Jones editors, revealing a missing contextual speech excerpt that partially justifies the feature's framing, but still leaves crucial aspects unaddressed. The article highlights the dangers of inadvertently creating hype while attempting to debunk it and questions the journalistic rigor of the Mother Jones piece.
records.quote: There’s a moment in the life of every generation, when that spirit has to come through if we are to make our mark on history. And this is our moment. This is our time.

records.title: National Explainer
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the success of "The Giant Pool of Money," a This American Life episode explaining the mortgage crisis.  Rosen argues that the episode's effectiveness stems from its prioritizing of explanation over simply reporting facts. He contends that traditional journalism often fails to provide the necessary background context for understanding complex news events, leading to audience disengagement.  He proposes a shift in journalistic priorities, advocating for the creation of more explanatory pieces that serve as prerequisites for understanding subsequent news reports, thereby increasing audience engagement and comprehension.
records.quote: If explanation is required for information acquisition, then the explainer comes before the informer as a pre-requisite.

records.title: Three Questions For ABC News About Its Anthrax Reporting
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen and Dan Gillmor press ABC News to answer questions about its anthrax reporting, including whether sources misled the network into linking the attacks to Iraq.
records.quote: Dan Gillmor and I are posting these questions simultaneously.

records.title: "The Whole Anthrax Case Would Make For a Good Journalism Class." Brian Ross Responds.
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes Brian Ross's response to questions regarding ABC News's inaccurate anthrax reporting in 2001.  Rosen presents a fictional Q&A summarizing Ross's responses, highlighting inconsistencies and raising concerns about the network's handling of the situation, lack of corrections, and potential implications for the relationship between media, government, and the public. The piece also discusses the broader implications of the incident for journalism and its relationship with power in Rosen's post-Iraq War era.
records.quote: The watchdog press died under Bush. We may have a watchdog press again some day, it could be reborn. But it died. And really the only way we’re going to know that full story is through some kind of, almost like a media truth and reconciliation commission, which I have no hope for.

records.title: Three Vital Questions for ABC News About its Anthrax Reporting in 2001
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen details a coordinated effort by bloggers and journalists to hold ABC News accountable for its 2001 anthrax reporting, which falsely linked Iraqi involvement.  Rosen, Jay Rosen, and Dan Gillmor posed three key questions to ABC News regarding the sourcing and accuracy of their reporting, emphasizing the importance of transparency and accountability when confidential sources mislead. The response from ABC News, along with commentary from various journalists and publications, highlighted the ethical dilemmas surrounding confidential sources and the need for investigative journalism to correct the record in cases of significant misinformation.
records.quote: A substantially false story that helps make the case for war by raising fears about enemies abroad attacking the United States is released into public debate because of faulty reporting by ABC News.

records.title: A Most Useful Definition
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen explores the definition of citizen journalism, focusing on Rosen's concise definition: "When the people formerly known as the audience employ the press tools they have in their possession to inform one another, that’s citizen journalism." Rosen discusses various perspectives on the term, including those from bloggers and other media analysts, and highlights the implications for the traditional news media, suggesting that citizen journalism represents a shift in how information is created and disseminated, moving away from a model of the press as a singular information pipeline.
records.quote: When the people formerly known as the audience employ the press tools they have in their possession to inform one another, that’s citizen journalism.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Big Daddy Newspaper Has Gone and Left Journalism
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen contrasts two responses to the decline of traditional newspapers.  One is the curmudgeonly resistance of veteran journalists clinging to the past, exemplified by the hostile reactions to a young intern's positive assessment of her editor's restructuring plans. The other is a proactive approach, represented by the Tree House Media Project, which empowers journalists to become self-publishers and adapt to the changing media landscape.  Rosen argues that the future lies in embracing self-reliance and abandoning the 'mass' identity of traditional media in favor of more human-scale approaches.
records.quote: No longer does one need a printing press to publish, only a personal computer, an Internet connection and an idea.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Migration Point for the Press Tribe
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This 2008 essay by Jay Rosen uses the metaphor of migration to describe the transformation of journalism in the digital age. Rosen argues that professional journalists, facing the decline of their traditional business model, must adapt to a new media landscape characterized by two-way communication, horizontal sharing, and the rise of citizen journalism. He highlights the challenges of this transition, including resistance from within the profession and the need to integrate professional and amateur journalism practices. Rosen uses the example of OffTheBus, a project he co-founded with Arianna Huffington, as an illustration of a distributed reporting model for campaign coverage.
records.quote: The land that newsroom people have been living on—also called their business model—no longer supports their best work.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: When Bill Clinton Met Mayhill Fowler on the Rope Line
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen defends Mayhill Fowler's OffTheBus reporting on Bill Clinton's rope-line comments, arguing that campaign journalism can include a valid citizen-reporter ethic outside traditional newsroom rules.
records.quote: Last week OffTheBus brought you another case with Mayhill Fowler in the middle of it.

records.title: Update on Beatblogging.org Six Months In
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This post updates the progress of Beatblogging.org, a project exploring whether beat reporters can improve their work by using social networks.  David Cohn, the original editor, has secured funding for a new project, spot.us, and Patrick Thornton has taken over Beatblogging.org.  The project will continue to profile beat reporters using networked approaches and collaborate with WiredJournalists.com to reach a wider audience of innovative journalists.
records.quote: Maybe a beat reporter could do a way better job if there was a ‘live’ social network connected to the beat, made up of people who know the territory the beat covers, and want the reporting on that beat to be better.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: The McCain News Hunt
records.author: Jay Rosen and Gabriel Beltrone
records.summary: Rosen details a collaborative project, the "McCain News Hunt," which utilized NewsTrust, a platform for rating and sharing news stories, and OffTheBus to crowdsource the best journalism about John McCain during a specific week. Participants rated 233 stories, resulting in a ranked list highlighting the top-rated pieces and demonstrating the potential of social media and collaborative filtering to improve news discovery and quality in a proliferating media landscape.
records.quote: The results aren’t spectacular or surprising, and I make no large claims for them. They do show that people really like accountability journalism and that Charlie Savage, now of the New York Times, wrote the most important McCain piece that week.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Scott McClellan And The Opacity Agenda
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen uses Scott McClellan's memoir to argue that Bush and Cheney preferred an opaque executive branch and that McClellan's limits as press secretary served that secrecy agenda.
records.quote: These words have a strange poignancy today.

records.title: PressThink: When Mayhill Fowler Met Bill Clinton at the Rope Line
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes a case involving Mayhill Fowler, a citizen journalist contributing to OffTheBus, who obtained an off-the-record comment from Bill Clinton.  The incident sparks a debate about the ethics and implications of citizen journalism, particularly concerning transparency, the changing nature of 'off the record' interactions, and the relationship between professional and citizen journalists. Rosen explores the evolving media landscape and questions traditional journalistic practices in light of the increased accessibility of information and the blurring lines between professional and amateur reporting.
records.quote: Professional reporters are going to have to decide whether they want to view citizen journalists as unfair competition, which is one option, or as extending the news net to places that pro reporters can’t, won’t or don’t go, which is another—and I think a better—way to look at it.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: McClellan has his revenge on all who underestimated him
records.author: Kathleen Parker
records.summary: Syndicated column by Kathleen Parker citing New York University journalism professor Jay Rosen's “rollback” theory that the Bush administration wanted to downgrade the press within the executive branch and make it less important in running the White House and governing the country.
records.quote: downgrade the press as a player within the executive branch, to make it less important in running the White House and governing the country.

records.title: McClellan wasn't merely bad
records.author: Kathleen Parker
records.summary: Syndicated column by Kathleen Parker citing New York University journalism professor Jay Rosen's “rollback” theory that the Bush administration wanted to downgrade the press within the executive branch and make it less important in running the White House and governing the country.
records.quote: downgrade the press as a player within the executive branch, to make it less important in running the White House and governing the country.

records.title: Revenge of the D.C. nerd, but is it sweet for Scott McClellan?
records.author: The Birmingham News
records.summary: Article discusses Scott McClellan's book and analyzes George W. Bush's administration and media strategy. Jay Rosen is mentioned in the context of his theory on the Bush administration's approach to the press.
records.quote: The Bush administration treated the press not as a channel for informing the public but as an obstacle to be managed, a strategy Jay Rosen theorized as defining the White House's relationship with the media.

records.title: Is Scott McClellan dishonorable?
records.author: Kathleen Parker
records.summary: Syndicated column by Kathleen Parker citing New York University journalism professor Jay Rosen's “rollback” theory that the Bush administration wanted to downgrade the press within the executive branch and make it less important in running the White House and governing the country.
records.quote: downgrade the press as a player within the executive branch, to make it less important in running the White House and governing the country.

records.title: PressThink: The Jerk at the Podium: Scott McClellan Steps Away
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes Scott McClellan's tenure as White House press secretary, arguing that his role was not to communicate effectively but to actively frustrate and delegitimize the press. McClellan's ineffectiveness, far from being accidental, was a deliberate strategy – part of a broader 'Rollback' policy to diminish the press's influence and enhance executive power. This involved minimizing communication, refusing detailed answers, and promoting an environment of non-engagement to reduce the press's ability to hold the administration accountable.
records.quote: McClellan’s job was to contest or deny the ‘terrain of fact,’ the empirical evidence, as traditionally defined.

records.title: PressThink: What Happened to Scott McClellan in Longer Perspective: 100 Years of the White House Press
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes Scott McClellan's post-White House reflections, connecting his experience as press secretary to a broader shift in White House communication strategies under the Bush administration.  Rosen argues that the Bush administration strategically employed non-communication and opacity, rejecting the traditional role of the press as an interlocutor between the presidency and the public. This departure from the Roosevelt-era model, where the president actively engaged with the press, represented a calculated effort to enhance executive power by controlling information flow and avoiding accountability.  McClellan's regret and public acknowledgment of his role in this strategy highlight the consequences of this approach and its ultimate failure in maintaining public support.
records.quote: The ruining of Scott McClellan was part of something way bigger, and to understand it we have to go back to the beginning of the White House press corps.

records.title: Looking for the Mouse in Media: Clay Shirky on Deploying the Cognitive Surplus for Public Good
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen discusses Clay Shirky's concept of "cognitive surplus," the vast amount of free time previously consumed by television, and its potential for productive online activity.  Rosen uses Shirky's ideas to explore the shift from passive media consumption to active participation and creation, exemplified by his daughter's blogging activities. He contrasts the passive nature of traditional media with the interactive possibilities of the web, highlighting the need for new media projects to utilize this untapped potential for social good.
records.quote: Someone working alone, with really cheap tools, has a reasonable hope of carving out enough of the cognitive surplus, enough of the desire to participate, enough of the collective goodwill of the citizens, to create a resource you couldn’t have imagined existing even five years ago.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: The Presses Stop But the Press Goes On: Capital Times Lives on the Web
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen details the transformation of the Capital Times, a Madison, Wisconsin newspaper, from a daily print publication to a primarily online news outlet with two weekly print editions. The shift, driven by economic pressures and the changing media landscape, involves job losses, a move to a digital-first strategy, and a re-evaluation of the paper's role in the community. Rosen analyzes the challenges and potential opportunities presented by this transition, considering the competitive online environment and the paper's legacy as a progressive voice in Madison.
records.quote: The presses have stopped but the press goes on.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: They Were Undercover Campaign Volunteers
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen points readers to two Philadelphia City Paper writers who went undercover as Clinton and Obama volunteers, framing their reports as revealing evidence about campaign organizing despite ethical questions.
records.quote: But we're not the only ones trying to do that.

records.title: Newspapers and the Net: Where’s the Business Model, People?
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen explores the crisis facing newspapers due to the internet's disruption of their traditional business models.  Rosen discusses the challenges of transitioning from an advertising-subsidized model to sustainable alternatives, questioning whether the public good of quality journalism can be maintained. He examines various approaches, including non-profit models like ProPublica, innovative ventures like The Politico, and the potential for filtering and repackaging online content. The article also touches upon the inherent inefficiencies of advertising and the need for increased public understanding of the true cost of serious journalism.
records.quote: The traditional newspaper formula has been patently unworkable for years, but too many newspaper leaders don’t understand that.

records.title: Mayhill Fowler and the Uncharted Territory of Citizen Journalism
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen discusses the case of Mayhill Fowler, an Obama supporter and citizen journalist who reported on comments made by Obama at a fundraiser.  Her report, published on the Huffington Post's OffTheBus blog, was picked up by major news outlets but was subsequently downplayed by Meet the Press, leading to a discussion about the evolving role of citizen journalism in political coverage and the challenges faced by traditional media in navigating this new landscape. The article explores the blurred lines between citizen journalist, campaign supporter, and news reporter, highlighting the lack of established frameworks for understanding this emerging phenomenon.
records.quote: The issue is less the distinction between “citizen” and “journalist” and more whether the Founding Fathers ever contemplated such a distinction in the first place.A close reading of the First Amendment and centuries of legal precedent says “no.”
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: The Uncharted: From Off The Bus to Meet the Press
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: An account of how OffTheBus, the citizen journalism project, grew from an experimental Huffington Post blog into a platform that broke real news during the 2008 campaign, including its relationship with traditional outlets like Meet the Press.
records.quote: OffTheBus grew from an experimental Huffington Post blog into a citizen journalism platform that broke real news during the 2008 campaign, demonstrating that distributed reporting could compete with and complement traditional outlets.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Ethics of Linking: Jay Rosen
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Jay Rosen explains the ethic of linking in blogging and news media.
records.quote:
# Ethics of Linking: Jay Rosen

Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RIMB9Kx18hw
Speaker: Jay Rosen
Upload date: 2008-04-08
Duration: 261 seconds
Publisher: Carnegie Council for Ethics in International Affairs

records.title: Love Affair: McCain and the Press
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: An analysis of the press corps's long-standing favorable relationship with John McCain, examining how the senator cultivated reporters through access and candor, and what this meant for coverage of his 2008 presidential campaign.
records.quote: John McCain cultivated the press through extraordinary access and candor, and reporters rewarded him with favorable coverage — a transactional relationship that shaped how his 2008 presidential campaign was framed long before voters weighed in.

records.title: PressThink: The Love Affair Between McCain and the Press Sprains the Brain of the Liberal Blogosphere
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the emerging conflict between liberal bloggers and mainstream media regarding their coverage of John McCain's presidential campaign in 2008.  Rosen questions whether a declared 'blogospheric war' against the media is truly underway, or if the situation is more nuanced and dynamic.  The piece examines the media's perceived favoritism towards McCain, the bloggers' strategies to counter this narrative, and the potential impact of McCain's unprecedented openness to press questioning on the campaign.
records.quote: This campaign is not going to be between the Democrats and the Republicans, said Philadelphias Duncan Black, who writes under the name Atrios and whose highly popular progressive political blog, named Eschaton, inspired the gathering of bloggers and political activists called Eschacon ‘08.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: The News about the news: Jay Rosen
records.author: Christopher Lydon
records.summary: The program features a discussion with media critic and NYU professor Jay Rosen about the current state of news and its role in a divided America. It highlights the business aspects of news in the digital age, while also acknowledging its importance as a public good. The conversation centers on the challenges facing journalism, including shrinking newsrooms, rising disinformation, and declining trust. Rosen advocates for a shift in journalistic approach, urging the press to move beyond objectivity and neutrality to actively defend democracy by calling out misinformation and supporting democratic norms. The discussion also includes the impact of AI on journalism, the future of local news, and the challenge of rebuilding public trust.
records.quote: The idea that there is this large, untapped audience of people in the middle who are just waiting for a news organization to come along and give it to them straight, that’s a fantasy.
concepts: Not the odds but the stakes

records.title: Where Did McCain Get What He's Got "in the Bank" with the Press?
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen asks why Chuck Todd said John McCain had enough credibility 'in the bank' with the press after falsely linking Al Qaeda in Iraq to Iran, arguing that banked capital came from McCain's open, on-the-record ease with reporters on the Straight Talk Express rather than demonstrated foreign-policy mastery.
records.quote: First came John McCain's strange assertion that Al Qaeda in Iraq was being trained and supported by the Iranians.

records.title: PressThink: Just How Did John McCain Obtain What He Has in the Bank with the Press?
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the unusually positive relationship between John McCain's presidential campaign and the press corps.  Rosen argues that McCain's willingness to engage in extensive, off-the-record conversations with reporters, even when facing tough questions, cultivated a sense of rapport and trust, creating a 'reputational capital' that shielded him from harsher criticism.  Rosen contrasts this with other candidates' more guarded approaches, highlighting how McCain's openness, while potentially containing strategic elements, inadvertently humanized both him and the reporters, resulting in more favorable coverage. The article also explores whether Barack Obama should adopt a similar strategy.
records.quote: The currency in which reporters trade is questions actually answered, QAA. McCain simply realized that the QAA system allowed him to print money, as in: ask all the questions you want!And where does that currency go? Straight into Chuck Todd’s Presumptive Credibility Bank.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Obama tells the Best Political Team on Television: You Have a Choice
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This post critiques CNN's Wolf Blitzer's analysis of Barack Obama's speech addressing the Jeremiah Wright controversy. Rosen argues that Blitzer's interpretation, focusing solely on political strategy, misses the speech's deeper message urging a transcendence of divisive political discourse and a more nuanced understanding of race. Rosen contrasts Blitzer's shallow analysis with the insightful observations of Greg Sargent and Charles Murray, highlighting Obama's direct challenge to the media's role in perpetuating a spectacle-driven, race-focused narrative.
records.quote: It is so far above the standard we’re used to from our pols… rhetorically, but also in capturing a lot of nuance about race in America.

records.title: Obama Tells the Best Political Team on Television: You Guys Have a Choice...
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes Barack Obama's 2008 campaign narrative, arguing that Obama succeeded because he told a more compelling political story than his opponents — one that connected personal biography to national purpose.
records.quote: Obama succeeded because he told a more compelling political story than his opponents — one that connected personal biography to national purpose.

records.title: Walter Pincus of the Post: Our Neutered Newsrooms are a Poor Example to the Rest of the World
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen argues that neutrality claims like Clark Hoyt's defense of the Times trap the media-bias debate, and that journalists must recognize the politics in their work and make it transparent, as Josh Marshall's TPM does by joining accountability reporting to an open display of political conviction.
records.quote: It is rare that a single article advances American press think.

records.title: Pincus, Neutrality, and the Politics of News
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen critiques the prevailing notion of journalistic neutrality, arguing that it hinders effective political reporting and undermines democratic processes. It uses examples like Clark Hoyt's defense of the New York Times' neutrality, Josh Marshall's TPM's transparently liberal approach, and Walter Pincus' call for journalistic courage to illustrate the need for a more politically engaged and self-aware press. The piece emphasizes the importance of fairness over neutrality, advocating for transparency about reporters' political affiliations and a reevaluation of the power dynamics between the press and government, particularly addressing the legacy of controlled messaging started during the Reagan administration.
records.quote: “The biggest reason to go open kimono is that the present system does what journalism should never do: it perpetuates a lie.”

records.title: PressThink: "An Attractively Against-the-Grain Enterprise..."
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: The article analyzes instances where news organizations, particularly The New York Times and The Washington Post, engage in 'misguided contrarianism' by publishing provocative or seemingly iconoclastic pieces that ultimately serve to promote the paper's self-image rather than contribute meaningfully to public discourse. It critiques the pressure to 'find something' on all political candidates and the tendency to prioritize staff morale or economic concerns over journalistic integrity.
records.quote: The paper is not so much a paper anymore; it is itself a candidate.

records.title: When Dumb Articles Happen to Smart Newspapers
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen follows up on his candidate-vetting pattern exercise with reader responses and a critique of Washington Post and New York Times stories that revealed newsroom self-image problems. He argues that smart newspapers produce dumb articles when narrative rituals and institutional self-regard overwhelm evidence.
records.quote: Thursday I posted a little exercise in pattern recognition at the New York Times.

records.title: PressThink: Three Vetting Stories Went Awry at the New York Times: Find the Pattern.
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Jay Rosen questions the New York Times' decisions to investigate Obama's drug use, Hillary Clinton's marriage, and John McCain's lobbyist ties. He argues that each story went "weirdly wrong" and asks Romenesko readers for insights into what might have been the common factors behind these editorial choices during the vetting process of presidential candidates.
records.quote: Each was part of the “vetting” ritual in which the press imagines itself asking the hard questions of candidates who would be president. Each has a touch of the bizarre to it.

records.title: When Candidate "Vetting" Runs off the Rails
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen asks readers to find the pattern among three New York Times candidate-vetting stories about Obama, Hillary Clinton, and John McCain. The short prompt says each story went weirdly wrong, left readers wondering what the editors were thinking, and reflected a vetting ritual with a touch of the bizarre.
records.quote: Huff Post readers, bloggers, journalists, talk show hosts, onlookers: help me out.

records.title: Cliff Notes Ver.
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This is a distillation of a New York Times Q&A with readers regarding their explosive report on John McCain's involvement with lobbyist Vicki Iseman. The NYT defends its reporting choices, addressing concerns about anonymity, the inclusion of potentially unverified information about a romantic relationship, the timing of the story, and the potential impact on McCain's campaign. They maintain the story's accuracy and their commitment to thorough investigative journalism, despite the significant backlash.
records.quote: We publish stories when they’re ready. Period. No matter when we publish them people see dark motives.

records.title: PressThink: Public Editor to Bill Keller: "You Haven't Got it."
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the New York Times' handling of a story suggesting John McCain had an affair. Rosen criticizes the Times' editors for lacking political awareness, failing to understand the potential consequences of their reporting, and clinging to journalistic codes that prevented them from recognizing the political realities of the situation. He argues that the Times' readers exhibited a more nuanced understanding of the political implications than the editors, highlighting a credibility gap between the newspaper and its audience.
records.quote: If a newspaper is going to suggest an improper sexual affair, whether editors think that is the central point or not, it owes readers more proof than The Times was able to provide.

records.title: For the New York Times: An Assignment
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen proposes a specific editorial assignment for the New York Times, arguing that the paper's journalism would improve if it approached certain stories with different methods and greater accountability.
records.quote: Rosen argues that the New York Times could produce better journalism by approaching certain stories with different methods and a stronger commitment to accountability, rather than defaulting to the conventions of detached, view-from-nowhere reporting.

records.title: 'Anonymous' McCain story backfires on Times
records.author: Connecticut Post
records.summary: Article discusses the backlash against the New York Times for publishing a story based on anonymous sources regarding John McCain's alleged relationship with a lobbyist. Mentions Jay Rosen's commentary on the story on NYTPicker.com.
records.quote: The Times' reliance on anonymous sources in the McCain story generated backlash that overshadowed the reporting itself, illustrating how sourcing decisions can become the story.

records.title: For the New York Times, Too, Self-Confidence on Ethics Poses Risks
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This blog post analyzes the New York Times's reporting on John McCain's alleged affair, questioning the timing of the story in relation to the paper's endorsement of McCain. Rosen raises concerns about the reliance on anonymous sources, the potential impact on the 2008 election, and the broader implications for media ethics and the relationship between the newsroom and editorial page. The piece also highlights the ensuing culture war and the Times's discomfort with defending its journalistic choices in the court of public opinion.
records.quote: For the New York Times, self-confidence on ethics poses its own risks, as well.

records.title: The Beast Without a Brain: Why Horse Race Journalism Works for Journalists and Fails Us
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Jay Rosen critiques horse race journalism, arguing that the campaign media operates as a 'herd of independent minds' lacking a central direction or capacity to learn from mistakes. This mindlessness results in superficial coverage focused on predicting outcomes rather than understanding the stakes, leading to inaccurate narratives and a failure to inform the public effectively.
records.quote: Campaign reporters tend to be massively other-directed. The reality-check is what the rest of the press is doing.

records.title: Filter the Best Stuff to the Front Page
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: An examination of the OffTheBus/NewsTrust collaboration to crowdsource quality political coverage, describing a test of filtering the best citizen journalism to the front page during the 2008 campaign.
records.quote: The OffTheBus/NewsTrust collaboration tested whether crowdsourced filters could surface the best citizen journalism to a front page during the 2008 campaign, treating quality political coverage as something readers could help identify, not just consume.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: "Most of them are not ideologically driven; they just want to get on the front page."
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the contrasting views of the conservative elite and the conservative base regarding the media. While the base often perceives the press as monolithic, liberal, and against the Bush administration, key figures like Karl Rove and Dan Bartlett, having gained insider experience, recognize a more nuanced reality. They acknowledge the press's inherent desire for compelling stories and its oppositional stance towards power, irrespective of party affiliation. This divergence highlights a strategic utilization of the base's perception of media bias to serve political goals, while insiders operate with a more pragmatic understanding of journalistic motivations.
records.quote: The press is generally liberal, he argued, but “I think it’s less liberal than it is oppositional.”

records.title: Yahoos Within the GOP Coalition Challenged on their Media Think
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen argues that Mike Huckabee's rise exposed contempt for social conservatives among conservative elites while hard-line liberal-media claims persisted in other parts of the GOP coalition. He contrasts that thesis with Dan Bartlett, Karl Rove, and Ari Fleischer treating the press as more professional, varied, and independent than the yahoo version allows.
records.quote: John Cole ("Enjoy your new GOP, folks...") and Andrew Sullivan ("This is their party. And they asked for every last bit of it...") pounced on the squirming shown as Huckabee climbed in the polls during December.

records.title: The Hill Restores Armstrong Williams to Legitimacy. Why?
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen questions The Hill's decision to restore Armstrong Williams as a pundit after the 2005 Department of Education payola scandal. Through a Q&A with editor Hugo Gurdon, he presses whether Williams's undisclosed government contract made his journalism, broadcasting, public relations, and government contracting work ethically fraudulent.
records.quote: He didn't disclose the deal because he couldn't disclose it without exposing the contract as fraudulent.

records.title: A Stooge Figure Speaks
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Jay Rosen argues that Scott McClellan's role as White House press secretary under George W. Bush was not simply to disseminate information, but to actively frustrate and belittle the press, hindering genuine communication and increasing the opacity of the executive branch. McClellan's actions, Rosen contends, were part of a broader strategy by the Bush administration to reduce constraints on presidential power and limit accountability through strategic non-communication, rather than outright lying or traditional spin.
records.quote: McClellan’s specialty was not lying, or the traditional art of spin, but what I have called “strategic non-communication.” Lying we understand; spin we have to come to grasp. Non-communication we still do not appreciate. Its purpose is to make executive power less legible.

records.title: PressThink: These Beat Reporters Will Try the Social Network Way
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Jay Rosen announces the launch of Beatblogging.org, a project involving 13 news organizations and their reporters who will experiment with integrating social networks into their beat reporting.  The goal is to explore whether a collaborative, pro-am approach to journalism, using social networks to connect with experts and the public, can improve the quality and reach of beat reporting.  The project will run for a year, with participating organizations including the Houston Chronicle, Star-Ledger, Wired.com, and others, each focusing on a different beat.
records.quote: The reporter was a gatekeeper before only the expertise he chose would make it to the public in print. But now the role of the reporter can and should be different: as a moderator, vetter, enabler, encourager.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Out in the Great Wide Open
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the implosion of Wide Open, a political blog run by the Cleveland Plain Dealer.  The blog's demise stemmed from a contributor's political donation to an opponent of a Congressman, leading to the newspaper's decision to sever ties with the contributor, and ultimately, the shutdown of the blog. Rosen critiques the newspaper's handling of the situation, arguing that prioritizing traditional journalistic ethics over transparency exacerbated the crisis and reveals a fundamental misunderstanding of the blogosphere's dynamics.  Rosen advocates for transparency as a more suitable approach for online opinion pieces.
records.quote: Transparency is not some new media buzzword but an alternative means of generating trust.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Beat Reporting With a Social Network: Can it Work?
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen proposes an experiment to improve beat reporting by integrating social networks. Rosen seeks 12 beat reporters to create online communities around their beats, allowing for collaboration with experts and stakeholders outside the newsroom. The goal is to enhance reporting quality and explore new models for journalistic practice in the digital age using tools like blogs, wikis, and forums.
records.quote: Maybe a beat reporter could do a way better job if there was a live social network connected to the beat, made up of people who know the territory the beat covers, and want the reporting on that beat to be better.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Okay, Ready? My Coordinates for a Successful News Site
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen outlines a model for successful online news organizations, focusing on features like high-quality aggregation, blogging platforms, original reporting with amateur and professional collaborations, beat blogging, comprehensive features, interactive forums, data visualization, community publishing, reverse publishing, crowdsourcing, breaking news coverage, geo-tagged information, search-optimized content, and comprehensive topic pages. Rosen presents this as a list of coordinates, not a rigid formula, for the future of online news.
records.quote: Like my coordinates for distributed journalism, these are the coordinates I see for the emerging model of a successful online news organization.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: What I Learned From Assignment Zero
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen reflects on the lessons learned from Assignment Zero, a collaborative journalism project with Wired.com that aimed to explore the potential of pro-am journalism. Rosen analyzes the challenges and successes of the project, highlighting the importance of proper division of labor, understanding contributors' motivations, managing coordination costs, and ensuring clear connections between individual contributions and the overall narrative. Key takeaways include the need for appropriately sized tasks, inspiring participation rather than commanding it, and leveraging existing online communities for efficient distributed reporting.
records.quote: Newsrooms developed as monasteries not because reporters were anointed (though many believe they were and are) but because there wasn’t really any frictionless way to include the public in the reporting enterprise. Now there is.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Rather Unbound
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen reads Dan Rather's lawsuit against CBS as a theatrical attempt to replay Rathergate and revive Rather's self-image as a driven reporter. He argues that the case is less about money than about putting CBS, the Bush National Guard story, and Rather's own legacy back on stage.
records.quote: If I were to underline one thing about Dan Rather's $70 million suit against CBS, it's the _theatricality_ of it, which is also the key to understanding Rather himself.

records.title: PressThink: Rather Unbound Will Redo the Killian Memos Story
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes Dan Rather's $70 million lawsuit against CBS, focusing on the theatricality of the event and its reflection of Rather's personality and career.  Rosen explores Rather's self-perception as a hard-news investigative reporter despite his role as a prominent anchor, examining his motivations for the lawsuit as a final attempt to reclaim his journalistic integrity and expose alleged collusion between CBS and the Bush administration in the Killian memo controversy.  The piece also considers broader implications regarding the role of anchors, the accountability of mainstream media versus bloggers, and the changing landscape of journalism.
records.quote: Rather told King he “would like the legacy of this lawsuit to be not that I made tons of money out of it, but that we kept the little flame, the flickering flame of hard-nose investigative reporting alive.”

records.title: Court of the Web Rules Against Times-Select
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the New York Times's decision to shut down TimesSelect, framing it as a verdict by "the court of the web" against paywalling opinion content, and what it means for the future of newspaper business models.
records.quote: The New York Times's decision to shut down TimesSelect was a verdict by 'the court of the web' against paywalling opinion content — a ruling that exposed the limits of newspaper subscription models in an era of open information.
