concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: RIP Times Select
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the New York Times' decision to shut down TimesSelect, its paywalled content section.  Rosen argues that the failure of TimesSelect demonstrates the futility of charging for online content in the face of the open web's link-based economy and the power of search engine optimization.  The Times' shift towards an open model, embracing search engine traffic and blogosphere participation, is presented as a strategic necessity for long-term success and revenue generation through advertising tied to search.
records.quote: The professional premium is better located there.

records.title: PressThink: Note From the Castle: White House Correspondent Writes to PressThink, Explains the Body Watch
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This is a blog post presenting a dialogue between Jay Rosen and a White House correspondent (“Hack”) regarding the role and limitations of the White House press corps. The correspondent challenges Rosen’s criticism of the corps’ coverage of the President’s trip to Iraq, arguing that the “body watch” – the constant monitoring of the President for safety reasons – necessitates their presence, even in potentially propagandistic settings. The discussion expands to explore the overreliance on the White House for news, the influence of access and “insider” information, and the need for a more balanced approach incorporating outside perspectives.
records.quote: What we are responsible for is making sure that, if he collapses, or is shot at, we are in a position to get that information to your viewers/listeners/readers.

records.title: The Master Narrative that Went Missing During the Bush Presidency
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen argues that Bush-era coverage lacked the master narrative of executive-power expansion. He points to Charlie Savage, Jack Goldsmith, and the Cheney project as evidence that the press needed a connecting story about maximal executive power rather than isolated campaign and policy episodes.
records.quote: Some new developments this week in the continuing story of how the press was overawed by the Administration of George W.

records.title: PressThink: The Master Narrative that Went Missing During the Bush Years Turns Up in Charlie Savage's Book
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the failure of the press to adequately cover the Bush administration's expansion of executive power. It highlights Charlie Savage's work in uncovering the administration's agenda of concentrating unchecked power in the White House, arguing that this 'master narrative' was crucial for understanding various seemingly disparate events. Rosen criticizes the press for failing to connect these events and for accepting a superficial understanding of the Bush administration's political strategy. He emphasizes the long-term consequences of this unchecked expansion of presidential power, regardless of future administrations' actions.
records.quote: The administration, from its very beginning, had set out to set precedents and take actions that would permanently expand presidential power for the long-term, even when such tactics brought them extra short-term difficulties.
concepts: Not the odds but the stakes

records.title: "Would You Guys Like us to Come Without You?"
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen criticizes White House reporters for accepting President Bush's surprise Iraq trip as a necessary assignment even when it functioned as a managed propaganda event. He argues that the press corps lacked the independence to deny the president a spin zone with an Iraq dateline.
records.quote: National Security Adviser Stephen Hadley had a good question for the White House press corps Monday, when the President--surprise!--flew to Iraq.

records.title: PressThink: When We Try to Explain the Rout of the Press under George W. Bush
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the failure of the Washington press corps to adequately cover the Bush administration, arguing that their adherence to established methods and a cyclical view of politics left them unprepared for the administration's radicalism.  Rosen critiques the press's deference to figures like Karl Rove, attributing it not solely to personal admiration but also to a lack of imagination and preparedness for unconventional political tactics.  The article uses the examples of the Iraq War coverage and the underreporting of Dick Cheney's power to illustrate the shortcomings of the press's approach.
records.quote: The media virtually never takes seriously any administration lawbreaking and corruption scandals because the people at the center of those scandals are those whom they deeply admire.

records.title: Blowback: The journalism that bloggers actually do
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This is a response to Michael Skube's opinion piece in the Los Angeles Times criticizing blogs' journalistic value.  Rosen challenges Skube's claims by providing numerous examples of blogs engaging in thorough fact-finding and investigative reporting. He argues that the traditional journalistic gatekeeping system is being challenged by the rise of citizen journalism and that the act of reporting is inherently democratic and not limited to professionally trained journalists.
records.quote: If you have a blog, you never know when you might be called on to also be a journalist.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: The journalism that bloggers actually do
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen responds to Michael Skube's LA Times op-ed dismissing blogs as 'noise that fits,' arguing that bloggers like Joshua Micah Marshall do substantive investigative journalism — and noting that Skube wrote about blogs without having read them.
records.quote: Rosen critiques Michael Skube's dismissive opinion piece about blogs and their role in journalism, arguing bloggers do real investigative and verification work.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Help Make my Blowback Post to Michael Skube a Little More Sound; LATimes.com to Run With It
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This text is a draft of a response by Jay Rosen to Michael Skube's critique of blogs. Rosen compiles a list of examples showcasing various instances of citizen journalism and blog-based investigative reporting to counter Skube's arguments. The examples highlight blogs' contributions to newsgathering and information dissemination across diverse fields, including politics, technology, and consumer affairs, demonstrating their capacity for in-depth investigations and breaking news.
records.quote: Pet owners frustrated with the limitations of the news media self-organize into a national network of sites and share news about tainted foods that may have killed thousands of pets across the country.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: My advice? Retire.
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This is a short, angry blog post directed at an unnamed journalist.  Rosen accuses the journalist of being an embarrassment to the profession, calls for their resignation, criticizes their reporting (specifically citing the Los Angeles Times and Walter Reed Army Medical Center coverage), and implies a lack of commitment to learning and reporting.
records.quote: You’re an embarrassment to my profession, to the university where you teach, and to the craft of reporting you claim to defend.

records.title: PressThink: Karl Rove and the Religion of the Washington Press
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen argues that the vulnerability of the American press to manipulation by figures like Karl Rove stems from an unspoken ideology of 'savviness' within journalism. Rosen contends that journalists prioritize shrewdness and winning, even at the expense of honesty, fairness, and ethical considerations. He uses Karl Rove's career and the press's coverage of his resignation as examples to illustrate how this prioritization of savviness allowed Rove to exploit and manipulate the media.
records.quote: Savviness—that quality of being shrewd, practical, well-informed, perceptive, ironic, “with it,” and unsentimental in all things political—is, in a sense, their professional religion.

records.title: Karl Rove and the Cult of Savviness in Our Political Press
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen examines Karl Rove's media strategy and the "cult of the insider" in Washington political journalism, where access to powerful sources becomes more valued than holding those sources accountable.
records.quote: In Washington political journalism, access to powerful sources has become more valued than holding those sources accountable — a dynamic Karl Rove exploited to near-perfection.

records.title: Why Do We Suck? and Other Questions Political Journalists Asked Themselves at YearlyKos
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen reviews press coverage of YearlyKos and finds more respect between political reporters and the liberal blogosphere than in earlier years. He argues that reporters are absorbing Dan Gillmor's lesson that readers know more than they do, though wariness and Iraq-war accountability remain unresolved.
records.quote: My main conclusion: more respect expressed for the blogosphere, and a little less wariness between the two groups.

records.title: PressThink: Why Do We Suck? and Other Questions Political Journalists Asked Themselves at YearlyKos
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen discusses the evolving relationship between mainstream media and the blogosphere in 2007, focusing on political journalism.  Mainstream journalists are increasingly acknowledging the value of blogosphere input, recognizing that readers often possess more knowledge than reporters. However, the piece also critiques the tendency of some journalists to prioritize appearing politically neutral over truthful reporting, leading to a superficial and often misleading approach to news coverage.  Rosen uses examples from YearlyKos and various journalists' comments to illustrate how the pressure to avoid partisan labels can compromise journalistic integrity.
records.quote: Simply put, news is no longer a one-way process. It is now much more of a conversation between journalist and reader.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: The Press Lives "Off" Politics, The Kossacks Live For It
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen reflects on the 2007 Yearly Kos convention, highlighting the growing influence of online political blogging and its impact on the relationship between politicians, the press, and the public.  Rosen emphasizes the role of Daily Kos and its community in shaping political discourse, arguing that its participatory nature prioritizes argument and engagement over purely informational reporting, a contrast to traditional journalism's approach.  Rosen notes the acknowledgment from journalists like Matt Bai of the press's failures, particularly during the Iraq War, and the evolving relationship between bloggers and traditional journalists.
records.quote: We the press failed you, the people whom Bush actively misled. We failed by not stopping him.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: The Agitators: Notes From Day One of YearlyKos
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Reporting from YearlyKos, Rosen argues that Gina Cooper and the netroots volunteers, not only Markos Moulitsas, built the event's political force. He links the convention's influence to bloggers' aggregated attention, participation, and OffTheBus's open campaign-reporting model.
records.quote: And I don't mean for a second that Kos is the CEO with the ideas and Cooper the efficient aide who carries out those ideas.

records.title: Tips on How to Write a Post for OffTheBus and Possibly Make the Front Page
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This FAQ post provides guidance to contributors of OffTheBus, a collaborative project between Huffington Post and New Assignment, on how to create effective blog posts for a campaign journalism platform. It emphasizes the importance of providing original information, conducting original reporting, and filling gaps in existing news coverage rather than simply offering opinion or commentary. Rosen's post offers examples of successful posts and suggests developing a specific beat for consistent contributions.
records.quote: One of the keys to a successful “norg” — and saving the endangered jobs of American journalists like me — will be to stop talking down to or even insulting our so-called “audience” of readers — but forming a working partnership with everyday citizens who care about good journalism.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Tips on How to Write a Post for OffTheBus & Possibly Make  the Front Page
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen offers contributors guidance on writing effective OffTheBus posts, emphasizing original reporting, timeliness, sourcing, and how to get a piece promoted to the front page.
records.quote: As things start rolling at OffTheBus, we're getting a lot of inquiries about effective blog posts, which is good.

records.title: All the Questions Citizens Got to Ask in the YouTube Debate
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A complete transcript and analysis of all citizen-submitted questions from the CNN/YouTube Democratic presidential debate in Charleston, SC, examining what this format revealed about the gap between what citizens and journalists consider important.
records.quote: The gap between the questions citizens chose to submit and the questions professional journalists would have asked reveals a persistent disconnect between press values and public concerns.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: The Hair Beat, the Politics of No Politics, and the Mystery Driver for OffTheBus
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: In a Q&A with Spokesman-Review columnist Frank Sennett, Rosen discusses OffTheBus's rolling launch, contributor standards and support, reporting structure, and editorial identity within its Huffington Post partnership.
records.quote: Now Blogspotter ("making sense of the blog world so you don't have to") and Hard 7 ("the culture of politics and the politics of culture") are both Sennett spaces.

records.title: Did Your Experiment Work? Q and A with Leonard Witt and Jay Rosen
records.author: Jay Rosen and Leonard Witt
records.summary: This Q&A discusses the lessons learned from Assignment Zero, a crowdsourced journalism project, and how those lessons are being applied to OffTheBus, a new open platform campaign news bureau. Key takeaways include the importance of clear task assignments, aligning tasks with contributors' motivations, and the limitations of a purely “gift economy” model for news. The discussion also touches upon the nature of political journalism and the challenges of synthesizing large amounts of crowdsourced material.
records.quote: People will contribute only because they want to, because the work stirs a passion they have, or is inherently interesting or they find the community of people, a great group of people and everything starts from there, not from “what needs to be done,” but the motivations and interests of the people joining the project.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Inquire. Discover. Inform Others.
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A companion piece to the OffTheBus launch, defining the project's editorial mission — "Inquire. Discover. Inform Others." — and articulating what citizen journalism at its best should look like.
records.quote: Citizen journalism at its best follows a simple but demanding mandate: inquire into what matters, discover what's actually true, and inform others clearly and honestly.

records.title: Guidelines for OffTheBus Bloggers
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen publishes editorial guidelines for OffTheBus, the citizen journalism project he co-founded with Arianna Huffington for the 2008 presidential campaign, establishing standards for volunteer bloggers.
records.quote: To earn the trust of readers, citizen journalists must hold themselves to the same standards of accuracy, transparency, and fairness that define credible reporting at any level.

records.title: About OffTheBus
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: OffTheBus is introduced as an open, pro-am campaign news bureau created by NewAssignment.Net and the Huffington Post, combining unedited citizen blogs with filtered, edited sections and collaborative reporting projects.
records.quote: Off The Bus is a news and opinion site about the 2008 election and the race for the White House.

records.title: Just the Sum of Us: James Surowiecki On What Crowds Can and Cannot Do
records.author: Emily Gordon
records.summary: This article features an interview with James Surowiecki, author of "The Wisdom of Crowds."  The conversation explores the implications of crowdsourcing and online collaboration, particularly regarding the aggregation of opinions to form collective judgment.  Surowiecki distinguishes between the rise of individual bloggers and the true wisdom of crowds, emphasizing the need for mechanisms to aggregate diverse opinions effectively.  The discussion also touches upon the digital divide, the role of past experiences in collective wisdom, the potential for online participation to translate into real-world activism, and the application of the wisdom of crowds to address complex issues like global warming.  Finally, Surowiecki reflects on his career transition from book critic to business columnist, highlighting the opportunities presented by the internet and the ongoing public interest in business and economics.
records.quote: You only get real collective wisdom when you have some way of aggregating lots of different individual opinions to produce a collective judgment.

records.title: Printing Press Progressives at Mother Jones Try to Debunk the Political Web
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen criticizes Mother Jones's framing of its Politics 2.0 package as simplistic, hype-driven false alternatives while praising the package's interviews as more grounded.
records.quote: Mother Jones_ magazine has come out with a special Politics 2.0 package.

records.title: PressThink: "Mother Jones invites you to question if the Politics 2.0 revolution really lives up to its hype."
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen critiques Mother Jones magazine's coverage of "Politics 2.0," arguing that their framing of the topic as a simple "it'll change everything/it'll change nothing" dichotomy is simplistic and misses the nuances of the impact of the internet on politics. Rosen contends that Mother Jones relies on tired journalistic tropes instead of offering a thoughtful analysis, ignoring insightful observations from their own interviewees. He highlights the missed opportunity to explore the generational conflict within political campaigns regarding internet usage and the evolving role of gatekeepers in the digital age.
records.quote: What they have accomplished in just a few years is astonishing. Already, the netroots are the most significant mass movement in U.S. politics since the rise of the Christian right more than two decades ago. And, by all appearances, they are far from finished with their task: recreating the Democratic Party in the image of the conservative machine they have set out to destroy.

records.title: PressThink: OffTheBus Hires Two People Who Know How to Organize 200: Amanda Michel and Zack Exley
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen announces the launch of OffTheBus.Net, a collaborative campaign journalism project spearheaded by Jay Rosen, Arianna Huffington, and the Huffington Post.  The project aims to create a more open and participatory approach to covering political campaigns, utilizing a blogging platform where volunteers can contribute.  While acknowledging potential biases due to the project's origins within a liberal-leaning online environment, the authors emphasize a commitment to accuracy and quality across all contributions. The article also discusses the challenges and potential benefits of this open, participatory model of journalism, contrasting it with traditional newsroom structures.
records.quote: They both understand that the falling costs for like-minded people to find each other, share information and collaborate on good works (as well as works of evil….) probably means we can do new and exciting things in political journalism, but it is still very hard to do those things because our knowledge of how to organize scattered people with limited time and definite interest is still primitive.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: OffTheBus.Net Hires Two People Who Know How to Organize 200
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen announces that OffTheBus.Net, a citizen-campaign-journalism venture with the Huffington Post, has hired Amanda Michel and Zack Exley to organize volunteer coverage of the 2008 presidential race.
records.quote: Some big news today for OffTheBus.Net, the joint venture in campaign journalism I have undertaken with Arianna Huffington and the Huffington Post.

records.title: Zack Exley and Amanda Michel Join OffTheBus.Net. Press Release, June 19, 2007
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Huffington Post and NewAssignment.Net announce that Internet organizers Amanda Michel and Zack Exley have joined OffTheBus.Net as project director and senior adviser for the 2008 campaign cycle.
records.quote: Michel will be Project Director; Exley will be Senior Adviser and a traveling correspondent.

records.title: PressThink: Who's Ahead? No, Seriously...
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen critiques the prevalent "horse race" narrative in political campaign reporting, arguing that it prioritizes who's winning over substantive policy discussions.  Rosen proposes an "Idea Race" alternative, where candidates are ranked based on their policy proposals and engagement with key issues. This approach aims to shift the focus from mere electability to the merits of different policy platforms and fosters a more informed public discourse. The piece also touches upon the challenges of changing ingrained journalistic practices and the potential biases in media coverage.
records.quote: Most people who pay attention to politics know that candidates who cannot win are safely ignored by the press until they threaten to affect the outcome.

records.title: Who's Ahead?  No, Seriously...
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen critiques the horse-race frame of campaign coverage and asks which candidates are 'ahead' on substantive issues such as health care, civil liberties, education, and the Internet rather than on polls alone.
records.quote: It's nice to know that Mitt Romney has pulled ahead in New Hampshire, seven months before the primary voting.

records.title: Twilight for the Curmudgeons
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen responds to Neil Henry's call for Google reparations to old media and argues that the curmudgeon class in newsrooms and journalism schools has lost the people best able to save the business.
records.quote: Link rot must not be allowed to set in, for this is a document.

records.title: Curmudgeon NH
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen discusses the tension between veteran journalists and the emerging digital media landscape.  Veteran journalists, exemplified by Neil Henry's critique of Google's role in the decline of traditional news, express resentment towards search engines and online platforms for profiting from journalistic content without sufficient reciprocal support.  Younger journalists and commentators, however, argue that the problem lies not with technology but with the outdated business models of traditional media. The piece highlights the generational divide, contrasting the anxieties of older journalists with the more optimistic adaptation of younger ones to the digital world.
records.quote: Technology isnt destroying journalism. Its simply destroying the business that subsidized journalism.

records.title: When the Press Fails…
records.author: W. Lance Bennett, Regina G. Lawrence, and Steven Livingston
records.summary: This article critiques the American press's failure to maintain independence and accurately report on significant events, particularly the Iraq War.  The authors argue that the press's reliance on official sources, pursuit of insider politics, and adherence to a flawed notion of objectivity led to complicity in the administration's manipulation of the news.  They highlight instances where the press missed or downplayed crucial information, contributing to public misinformation and a lack of critical scrutiny of government actions. The authors suggest that the press's ingrained dependence on government for legitimacy prevents it from effectively challenging power, even when recognizing its own failings.
records.quote: Legions of critics and off-duty journalists are searching for answers to why it is so difficult to be independent and get stories straight. Why is it so hard to resist the ever-present spin of those in power?

records.title: A Blog is a Little First Amendment Machine
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen uses five stories as parables to argue that blogging acts as a 'little First Amendment machine,' disrupting one-way mass media and opening democratic possibilities for journalism.
records.quote: When in the eighteenth century the press first appeared on the political stage the people on the other end of it were known as the public.

records.title: Howard Kurtz: The Humble Interview Under Assault
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A response to Howard Kurtz's column about the decline of the traditional media interview, examining how the internet and blogging have changed the power dynamics between journalists and their subjects.
records.quote: The internet and blogging have shifted the power dynamics between journalists and their subjects, putting the traditional media interview — and the journalists who conduct it — under new forms of pressure.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Howard Kurtz Sez: "The humble interview, the linchpin of journalism for centuries, is under assault."
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This is a transcript of an email interview between Jay Rosen and Howard Kurtz, discussing the changing nature of the interview in the context of the rise of the internet and citizen journalism. Rosen argues that the traditional interview is not obsolete, but the balance of power has shifted due to sources having more direct access to audiences. He discusses his experiences with interviews, the limitations of soundbites, and the challenges of collaborative journalism projects like Assignment Zero and Off the Bus, which aim to incorporate citizen contributors into news coverage.
records.quote: What’s missing is any openness to the idea that an interview can be truly dialogic - that the interviewer has as much to learn as the interviewee.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Interview Week at Assignment Zero: Anna Haynes is Questioning SusanG of Daily Kos
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen presents an interview with Susan Gardner of Daily Kos about crowdsourced journalism.  Gardner discusses the potential of crowdsourcing for analyzing large datasets (like proposed legislation or email dumps), the motivations of contributors (a sense of civic duty and frustration with mainstream media), and the challenges of managing crowdsourced projects (coordination, avoiding excessive research tangents, and defining success).  She highlights the importance of clear roles, strong collaborative software, and a balance between researchers and writers in successful projects.  The interview is presented as a work-in-progress, soliciting further questions and input from readers.
records.quote: I think its also a revival of the notion of participatory democracy. Those who are gifted with analysis, research and interpretive skills feel they’re giving something back to the country by exposing corruption.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: "Something Quite Breathtaking." My Exchange with Neil Lewis of the New York Times
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Jay Rosen publishes an on-the-record exchange with New York Times correspondent Neil Lewis about press ethics, the White House Correspondents' Dinner, and the American press's failure to challenge the run-up to the Iraq war.
records.quote: Neil Lewis, a Washington correspondent for the New York Times, wrote me about my criticisms of his colleague, Jim Rutenberg, in a previous post.

records.title: PressThink: An Exchange with Neil Lewis of the New York Times
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen presents a correspondence between Jay Rosen and Neil Lewis of the New York Times. Lewis objects to Rosen's criticism of a colleague's interview practices, arguing that editing and condensing are inherent to journalism. Rosen clarifies his criticism, focusing not on the editing itself but on the reporter's framing of a discussion about the White House Correspondents' Dinner within a misleading 'bloggers vs. journalists' narrative. Rosen contends that this framing obscures a larger issue: the failure of the press to adequately confront its relationship with the Bush administration and its role in the Iraq War.
records.quote: The failure of much of the American press to uncover — and provide some prominence to — the private doubts and even the public case against the war was, in my view, it’s most egregious failure in my 50 years in journalism.

records.title: PressThink: Assignment Zero, Updated. With Initial Results...
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen details the progress and challenges of Assignment Zero, a collaborative journalism project exploring crowdsourcing and peer production. The project, initially focused on a broad investigation of wisdom-of-the-crowd efforts, shifted to a more focused approach involving five key topics and an "Interview Week" to gather information from key figures. The project utilized a Creative Commons license, emphasizing transparency and open collaboration. Challenges included creating a user-friendly platform for contributors and initially selecting a complex first story. Despite setbacks, the project aimed to produce five feature stories and numerous Q&As for Wired.com, with support from the Online News Association.
records.quote: Whether Assignment Zero worked or not is ultimately in the journalism.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: That Man Tried to Run You Over. Why Are You Having Dinner With Him?
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen welcomes the New York Times' withdrawal from the White House Correspondents Association dinner as a symbolic rejection of the Bush-era consensus that marginalized the press, and criticizes journalism's reluctance to confront that structural failure.
records.quote: It's good news that journalists at the New York Times will no longer participate in the bloated and compromised White House Correspondents Association dinner.

records.title: When Fairness Really Bites
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen critiques the White House Correspondents' Dinner, arguing that it symbolizes the failure of the press to hold power accountable, particularly during the Bush administration. Rosen discusses the changing relationship between the press and the White House, noting the Bush administration's attempts to marginalize and discredit the press. Rosen also reflects on his own experiences being interviewed for news stories, highlighting the power dynamics between reporters and sources and the limitations of traditional journalistic interviews in the age of blogging.
records.quote: In our democracy, the people who represent the public stood for election… I don’t believe you have a check-and-balance function.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: News, Improved: Learning to Change
records.author: Michele McLellan and Tim Porter
records.summary: This article discusses the necessary changes in newsroom leadership, culture, and training for newspapers to survive in the digital age.  It highlights the shift from autocratic management styles to collaborative leadership, emphasizing the need for communication, coaching, and risk-taking. The authors also detail the importance of transitioning from defensive newsroom cultures to adaptive ones that foster creativity and initiative, suggesting strategies such as increased training and staff-level decision-making.
records.quote: The future of news will belong to those who build it.

records.title: PressThink: Participate in Politics by Covering the Campaign: NewAssignment.Net and Huffington Post Team Up
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Jay Rosen and Arianna Huffington announce a joint venture in campaign journalism, involving a large network of contributors covering various presidential candidates. The project, housed on NewAssignment.Net and affiliated with the Huffington Post, aims to provide diverse perspectives on the campaign beyond traditional media's limitations, utilizing a ‘pro-am’ model with volunteer contributors and a Creative Commons license. While the initiative embraces the potential of many voices, concerns are raised about the potential for the project to still reflect dominant perspectives rather than genuinely diverse ones.
records.quote: So instead of one well-placed reporter trailing John Edwards wherever he goes (which is one way of doing it) some 40 or 50 differently-placed people tracking different parts of the Edwards campaign, all with peculiar beats and personal blogs linked together by virtue of having a common editor and a page through which the best and most original stuff filters out to the greater readership of the Web, especially via the Huffington Post.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Participate in Politics by Covering the Campaign
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen announces a Huffington Post/NewAssignment.Net partnership for the 2008 campaign that will enlist many volunteer contributors to cover candidate beats, proposing a distributed, pro-am alternative to traditional bus journalism.
records.quote: Arianna Huffington and I are announcing today a new joint venture in campaign journalism.

records.title: PressThink: Assignment Zero, Day Six: Help Wanted Section
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This is a call to action, recruiting journalists and other skilled individuals to volunteer for Assignment Zero, a crowdsourced journalism project.  The project aims to collaboratively report on the spread of crowdsourcing and peer production methods, breaking down a large story into manageable parts for a team of professional and amateur contributors.  Rosen highlights the need for editors, reporters, web-savvy journalists, organizers, and developers to help manage the project's complexity and scale, emphasizing the innovative, pro-am model of journalism.
records.quote: Journalism by the many, edited by a few, requires great efficiency and strong systems.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Assignment Zero
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen announces Assignment Zero, a collaborative journalism project exploring the potential of crowdsourcing and peer production in newsgathering.  The project aims to investigate the spread of crowdsourcing, using a pro-am model involving professional journalists and citizen journalists working together to report on a topic at a scale beyond the capabilities of a traditional newsroom.  The initiative highlights the shift in the relationship between journalists and audiences, leveraging the informational strengths of the 'people formerly known as the audience' and embracing radical transparency.
records.quote: Our hope is that a team of professionals, working with scores of citizen journalists, is capable of completing an investigative project of far greater scope than a team of two or three professionals ever could.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: They're Not in Your Club but They Are in Your League: Firedoglake at the Libby Trial
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes Firedoglake's coverage of the Scooter Libby trial, arguing that its live-blogging, driven by a committed community and a lack of official coverage, produced superior reporting to that of mainstream media.  Rosen contrasts the established journalistic norms with Firedoglake's success, highlighting the changing media landscape and the potential of online communities to generate reliable and impactful news coverage.
records.quote: Blogging allows us to go direct with our knowledge, experience and insights, without waiting for a reporter to ask us what we think.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Situation Grave and Deteriorating for the Agnewocracy
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen uses the Jamil Hussein/AP dispute and conservative admissions by Rich Lowry and Max Boot to argue that the conservative "Agnewocracy" bias campaign left many on the right unable to accept bad news from Iraq, while the mainstream press proved the more reliable reality check.
records.quote: A first-class hate object, as they were in '64.

records.title: PressThink: Grave and Deteriorating for the Children of Agnew
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the conservative backlash against the mainstream media, particularly focusing on the Iraq War.  It argues that the distrust of the mainstream media among conservatives, fueled by partisan loyalty to President Bush and a desire to discredit perceived liberal bias, led to a detachment from reality regarding the situation in Iraq.  Rosen highlights how this rejection of empirical evidence hampered effective policy and contributed to the war's failure, contrasting the actions of conservatives with the more realistic assessment offered by some conservative voices like Rich Lowry, who acknowledged the mainstream media's accuracy in reporting on the war's dire conditions. The article uses the Jamil Hussein controversy as a case study to illustrate these broader points about political polarization and the role of media.
records.quote: “Realism is essential in any war, and it is impossible without an ability to assimilate bad news, even bad news that comes from distasteful sources.”

records.title: PressThink: Check out Placeblogger.com. It's About All Those Hyperlocal News Sites Springing Up...
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen discusses the launch of Placeblogger.com, a website designed to connect and promote hyperlocal blogs.  Rosen highlights the significance of placeblogs as a form of community-based journalism, emphasizing their focus on lived experience and local news beyond the scope of traditional media.  The article also features commentary from various individuals in the blogosphere and traditional media, discussing the potential impact of placeblogs on the future of journalism and the changing media landscape.
records.quote: Placeblogs represent the lived experience of a place; newspapers reflect the tiny slice of that experience that is news.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: The Retreat from Empiricism and Ron Suskind's Intellectual Scoop
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen argues that political journalism has retreated from empiricism — the commitment to verifiable facts — in favor of he-said/she-said balance that treats all claims as equivalent regardless of evidence.
records.quote: Political journalism has abandoned its commitment to verifiable facts in favor of a false balance that treats all claims as equally credible, substituting the appearance of fairness for the harder work of determining what is actually true.

records.title: PressThink: Retreat from Empiricism: On Ron Suskind's Scoop
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes Ron Suskind's article "Without a Doubt," focusing on the Bush administration's rejection of "reality-based community" decision-making.  Rosen argues that the Bush administration prioritized action over evidence-based policy, actively shaping reality through its actions and suppressing dissenting voices.  He contrasts this approach with traditional policymaking and discusses the implications for the press and the setting of public narratives about events like the Iraq War.
records.quote: We’re an empire now, and when we act, we create our own reality. And while you’re studying that reality — judiciously, as you will — we’ll act again, creating other new realities, which you can study too, and that’s how things will sort out.

records.title: PressThink: Newspaper Chain Goes Creative Commons: GateHouse Media Rolls CC Over 96 Newspaper Sites
records.author: Lisa Williams
records.summary: GateHouse Media, a newspaper conglomerate, is adopting Creative Commons licenses for nearly all its Massachusetts newspapers and TownOnline sites, a move toward greater openness on the web. This decision, though using a restrictive non-commercial license, is significant as few major media outlets have embraced CC licensing. The company is also incorporating user-generated content and open-source software (Zope) into its platforms, potentially impacting newsroom jobs but also presenting opportunities for innovation and revenue generation through increased online traffic and potential software sales. The article discusses the implications of this open approach, including potential challenges and the intriguing reception from investors who see it as an internet-style business model.
records.quote: For a major publisher with significant numbers of people reading to be doing this is great.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: "A Collection of Journalists Who Have Distinctive Signatures." That's What John Harris Has in Mind.
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This is a Q&A with John Harris and Jim VandeHei, who left the Washington Post to start a new “multi-platform” political news operation.  The conversation centers on their reasons for leaving, their vision for a new kind of political journalism that emphasizes individual journalist signatures, in-depth reporting beyond the “front story,”  a more conversational and transparent style, and a multi-platform approach leveraging web and broadcast partnerships. They aim to fill a perceived niche in political news by providing insightful context and behind-the-scenes reporting that other outlets are not consistently delivering.
records.quote: We believe that for people who want this type of stability, journalism is not going to remain an attractive profession for much longer. But people who adapt will thrive and end up having more fun than in the old days.

records.title: Extra!  Extra! John Harris and Jim VandeHei to Pull Back the Curtain on Official Washington!
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen examines John Harris and Jim VandeHei's move from the Washington Post to an Allbritton political news venture and argues that its "next generation" rhetoric masks a conventional insider model rather than a genuine break with traditional political journalism.
records.quote: It will correspond to a new Washington newspaper, the Capitol Leader, which will publish three days a week and only when Congress is in session.

records.title: PressThink: This Just In: John Harris and Jim VandeHei to Pull Back the Curtain on Official Washington
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the departure of John Harris and Jim VandeHei from the Washington Post to launch a new multi-platform political news operation with Allbritton Communications.  Rosen questions the novelty of their proclaimed "next generation" approach, which emphasizes transparency and interactivity but appears to rely on traditional journalistic practices and insider access.  The core innovation seems to be a willingness to break established norms regarding source disclosure and the unspoken agreements within political reporting.
records.quote: There’s little question we’re in the midst of a period of profound change, and the moves by Harris and VandeHei are a fascinating reminder of that fact.

records.title: PressThink: Pro Thinks Pro-Am Reporting Could Work: John McQuaid Interview, Part Two
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This interview between Jay Rosen and John McQuaid discusses the evolving role of technology and citizen participation in investigative journalism. McQuaid highlights the potential of online communities and networks for collaborative reporting, enabling journalists to access diverse perspectives and expertise. Rosen and McQuaid debate the limitations of traditional “he said, she said” journalism and advocate for more assertive investigative reporting that draws conclusions and challenges established narratives, even acknowledging the potential backlash from ideologically committed groups. The discussion centers on the need for innovative reporting techniques to maintain public confidence and deliver impactful, explanatory journalism in a rapidly changing media landscape.
records.quote: Journalists are in the business of assembling and refining knowledge — not just facts, but ideas — and we need allies of all stripes.

records.title: PressThink: Top Pro Thinks Pro-Am Reporting Has Promise
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This is an interview with John McQuaid, a Pulitzer Prize-winning investigative journalist who left the Times-Picayune due to cost-cutting and the changing landscape of journalism.  McQuaid discusses his transition to online investigative journalism, reflecting on the limitations of traditional newspaper models and the potential of the web for in-depth reporting. He highlights the shift in access to information, the changing role of the reader, and the challenges and opportunities of adapting investigative journalism to the dynamic nature of the internet.
records.quote: Newspaper journalists watched the revolution unfold on their desktops along with everyone else, and rejoiced. But, of course, without knowing it, we were also watching our own relevancy decline.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Polling Place Photo Project: An Open Source Photo Essay
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen discusses the Polling Place Photo Project (PPPP), an open-source initiative aiming to document the American voting experience through citizen-generated photographs. The project, a collaboration between AIGA, Design Observer, and NewAssignment.Net, seeks to improve the accuracy and understanding of the voting process by supplementing traditional media coverage with firsthand visual accounts. It also serves as a test case for the feasibility and ergonomics of large-scale, volunteer-based, open-source data collection and social network reporting.
records.quote: The project’s goal, according to its designer and prime mover William Drenttel, is “an archive of photographs that captures the richness and complexity of voting in America.” A second aim is to “encourage research into how voting happens and how voting can be made easier, clearer, less confusing, more reliable.”
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Political Ergonomics and the Launch of an Open Source Photo Essay
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen introduces the Polling Place Photo Project, an open-source photography effort to document Americans voting, and frames it as an exercise in political ergonomics that could improve how elections are understood and experienced.
records.quote: When Americans vote on November 7th, what will it look like?

records.title: Stephen Harper’s Press Gallery Put Down
records.author: Ira Basen
records.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Stephen Harper's deliberate strategy to undermine the Ottawa press gallery is analyzed. Harper, mirroring George W. Bush's approach, aimed to diminish the press's influence by limiting access and promoting alternative channels of communication. This involved restricting press conference question selection, favoring one-on-one interviews with handpicked journalists, and utilizing alternative media like podcasts and websites to bypass traditional media filters. While initially met with a walkout by the press gallery, Harper's strategy aimed at 'de-certifying' the press, thereby weakening its ability to hold the government accountable. The article contrasts this with the relatively positive press coverage Harper received, highlighting the strategic nature of his actions rather than a response to actual grievances.
records.quote: Harper wanted to see if he could fundamentally change the relationship between his government and the people who cover it.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Spouse on Campaign Payroll? Sunlight's New Tool
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This blog post discusses Sunlight Foundation's new project, "Find out if Congress is a Family Business," which uses a distributed reporting model to investigate whether members of Congress employ their spouses on their campaigns. The project highlights the potential of citizen journalism and networked tools to enhance transparency and accountability in government. Rosen's post also touches on broader themes in journalism, including the need for innovation, the challenges facing traditional news organizations, and the evolving relationship between citizens and the media in the digital age.
records.quote: “Members who hire spouses to work on their campaigns pay them from the campaign contributions they raise from special interests— in effect, allowing their political fundraising to add to their personal income,” said the press release from Sunlight.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Citizen Journalism Expert Jay Rosen Answers Your Questions...
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen features a Q&A with Jay Rosen, discussing the role of newspapers in the age of online media and citizen journalism.  Rosen analyzes Bluffton Today, an experimental newspaper that reversed the traditional print-to-web workflow, highlighting its attempt at community-driven journalism. He addresses concerns about the lack of respect for online journalism compared to established media, arguing that the failure is not just suppression of truth but a failure of imagination and methodology within traditional journalism. Finally, he discusses challenges and safeguards for ensuring accuracy and preventing misinformation in open-source reporting models.
records.quote: The people formerly known as the audience (as I call them) are now a producer force to be reckoned with, and Big Media has just started that reckoning.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: All the news that's fit to open-source - CNET
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This text describes an early experiment in citizen journalism, NewAssignment.net, funded by Reuters. The initiative, spearheaded by Jay Rosen, aimed to collaborate amateur and professional journalists on investigative reports using open-source methods. The funding would support the site's first editor, with an anticipated launch the following spring. Blog community responses expressed excitement and optimism about the potential for this collaborative approach to transform journalism.
records.quote: What's more important is to help journalists figure out how to interact with the blogosphere--that big global, interactive, viral conversation about the things that matter to people.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Editing Horizontally: Thanks to Reuters, NewAssignment.Net Can Hire Someone
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Reuters is giving $100,000 to NewAssignment.Net, an experiment in open source journalism where people collaborate peer-to-peer in the production of editorial goods. The money will underwrite the costs of hiring the project's first editor. The aim is to draw smart crowds into collaboration and get stories done that aren’t getting done now, pooling intelligence and dividing up the work. The project seeks a middle path between traditional journalism and new forms like blogging and social media, exploring ways to augment and accelerate the creation of quality journalism.
records.quote: Ultimately, journalism is about the story and the pursuit of truth; it is not about the news industry, a j-school or a traditional newsroom structure.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Sunlight Gives $10K to NewAssignment.Net
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen discusses the Sunlight Foundation's initiatives to promote citizen journalism and increase government transparency. It highlights projects like Exposing Earmarks and the Political Transparency Project, which utilize citizen volunteers to investigate and report on government activities. Rosen explores the potential of the internet to empower citizens as watchdogs, while acknowledging the challenges and risks associated with amateur journalism.
records.quote: The internet, and the platforms it provides, has revealed a much richer, more imaginative, eccentric, and curious populace than popular culture portrays.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Exploding By-Lines: Update on NewAssignment.Net
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This blog post discusses the development of NewAssignment.Net, a pro-am journalism project aiming to combine the work of professional and amateur journalists.  It explores the challenges and potential of networked journalism, using the Exposing Earmarks project and Robert Greenwald's fundraising for a documentary as case studies. Rosen's post also highlights the importance of ease of use, clear assignments, and managing user expectations for the success of such collaborative projects, while acknowledging uncertainties about its viability.
records.quote: One non-profit group, NewAssignment.Net, plans to combine the work of amateurs and professionals to produce investigative stories on the internet.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: The Era of Networked Journalism Begins
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This blog post discusses the Exposing Earmarks Project, a collaborative effort between various organizations (including conservative and liberal groups) and citizen journalists to uncover secret congressional spending. The project uses a networked journalism model, combining professional journalists with citizen participation to investigate and report on government earmarks. Rosen analyzes the project's successes and challenges, including its slow start and questions about its political neutrality, highlighting the evolving nature of pro-am journalism and the complexities of citizen engagement in investigative reporting.
records.quote: This is networked journalism (professionals and amateurs working together to get the real story) beginning to come of age, and it’s very much in the spirit in my initiative NewAssignment.Net.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: How Realistic is NewAssignment.Net?
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen responds to critiques of Rosen's proposed NewAssignment.Net, a platform for collaborative journalism funded by users and donors. Critics raise concerns about the feasibility of user-funded stories, the potential for ideological bias, and the challenges of balancing user input with editorial control. Rosen addresses these concerns by highlighting the role of editor reserve funds, the importance of establishing trust between editors and users, and the flexibility of the funding model. He also discusses the need for transparency and the possibility of incorporating other funding streams, such as advertising and syndication.
records.quote: The heart and soul is the connection, or bond, between a New Assignment editor and the community of users drawn to an editor’s portion of the site because they can participate in the coming together of important stories.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Liberation! On Creating the New Haven Independent
records.author: Paul Bass
records.summary: Paul Bass recounts his experience transitioning from traditional corporate journalism to founding the online, non-profit New Haven Independent. He details the challenges and rewards of this shift, emphasizing the increased reader engagement, interactive elements, and the return to a mission-driven approach to local news reporting. The article highlights the limitations of corporate media and the potential of a non-profit, community-focused model for online news.
records.quote: I’ve concluded that, yes, most conventional journalists can make the leap into the future of community journalism. They’ll be excited to discover that they can return to the mission that brought them to the business in the first place, while finding new ways to work alongside readers to report the news and rebuild a civic dialogue.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: The Pros Gonna Blog You Under the Table
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This satirical piece critiques mainstream journalism's self-congratulatory pronouncements about its supposed dominance over blogging. Rosen argues that journalists' attempts to incorporate blogging techniques are superficial and fail to capture the essence of what makes successful blogs thrive: passion, irreverence, consistent engagement, and genuine interest in the online conversation. He uses examples of prominent journalists abandoning their blogs and the lack of engagement from established news organizations' blogs to support his claim, highlighting the persistent gap between professional journalism's rhetoric and its actual practice in the digital space. Rosen concludes with observations about the poor competitive response of mainstream media to the challenges presented by online platforms and blogs.
records.quote: It would do us all good if the pros would stop predicting the demise of blogging, and get busy learning to use blogging in their reporting.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Nick Lemann's Amateur Hour
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This is a response to Nicholas Lemann's critique of citizen journalism, "Amateur Hour."  Rosen largely agrees with Lemann's concerns about the quality and reliability of citizen journalism but argues against a simplistic dichotomy between professional and amateur journalism. He emphasizes the historical continuity between blogging and earlier forms of citizen journalism and suggests that a more nuanced understanding is needed, recognizing both the potential and limitations of both professional and citizen journalism. Rosen also highlights the challenges of funding and sustaining high-quality citizen journalism initiatives, like his own New Assignment.Net.
records.quote: Journalism is enmeshed with and supported by the media, but has an older and more important purpose.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Journalism Professors Pass a Resolution
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Coverage of a resolution passed by the Association for Education in Journalism and Mass Communication (AEJMC), examining what the professional body's stance reveals about tensions within journalism education.
records.quote: When journalism educators pass resolutions, the document itself becomes evidence — of what the profession considers safe to say, what tensions it can acknowledge, and what contradictions it still cannot bring itself to name.

records.title: NewAssignment.Net: Part Two
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen discusses the potential challenges and benefits of NewAssignment.Net, a platform for crowdsourced journalism funding.  The central argument revolves around the crucial role of skilled editors in maintaining journalistic integrity and independence despite funding from interested parties.  Concerns about donor influence, the potential for biased reporting, and the reliability of crowd-sourced information are addressed, with Rosen emphasizing the importance of a strong editorial process and reserve funds to mitigate these risks.  The success of the platform hinges on the ability of editors to cultivate a network of reliable supporters, navigate conflicting interests, and maintain editorial control despite funding pressures.
records.quote: “The editor’s job at New Assignment is going to be as much about managing online community as about assigning stories, editing copy and mentoring reporters,” Scott writes. “That’s a demanding, but certainly not impossible, pile of responsibilities.”
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Introducing NewAssignment.Net
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen proposes NewAssignment.Net, a non-profit platform aiming to fund high-quality, original reporting through donations.  It leverages open-source methods, allowing for public participation in developing and refining story assignments before professional journalists are contracted to complete the work. This model aims to address the funding crisis in journalism by directly connecting interested citizens with investigative reporting projects, bypassing traditional media outlets. The platform intends to produce original journalism through collaboration between professional journalists and citizen contributors, and addresses funding challenges faced by the news industry.
records.quote: Journalism has always been subsidized, whether by the pure commerce of classified ads or the mass media monopoly of the old network newscasts.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Free Pass
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen critiques a Fortune magazine column by Justin Fox that argues publicly traded corporations are the best ownership model for newspapers.  Rosen contends that Fox's assertion is based on a misrepresentation of prevailing wisdom within the newspaper industry. He argues that Fox presents a fact-free observation, lacking quotes, examples, or links to support his claim that the industry universally believes local ownership is the solution to its problems. Rosen counters with numerous quotes from various journalists and commentators showing a much more nuanced and cautious perspective on local ownership, highlighting the lack of evidence for Fox's sweeping conclusion.
records.quote: There’s an upside, there’s a downside to local ownership. Reasons to be hopeful, reasons to be wary.

records.title: "We are Covering the War on Terror, It's a Classified War."
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen reflects on the New York Times and Los Angeles Times stories about secret government tracking of global bank transfers, arguing that the press's legitimacy depends on independence, verification, transparency, and truthtelling rather than on a claim to represent the public will.
records.quote: Since those headlines appeared on June 23rd storm conditions have prevailed over the big castle of press authority.

records.title: PressThink: It's a Classified War
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the intense backlash against the New York Times's publication of stories revealing secret government programs related to tracking global bank transfers and the war on terror. Rosen examines the legitimacy of the press in the face of government secrecy, the debate over journalistic ethics in covering classified information, and the political motivations behind the attacks on the press, connecting them to a broader strategy by the Bush administration to roll back the press's influence and expand executive power. Rosen also discusses the inadequacy of simple formulas like 'when in doubt, publish' and the lack of effective responses from journalism educators.
records.quote: Precisely because no one elected the press it must find other means of securing its legitimacy. These are inevitably political in nature; they involve persuasion and “public opinion” as well as the protections of law.

records.title: Networked journalism
records.author: Jeff Jarvis
records.summary: This article discusses two prominent issues in journalism: the challenges of journalists' social media use and the impact of Google's AI on news traffic.  It uses the example of Terry Moran's dismissal from ABC News for a critical tweet about Stephen Miller and Trump to illustrate the complexities of social media policies for news organizations. The piece also addresses Google's AI-powered search results significantly reducing traffic to news websites, suggesting that news organizations need to cultivate direct relationships with their audiences through subscriptions and newsletters to counteract this trend. Finally, it acknowledges the retirement of media critic Jay Rosen from NYU.
records.quote: In networked journalism, the public can get involved in a story before it is reported, contributing facts, questions, and suggestions.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen, written from the perspective of 'the people formerly known as the audience,' announces their existence and the shift in power dynamics due to the rise of digital media. It emphasizes that the audience is no longer a passive recipient of information but active participants with the ability to create, share, and control media. The article challenges traditional media's perception of the audience as mere 'eyeballs' and asserts the audience's autonomy and ability to engage on their own terms.
records.quote: Once the users take control, they never give it back.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: The People Formerly Known As The Audience
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen explores the shift in power dynamics between traditional media and its audience, now empowered by new technologies and participatory platforms. Rosen argues that the audience is no longer passive, but actively involved in creating, sharing, and distributing information, thus challenging the traditional one-way model of media communication. This shift necessitates adaptation from traditional media organizations, who are urged to embrace collaboration and recognize the audience's agency.
records.quote: The people formerly known as the audience are those who were on the receiving end of a media system that ran one way, in a broadcasting pattern, with high entry fees and a few firms competing to speak very loudly while the rest of the population listened in isolation from one another— and who today are not in a situation like that at all.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Case Study for an Unconference
records.author: Ken Sands
records.summary: Ken Sands, online publisher for The Spokesman-Review, discusses his newspaper's efforts to integrate user-generated content and social media into their journalism.  He argues that readers possess more knowledge than journalists and proposes experiments to leverage this collective intelligence, including webcasting news meetings, creating community blogs, and tapping into existing online fan networks.  Sands seeks collaboration and ideas from BloggerCon attendees to improve newsgathering and build a more sustainable business model.
records.quote: The readers and users know more than we do. How do we make from that better journalism?
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Users-Know-More-Than-We-Do Journalism
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen discusses the potential and challenges of "readers-know-more-than-we-do" journalism, also known as open-source journalism.  It explores how the internet and distributed knowledge can be used to break news, focusing on collaborative reporting and citizen involvement. Rosen questions how to effectively utilize social networks, collaborative editing, and citizen journalism to produce reliable and impactful news stories while addressing concerns about accuracy, reliability, and potential manipulation by partisan opponents.
records.quote: Participatory media matters because it’s where the most influential part of the mainstream media’s audience is increasingly turning, now and in the near future. And the news business does — and should — should care very much about the influence it wields, directly and indirectly.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: The Pledge: Philly Newspapers Bought by Local Big Shots
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen examines the Philadelphia newspapers' sale to local investors and the pledge to protect editorial independence, asking whether local, civic-minded ownership can sustain journalism that serves the city rather than purely commercial interests.
records.quote: The happy fact is we don't know the answer to questions like that.

records.title: The New War on Voting
records.author: Angie Coiro
records.summary: The June/July 2006 issue of *Mother Jones* magazine, accessible on archive.org, focuses on several key topics. The main feature investigates restrictions on voting access through voter ID laws and other methods. Additional articles explore how corporations benefit from public assistance programs and the human impact of the Iraq War. The issue, published by the Foundation for National Progress, also covers broader themes typical of the magazine, including environmental issues, corporate power, and social justice. The content is available for online reading and download in multiple formats, including PDF, EPUB, and Kindle.
records.quote: These are people who have risked everything to come to America, and they're willing to die for this country. That's a level of commitment that we shouldn't ignore.
concepts: Not the odds but the stakes

records.title: PressThink: A Prayer for the Philly Papers
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the sale of the Philadelphia Inquirer and Daily News to a local ownership group, focusing on the implications of a “pledge” of editorial independence from the new owners.  Rosen explores the uncertainty surrounding the success of this experiment in local ownership, contrasting the perspectives of those who are optimistic about a potential break from traditional ownership models and those who are skeptical based on the history of the newspapers and the new owner's past.  The article highlights the importance of not knowing the outcome and the need for a truly experimental approach, acknowledging the potential for both success and failure.
records.quote: The future of democracy is going to depend on how well the country is informed about its problems.

records.title: PressThink: That al Qaeda Doesn't Believe in Transparency is a Big Reason We Do
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes Tony Snow's debut as White House Press Secretary, contrasting his style with that of Scott McClellan.  Rosen argues that the Bush administration's approach to press briefings, characterized by limited transparency and control of the agenda, is inadequate for winning the 'war of ideas.' He proposes a dramatic increase in briefings, targeting diverse audiences including international and religious press, bloggers, and the general public, to counter the administration's perceived strategic communication failures and effectively engage in a global contest for public opinion.
records.quote: The only way we can lose this is if we lack political will to see it through.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: "Nice and Collegial and Relaxed:" Four Scenes From Tony Snow's First Meet with the Press
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen transcribes Tony Snow's first press gaggle as White House Press Secretary on May 12, 2006.  The transcript reveals challenges in managing the gaggle, including its unexpected early start and overcrowding, leading to adjustments in location and communication.  The Q&A session covers various topics, including the administration's credibility,  'Setting the Record Straight' strategy, international affairs, and an ongoing Justice Department investigation. Snow's responses often highlight his new role and limited knowledge of certain issues, while emphasizing his commitment to transparency and collaboration with the press.
records.quote: I’ll tell you what we will do then is we will move it back into the Briefing Room. I had this wonderful idea that this would be nice and collegial and relaxed, but it obviously at this point is just a mess.

records.title: Forecast for Snow
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the abrupt resignation of CIA Director Porter Goss and its implications for the relationship between the Bush White House and the press. Rosen speculates on whether the new White House press secretary, Tony Snow, will represent a change in strategy, moving away from the previous administration's attempts to de-certify and marginalize the press. Rosen discusses the White House's lack of transparency regarding Goss's departure and considers the possibility of the press corps boycotting White House briefings as a symbolic response to the administration's lack of reason-giving and contempt for the press.
records.quote: An Administration that doesn’t have to give reasons for what it is doing is unaccountable to the American people and their common sense, to world opinion— even to itself.

records.title: PressThink: Snow at the Podium, Rollback on the Rocks
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the Bush White House's strategic communication approach, characterized by a policy of 'Rollback' – starving the news media and disengaging from the press.  The appointment of Tony Snow as press secretary is interpreted as a shift away from this strategy, signaling a potential return to more conventional media engagement.  Rosen contrasts this approach with that of Theodore Roosevelt, who actively cultivated the press to enhance presidential power.  The article questions the effectiveness of the Rollback strategy and explores the broader implications of the White House's relationship with the media, particularly in the context of the 'War on Terror' and the battle for world opinion.
records.quote: The presidency itself had been made bigger by media.

records.title: PressThink: Murray Waas is Our Woodward Now
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen contrasts the investigative journalism of Bob Woodward with that of Murray Waas, arguing that Waas is the more effective and accurate reporter in uncovering the truth behind the Bush administration's justifications for the Iraq War. The piece highlights Waas's meticulous fact-checking, multiple sourcing, and outsider perspective, contrasting it with Woodward's perceived access journalism and apparent susceptibility to manipulation by the Bush administration. Rosen suggests that Waas's work represents a shift away from insider journalism and toward a more rigorous, fact-based approach.
records.quote: Not only is Woodward not in the hunt, but he is slowly turning into the hunted.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: No End to Any Argument: Keller on Transparency
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes New York Times executive editor Bill Keller's decision to avoid reading media blogs like Romenesko, framing it as a case study of the changing relationship between the established press and online media.  Rosen critiques Keller's view that engaging with online criticism leads to unproductive "self-absorption," arguing that it reflects a misunderstanding of the dynamic nature of online conversation and a failure to adapt to the evolving power dynamics of the news media landscape. Rosen suggests alternative strategies for engaging with online criticism, proposing the creation of a Times blog dedicated to addressing editorial decisions and fostering more constructive dialogue.
records.quote: If you don’t explain yourself, you just invite others to do the explaining of you for you.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Open Source Journalism
records.author: Richard Poynder
records.summary: This article presents an interview with Jay Rosen, a journalism professor, discussing the evolution from public journalism to citizen journalism and the potential of open-source journalism. Rosen argues that the press needs to collaborate with bloggers to create a new form of journalism where the public and professionals cooperate. He emphasizes that the web has shifted the debate, and journalists must adapt to the changing media landscape to remain relevant, sharing journalism with bloggers and developing a new collaborative relationship.
records.quote: All kinds of knowledge monopolies — and positions of authority based on them — are wearing away … [and] … the professionals who have gained control of institutions of various kinds — including politics — are not going to have that kind of control anymore.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Red America, RIP... and the Great Blogger Bake Off
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Following Ben Domenech's resignation from washingtonpost.com due to plagiarism accusations, Jay Rosen proposes an open online competition to select the next political blogger. He argues this would be a more innovative and transparent approach than the initial hiring process, showcasing the blogosphere's ability to vet and select credible voices while addressing the controversy surrounding Domenech's hiring and subsequent dismissal.
records.quote: The blogospheric “market” should reward or punish behavior and let us develop consistent with the expectations and preferences of our readers.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Twelve Newspapers in a State of Nature
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen discusses the precarious state of several newspapers following Knight-Ridder's sale to McClatchy. McClatchy's unwillingness to retain several papers creates an opportunity for local ownership models, potentially involving community groups, non-profit organizations, or educational institutions. Rosen urges journalists and community members to proactively seek alternative ownership structures rather than passively awaiting the outcome, highlighting examples of community-owned newspapers and advocating for a more active role in shaping the future of local journalism.
