records.quote: Rather than passively awaiting the outcome of Knight-Ridder's sale to McClatchy, Rosen urges journalists and community members to proactively seek alternative ownership structures—community groups, nonprofits, or educational institutions—as a path to preserving local journalism.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
Not the odds but the stakes

records.title: The Six Degrees of Newspaper Blogging and Why the Guardian is Ahead
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen uses the launch of the Guardian's comment-is-free site to argue that newspapers should move beyond simply starting blogs and instead create aggregator-style platforms that add value through reader engagement and local blogger participation.
records.quote: It's an aggregator for local bloggers in a town with a lot of them.

records.title: PressThink: Seeders of Clouds: Latest on Newspaper Blogging
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the impact of blogs on the local news landscape, focusing on how newspapers are responding to the rise of citizen journalism and online aggregation. It examines various approaches, from newspapers ignoring the digital shift (like the Buffalo News) to those actively embracing blogs and citizen contributions (like the Guardian and Houston Chronicle). The piece highlights the need for newspapers to create unique value online, move beyond simply replicating print content, and foster community engagement to remain relevant in the digital age.
records.quote: The internet was not invented just to show a replica of yesterday’s newspaper with a few banner advertisements.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Re-musing Ourselves
records.author: Brooke Gladstone; Jay Rosen
records.summary: On the Media segment with Rosen on Neil Postman, his mentor in the NYU Journalism Department and author of Amusing Ourselves to Death. Rosen counts Postman as both mentor and hero and explains why Postman's argument about the superiority of the printed word for sustaining ideas has only grown more relevant.
records.quote: It was in print that we learned how to make an argument cohere. It was in print that we learned that we could classify what we know.

records.title: PressThink's Blue Plate Special: Newspaper Blogging
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen announces the launch of PressThink's Blue Plate Special, a series focusing on newspaper blogging.  The first installment examines the best blogging newspapers in the U.S., featuring a chart analyzing the state of newspaper blogging and interviews with key figures.  A future installment will delve into the mechanics of successful blogs, using anthropological 'thick description' to understand how they work and why they succeed, inviting reader contributions.
records.quote: We plan a close-up look at a bunch of blogs that do work, successful uses of the form, in order to understand from them how they work, and the why of it.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: "What if Bush Changed the Game on You?" My 1,107-Word Question to the Political Press
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen argues that the Bush White House has deliberately changed the terms of engagement with the Washington press corps, weakening the old consensus in which presidents needed the press to communicate and journalists needed access to power.
records.quote: 11, but at the last minute Harris pulled the plug and decided against publishing the interview, which we had worked on for several weeks.

records.title: PressThink: Dick Cheney Did Not Make a Mistake By Not Telling the Press He Shot a Guy
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the Bush administration's, particularly Dick Cheney's, deliberate strategy of undermining the traditional relationship between the White House and the press. By ignoring established communication protocols and selectively releasing information, Cheney demonstrated a disregard for the press's role as a conduit to the public and a rejection of its perceived power. Rosen argues this represents a fundamental shift in the power dynamic, where the White House actively seeks to control the narrative and circumvent traditional journalistic practices, leaving the press weakened and unable to effectively hold power accountable.
records.quote: The public visibility of the presidency itself is under revision.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Introducing PressThink's Blue Plate Special
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen announces the launch of Blue Plate Special, a new online journalism project conceived by Jay Rosen. It will feature collaborative reporting on a monthly theme related to the intersection of the internet and journalism. The project is described as an experiment in online journalism, drawing inspiration from various successful examples of blog expansion, such as adding correspondents or creating spin-off sites. It also serves as a precursor to a planned overhaul of Rosen's PressThink website.
records.quote: Good information and multiple perspectives on a single theme— for now, that is the formula for a Blue Plate Special.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: It Was Not a Mistake When NBC Met Katrina
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Analysis of how NBC's coverage of Hurricane Katrina broke from the conventions of television news, arguing that the emotional directness of reporters like Brian Williams and Anderson Cooper was not a mistake but a return to honest reporting.
records.quote: The emotional directness of reporters like Brian Williams during Katrina was not a professional lapse but a return to honesty — proof that the conventions of detached television news can obscure reality as much as they reveal it.

records.title: Introduction to the Twentieth Anniversary Edition of Amusing Ourselves to Death
records.author: Andrew Postman
records.summary: Andrew Postman, son of Neil Postman, explores the continued relevance of his father's book, *Amusing Ourselves to Death*, twenty years after its initial publication. He argues that the book's critiques of television's impact on society remain strikingly pertinent in the age of the internet and ubiquitous technology, based on the reactions of college students assigned the book in their classes. While some students felt the book was outdated or offered no solutions, the overwhelming response indicated that Postman's observations about the trivialization of information and the dominance of entertainment continue to resonate.
records.quote: His questions can be asked about all technologies and media. What happens to us when we become infatuated with and then seduced by them? Do they free us or imprison us? Do they improve or degrade democracy? Do they make our leaders more accountable or less so? Our system more transparent or less so? Do they make us better citizens or better consumers? Are the trade-offs worth it? If theyre not worth it, yet we still cant stop ourselves from embracing the next new thing because thats just how were wired, then what strategies can we devise to maintain control? Dignity? Meaning?

records.title: PressThink: Brady, Hamsher, Reynolds, Jarvis, Rosen at the Post site. Plus: Elite Newspaper Divergence (END)
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen discusses an online roundtable on ethics and interactivity featuring Jim Brady (Washingtonpost.com), Jane Hamsher (Firedoglake), Glenn Reynolds (Instapundit), Jeff Jarvis (Buzzmachine), and Jay Rosen (PressThink). The discussion revolves around the Washington Post's handling of comments on their website, particularly after temporarily disabling them due to technical issues and a perceived lack of civility. The article highlights contrasting approaches to online reader engagement between the Washington Post and the New York Times, including the use of bylines linked to reporter email addresses, and the NYT's paywalled blog content. The differing viewpoints and heated exchanges during the roundtable, especially between Hamsher and Brady, underscore the challenges news organizations face in navigating online interactivity and reader engagement.
records.quote: Jim Brady told Dan Gillmor that more changes are coming at the Post site, once the Post fixes the problems it had last week.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Transparency at the Post: Q & A with Jim Brady of Washingtonpost.com
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: In a Q&A with Washingtonpost.com executive editor Jim Brady, Rosen explores the Post's decision to shut down comments on post.blog after the Deborah Howell controversy and asks what transparency means when online conversation is closed off.
records.quote: When Jim Brady decides to shut down the comments at post.blog to prevent even bigger problems we're going backwards in our ability to have a conversation with the Washington Post.

records.title: PressThink: Transparency at the Post: Q & A with Jim Brady of Washingtonpost.com
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Jim Brady, then managing editor of washingtonpost.com, temporarily closed the comments section of post.blog due to abusive and uncivil comments targeting Deborah Howell, the Washington Post's ombudsman.  This decision sparked a debate about the balance between online transparency, reader engagement, and maintaining a civil online environment.  The article presents a Q&A with Brady, exploring the reasons behind the decision, the challenges of moderating online comments, and the broader implications for online journalism and public dialogue.
records.quote: The issue here was civility.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: The Walter Winchell of Montclair
records.author: Debra Galant
records.summary: Debra Galant, founder of the hyperlocal news blog Baristanet.com, reflects on the differences between her experience in traditional journalism (at The New York Times) and her current work in online, community-based reporting. She contrasts the institutional authority of established newspapers with the informal, sometimes irreverent, nature of her blog, highlighting the advantages of real-time reporting, direct audience engagement, and the focus on local, often overlooked, news stories that resonate deeply with the community. While acknowledging the challenges of maintaining a certain standard while fostering community discussion and dealing with criticism, she ultimately celebrates the unique opportunities and rewards of hyperlocal blogging.
records.quote: But bigger still is the shift from top-down control of media to control from the bottom, from the people, who are tired of corporate ownership and meddling and just want to be served, want to have a greater voice.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Wrong When the Governor is Wrong
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the media's misreporting of the West Virginia Sago mine disaster, specifically focusing on CNN's three-hour broadcast of false information that 12 miners were alive.  Rosen contrasts the actions of a local reporter who stayed at the official briefing room, finding no confirmation of the reports, with the actions of national news organizations that rushed to the church where families were gathering, relying on unconfirmed rumors.  Rosen criticizes CNN and other outlets for failing to properly verify information, highlighting the lack of confirmation from the rescue operation itself, and questions the media's assertion that their mistakes were unavoidable. The piece also explores the role of the public in evaluating the reliability of news in the age of instant communication.
records.quote: It is unacceptable to me that for three hours of live television, with our top talent presiding, we’ve got twelve men alive reported as truth, and we never saw those men, no ambulances for them ever moved, and we had no real confirmation.

records.title: Wrong When the Governor is Wrong: A Small Detail in the Mis-reporting of the Miners' Deaths
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen examines how CNN and other outlets spread false reports that West Virginia miners had survived because they followed the governor's statements instead of staying at the official briefing site with the local reporter who kept asking questions.
records.quote:
Links to the explanations editors gave are here.)

What Becky Wagoner, the reporter for the local daily, did is stay put.

records.title: PressThink: "Today, we fell short." vs. "I'm not seeing any obvious missteps."
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the media's response to a false report that 12 miners had been rescued alive from a West Virginia mine.  It contrasts the differing responses of various news organizations to the erroneous information, highlighting the varied approaches to acknowledging mistakes and the importance of accurately reporting sources. Rosen emphasizes the need for a moral voice in admitting errors, prioritizing the reader's experience over internal journalistic justifications, and the crucial role of trust in the news-consuming public.
records.quote: Accuracy, which was achieved, is the more technical term, truth, which did not happen, is a moral category.

records.title: Jay Rosen | Edge.org
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This text provides a biographical sketch of Jay Rosen, highlighting his career in journalism education, his influential blog PressThink, his involvement with various media organizations, and his contributions to the field of journalism.
records.quote: He is the author of PressThink, a blog about journalism's ordeals in the age of the Web, which he launched in 2003.

records.title: PressThink: Times Public Editor: Bill Keller Stonewalled Me
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the controversy surrounding the New York Times' reporting on warrantless NSA eavesdropping.  It focuses on the criticism leveled by the Times' public editor, Barney Calame, against executive editor Bill Keller's handling of the situation, particularly regarding the lack of transparency in explaining the delayed publication. The piece discusses the tension between the Times' commitment to transparency and the demands of investigative journalism, contrasting the perspectives of various journalists, bloggers, and commentators. It highlights the debate over the role of the public editor, the pressures of national security concerns, and the evolving relationship between the mainstream media and the blogosphere in the wake of the story.
records.quote: My point is, the independence rests mainly in the character of the person who holds the job.

records.title: A Collection of Journalism Awards No Newsroom Would Want
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A compilation and analysis of journalism's notable failures, examining cases where news organizations got major stories wrong and what these episodes reveal about structural problems in how the press operates.
records.quote: When news organizations get major stories wrong, the failures are rarely individual lapses; they reveal structural pressures — toward access, toward speed, toward the consensus of the powerful — that operate across the press as a whole.

records.title: I'm Not Going to Talk About the War
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen examines New York Times editor Bill Keller's approach to press criticism, particularly around the paper's handling of the Iraq war and domestic surveillance stories, and his preference for letting "our pages" speak for themselves.
records.quote: Bill Keller's instinct was to let 'our pages' speak for themselves rather than engage press critics directly — a posture that treats accountability journalism as something the Times performs on others, not on itself.

records.title: PressThink: "I’m Not Going to Talk About the Back Story."
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen critiques Bill Keller's handling of transparency issues at The New York Times, specifically regarding the decision to publish a story about the Bush administration's secret lifting of limits on spying in the U.S. Rosen argues that the Times withheld key information about the story's background and the White House's attempts to suppress it, highlighting a lack of self-scrutiny and a resistance to engaging in open dialogue with its readers, despite internal recommendations to improve transparency.
records.quote: Heavyweights in journalism can’t figure it out. I certainly can’t. And the newspaper won’t say much.

records.title: Dan Froomkin on Attitude in White House Briefing
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen discusses the debate surrounding Dan Froomkin's White House Briefing column and whether its critical stance towards the Bush administration constitutes ideological bias or legitimate accountability journalism. Froomkin defends his approach, emphasizing his commitment to journalistic passion and accountability, regardless of the president's party. The piece also explores the tensions between traditional print journalism's emphasis on detachment and the more engaged style of online blogging, and the differing perspectives of print and online journalists at the Washington Post regarding this evolving media landscape.
records.quote: But its journalistic passion, not partisan passion. And what disturbs me is the suggestion that enthusiastically scrutinizing a Republican president is somehow de facto biased and liberal and therefore inadvisable for a reporter in a mainstream newsroom. I think thats toxic for the industry, and for democracy.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Froomkin Fallout: A Q&A
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This Q&A discusses the controversy surrounding Dan Froomkin's "White House Briefing" column on washingtonpost.com. The Washington Post's political staff expressed concerns that the column's title and presentation created confusion among readers about Froomkin's role as a commentator versus a reporter, potentially harming the paper's credibility. The debate centers on the line between opinion and news reporting in the online environment, the perception of Froomkin's column as having a liberal bias, and the broader challenges of maintaining journalistic objectivity in the age of the internet.
records.quote: What worries me is when I see headlines that suggest there’s a huge battle between the newspaper and the Web site.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Two Washington Posts May Be Better Than One
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen discusses the internal conflict at the Washington Post between its print and online newsrooms regarding the opinion column "White House Briefing" by Dan Froomkin.  The print side, concerned about perceptions of bias against the Bush administration, wanted the column's name changed, while the online side, led by Jim Brady, resisted, highlighting the tension between journalistic traditions and the dynamics of online readership and political pressures. Rosen uses this situation to argue for the benefits of maintaining a divided newsroom structure, allowing for a wider range of perspectives and a more dynamic approach to journalism in the digital age.
records.quote: What the brief struggle over White House Briefing showed me is the hidden advantages of a divided house.

records.title: PressThink: Grokking Woodward
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the controversy surrounding Bob Woodward's actions in the Valerie Plame leak investigation. It critiques Woodward's journalistic practices, particularly his close relationships with powerful sources and his seeming lack of critical analysis, arguing that his pursuit of access over truth hindered his ability to uncover the full story of the Bush administration. The piece contrasts Woodward's approach with the ideal of investigative journalism, highlighting the perspectives of various journalists and commentators, including David Broder, Eugene Robinson, Jane Hamsher, Nora Ephron, William Powers, and Joan Didion, to expose the limitations of Woodward's methods and the potential consequences of prioritizing access to power over investigative thoroughness.
records.quote: The best thing ever written about Woodward is nine years old, but its fundamentals still apply.

records.title: Grokking Woodward
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen examines Bob Woodward's role in the Valerie Plame affair, arguing that Woodward's transformation from accountability journalist to establishment insider reveals deeper problems with Washington's access journalism culture.
records.quote: Woodward's handling of the Plame affair shows how access journalism corrupts accountability journalism: once you become an insider, protecting sources and relationships crowds out the obligation to inform the public.

records.title: John Harris and Jim Brady: Politico.com
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: An interview-based piece examining the departure of John Harris and Jim VandeHei from the Washington Post to launch Politico, and the controversy over Dan Froomkin's White House Briefing column at washingtonpost.com.
records.quote: The departure of Harris and VandeHei from the Washington Post to launch Politico, alongside the controversy over Froomkin's column, illustrates the institutional tensions between traditional political reporting and the new norms emerging online.

records.title: PressThink: Guest Writer Liz George of Baristanet Reviews Backfence.com Seven Months After Launch
records.author: Judy Miller
records.summary: This article analyzes Backfence, a hyperlocal, user-generated content website. While touted as a leader in citizen journalism, Backfence's slow growth and low user engagement raise questions about the viability of its model. The author compares Backfence to their own successful hyperlocal site, Baristanet, highlighting the differences in community engagement and content generation. The article discusses the challenges of attracting and retaining users in a user-generated content platform, particularly the difficulty of achieving a critical mass of contributors to generate a vibrant online community. The lack of organic local flavor and the uniform design are cited as potential impediments to attracting and engaging users.
records.quote: You cannot franchise Baristanet until the two of you learn to clone yourselves — which is why your site has heart and soul and wit and credibility and Backfence has venture capital. Yours is a community news site. Theirs is a business plan.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Fortress Journalism Failed. The Transparent Newsroom Works.
records.author: Steven A. Smith
records.summary: This article contrasts the failing "fortress journalism" model with the author's experience implementing a transparent newsroom at the Spokane Spokesman-Review.  The author argues that the traditional model, characterized by secrecy and a separation from the community, is failing, while transparency, including openness about mistakes and engaging directly with readers, enhances credibility and builds trust.  He cites examples from his career at various newspapers and draws on research from the ASNE credibility project to support his claim that a two-way flow of information, involving citizens in news production, is essential for the future of journalism.
records.quote: Transparency—which includes being open about mistakes—can kill rumors and conspiracy theories that breed distrust. It can soften criticism, or at least direct it to the appropriate targets.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: The Main Street Strategy For Selling Knight-Ridder
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen proposes that Knight-Ridder avoid a Wall Street sale by breaking itself into locally owned papers, giving individual newsrooms and communities control rather than selling to a single national buyer.
records.quote: On November 14, Knight-Ridder Inc., announced that it would put it itself up for sale, and retained Goldman Sachs to advise it.

records.title: PressThink: If I Didn't Build it, They Wouldn't Come: Citizen Journalism is Discovered (Alive) in Watertown, MA
records.author: Jay Rosen, Lisa Williams
records.summary: Rosen reflects on the rise of citizen journalism in the mid-2000s, using Rosen's experience with her hyperlocal newsblog, H2otown, as a case study.  It contrasts the motivations and reward systems of citizen journalists with those of professional journalists, highlighting the entrepreneurial opportunities presented by the web for individuals to create local news sources.  Rosen also discusses the decline of traditional local newspapers and the resulting media void in many communities, proposing alternative business models for online news sources.
records.quote: I wanted to say to them, If you really want to do this, dont let a little thing like not getting a job stop you.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Truthtelling in the Style of Ed Meese:  Arthur Sulzberger, Jr. on Charlie Rose
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen criticizes Arthur Sulzberger Jr.'s appearance on Charlie Rose as evasive and damaging, comparing his refusal to acknowledge the Times' failures to the obfuscation associated with Ed Meese.
records.quote: Thursday night's interview with Charlie Rose was a low point in the public life of Arthur Sulzberger, Jr.

records.title: Will theTimes Ever Tell Us If Judy Miller Had a Security Clearance?
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen argues that Judy Miller's admission that she held a security clearance from the Pentagon undermines her credibility and that the New York Times must publicly correct or explain the claim rather than let Miller's account stand.
records.quote: It's been three weeks since the New York Times released its report, "The Miller Case," along with Judy Miller's first-person recollection of her grand jury testimony.

records.title: Jay Rosen: The Judy Miller SPJ Award
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the controversy surrounding the Society of Professional Journalists (SPJ) awarding Judith Miller its First Amendment Award. The award was given for Miller's 85-day jail sentence for refusing to reveal a confidential source, but the piece highlights concerns about Miller's questionable reporting on WMDs in Iraq and her handling of confidential sources, including a deal with Scooter Libby. Rosen explores the SPJ's justification for the award, emphasizing the advancement of a federal shield law as the overriding factor, despite concerns about Miller's professional conduct. The article also includes commentary on the implications of Miller's actions and the broader discussion around journalistic ethics and the use of confidential sources.
records.quote: Journalism has, as its core, the trust between reporters and editors, and reporters and the public. As that erodes, the whole enterprise starts to crumble.

records.title: PressThink: Guest Writer Ron Brynaert: Does the New York Times Have a Learning Disability?
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen critiques the New York Times' handling of several major controversies, including the Judith Miller case, the Wen Ho Lee case, and the Jayson Blair plagiarism scandal.  Rosen argues that the Times repeatedly failed to learn from its mistakes, despite internal investigations and reports recommending increased transparency and engagement with critics.  He highlights the newspaper's reliance on confidential government sources, its reluctance to acknowledge errors, and its insufficient response to reader concerns, ultimately questioning the organization's commitment to journalistic integrity and accountability.
records.quote: They learn, we learn, and then maybe well all get to where we need to go wherever that might be.

records.title: "We Regret Nothing."  Times Editorial Page Breaks Silence on Miller Case
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen criticizes the Times editorial page for breaking its silence only to reaffirm support for Judith Miller, ignoring internal dissent and Keller's regrets, while the paper still refuses to answer the security-clearance question.
records.quote: There was a break today in the silence that had fallen over the New York Times editorial page in the matter of Judith Miller.

records.title: Public Editor Tries to Find Out: Did Miller Have a Security Clearance?
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen notes that Times public editor Barney Calame could not confirm whether Judith Miller held a security clearance, treats Miller as an unreliable narrator, and argues the Times should sever ties with her.
records.quote: Significant news for readers of my post, Thanks for the Link, New York Times.

records.title: Thanks for the Link, New York Times.   Now Please Answer My Question.
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen praises the Times for linking to blogger discussion of its Miller report, then presses the paper to answer whether Judith Miller held special security clearances in 2003 and what editors knew about them.
records.quote: "Bloggers Discuss the Miller Case," said the headline at the Times site Tuesday.

records.title: Rosen is Unplugged for a While
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Jay Rosen announces a temporary hiatus from his PressThink blog to complete his book, "By the People." The announcement follows a series of seven posts criticizing Judith Miller and the New York Times' handling of her reporting, which are briefly summarized. Rosen expresses gratitude for the blog's readership and plans to return in December.
records.quote: Judith Miller may be the only investigative reporter alive who doesn’t care if you understand, because she does. She’s not aware of it when her stories do not add up. They cohere for her. In this sense she violates not the rules of journalism, but the reason we have it.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Bloggers Discuss the Miller Case
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the controversy surrounding Judith Miller's reporting on weapons of mass destruction in Iraq and her alleged security clearance.  Rosen questions whether Miller had a special security clearance that allowed her access to classified information beyond other reporters. He critiques the New York Times's response to inquiries about the matter, highlighting inconsistencies in Miller's statements and the lack of transparency from the newspaper. Rosen uses this case to discuss the role of bloggers in holding mainstream media accountable and the importance of journalistic transparency.
records.quote: What the New York Times has not figured out yet is that Judith Miller is an extreme example of the unreliable narrator. She increases our doubt in the story as she tells it.

records.title: The Era of Omniscience is Over
records.author: Andrew Heyward
records.summary: Andrew Heyward, President of CBS News, declared the "era of omniscience" over in mainstream news. He argued that news organizations must abandon claims to all-knowing objectivity and instead embrace the reality of multiple perspectives and a more authentic approach to reporting. This shift is driven by the empowered consumer and the rise of new media, forcing news outlets to adapt and acknowledge their limitations while maintaining accuracy and fairness. The article includes reactions from several writers who discuss the implications of this shift and its challenges for journalism.
records.quote: The strongest exemplars of mainstream commercial television news—60 Minutes, CBS News Sunday Morning, the network newscasts at their best—stand out not just by original reporting but also by avoiding these traps. And I’m convinced a consumer-empowered marketplace will reward authenticity over artifice.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Times Report on Judith Miller: Key Moments, My Comments, and What the Blogs Say
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen critiques the New York Times' handling of the Judith Miller case, arguing that Miller's actions, framed as a First Amendment struggle, effectively hijacked the newspaper's decision-making process.  Rosen contends that the Times' prioritization of Miller's principles over journalistic ethics and factual accuracy led to a disastrous outcome, hampered by Miller's lack of cooperation and the leadership's failure to properly investigate and oversee the situation.  Rosen highlights instances of Miller's questionable behavior, including memory loss regarding crucial details and unwillingness to cooperate with colleagues.
records.quote: By taking Miller’s secret-keeping “into” itself the Times took on more and more responsibilities not to speak, not to publish, not to report, not to inquire. All this is deadly for a newspaper, and the staff knew it.

records.title: PressThink: The Hypothesis: Notes on the Judy Miller Situation
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This post analyzes Judith Miller's silence and lack of cooperation with the New York Times reporters investigating her role in the Plame affair. It puts forward a hypothesis that Miller will not fully cooperate and examines evidence from various sources to support this claim. Rosen also critiques the Society of Professional Journalists (SPJ) for planning to give Miller a First Amendment award before the full story is revealed.
records.quote: I am delighted that the contempt order has been lifted, and Judy is now completely free to go about her great reporting as a very principled and honorable reporter,” said Robert Bennett, Ms. Miller’s attorney.

records.title: PressThink: The Times at Bay: Armchair Critic Speculates
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the New York Times's delayed reporting on Judith Miller's involvement in the Plame affair. Rosen speculates on the reasons for the delay, suggesting a combination of factors including the ongoing legal proceedings, the Times's own potential culpability, and the lack of cooperation from Miller herself. Rosen highlights the internal frustration and uncertainty within the Times newsroom, emphasizing the tension between the desire to publish a thorough investigation and the fear of publishing damaging information before all the facts are known. The piece ultimately questions the Times's handling of the situation and its implications for journalistic integrity.
records.quote: The New York Times is in a suspended state, editorially speaking. In fact, the entire organization—with the exception of a few lawyers, a few top executives, a few top editors, plus Jon Landman and his crew—is in the dark about Miller, uncertain of what a full investigation will find, unwilling to speak in the absence of knowledge now being gathered, fearful that the emerging story could be devastating.

records.title: PressThink: The Shimmer: Missing Data at the New York Times
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the New York Times's handling of the Judith Miller case, criticizing its lack of transparency and its failure to adequately explain its actions to the public.  Rosen points to inconsistencies in the Times' reporting, its delayed and inadequate explanations, and the contrast between its own actions and its usual standards of investigative journalism. The article highlights how the New York Times was scooped by other publications on crucial details of the Miller case,  raising concerns about the paper's internal processes and its capacity for self-reflection.  Rosen suggests that the Times' response reflects a broader, unidentified issue affecting its journalistic practices.
records.quote: “The news comes in code, and mostly the silences speak.” Last week, that’s how I described what happens when the New York Times reports about Judith Miller and her time in jail.

records.title: The Hypothesis:  Notes on the Judy Miller Situation
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen tests "The Hypothesis" that Judy Miller would not materially cooperate with the Times reporters investigating her, collecting evidence from news reports, editor statements, and Miller's own evasions to support it.
records.quote:
I wrote:

_Everything has to wait until the moment when Judy "'can be expected to tell what happened," as Landman so carefully put it.

records.title: The Times at Bay: Armchair Critic Speculates
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen speculates that the New York Times is in a "suspended state" over the Judith Miller affair: most of the staff is in the dark, Miller is not cooperating with the internal reporting team, and the paper's silence reflects fear of what Fitzgerald's investigation may reveal.
records.quote: There were some small breaks Wednesday in the matter of missing journalism at the New York Times.

records.title: The Shimmer:  Missing Data at the New York Times
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Examines the Times's missing and inconsistent reporting about Judith Miller's notes and grand-jury testimony, arguing that the newspaper had lost the capacity to tell the truth about itself while acting as a participant in the story.
records.quote: _When I talk about pictures in my mind I am talking, quite specifically, about images that shimmer around the edges.

records.title: News Comes in Code: Judy Miller's Return to the Times
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Explains why Rosen had come to rank The Washington Post above The New York Times, criticizing the Times for letting Judith Miller's return drive an opaque official narrative instead of reporting the larger story to readers.
records.quote: Just one man's opinion, but now is a good time to say it: The New York Times is not any longer--in my mind--the greatest newspaper in the land.

records.title: PressThink: News Comes in Code: Judy Miller's Return to the Times
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen critiques the New York Times' handling of Judith Miller's case, arguing that the paper prioritized protecting Miller over fulfilling its journalistic duty to inform the public.  Rosen contrasts the Times' perceived inaction and prioritization of its own narrative with the Washington Post's more proactive approach, highlighting a shift in his perception of the relative strengths of these newspapers.  He observes a lack of internal criticism and debate within the Times, comparing the situation to Soviet-style media control. Rosen concludes that the Times' editorial silence around Miller's actions represents a journalistic failure, questioning her understanding of journalistic ethics and the paper's subsequent defense of her.
records.quote: The Post, I believe, is our great national newspaper now; the Times is number two, with the Wall Street Journal close behind. Still a strong fleet.

records.title: PressThink: Judith Miller and Her Times
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the Judith Miller case and its impact on the New York Times. Rosen argues that Miller's actions, while framed as a principled stand for protecting sources, ultimately damaged the newspaper's credibility and ability to report objectively. He criticizes the Times's inconsistent messaging and its failure to provide clear and comprehensive reporting on the situation, highlighting the conflict between Miller's personal decision and the institutional implications for the newspaper.
records.quote: There is nothing intrinsically noble about keeping your sources’ secrets. Your job, in fact, is to expose them.

records.title: Judith Miller and Her Times
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Argues that Judith Miller's choices in the Plame investigation constrained The New York Times's reporting and muddled its claims about civil disobedience and a federal shield law, because other reporters had negotiated alternatives.
records.quote: When Jack Shafer calls it "the epic collision of first principles from which Judith Miller has just slunk away," he gets Thursday's news exactly right.

records.title: Some Bloggers Meet the Bosses From Big Media
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Reports on a roundtable between bloggers and major-media executives about the web transition, including newsroom funding, weak innovation, citizen-reporting verification, and the recognition that legacy news organizations must change.
records.quote: I was rushing by on my way to a roundtable at the nearby Museum of Television and Radio.

records.title: Some Bloggers Meet the Bosses From Big Media
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen recounts a roundtable discussion between bloggers and high-level executives from mainstream media organizations. The discussion reveals a lack of innovation and entrepreneurial spirit within established media, contrasted with the agility and conversational nature of the blogosphere. While Big Media acknowledges the shift to online platforms and the growing influence of blogs, concerns remain about sustainable business models and the perceived lack of credibility in citizen journalism.
records.quote: “The world has really, really changed and will keep changing and we in mainstream media may not like it but its a fact and we have to embrace it or we will die.”
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Charging for Columnists: Notes and Comment on the Launch of TimesSelect
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the New York Times' launch of TimesSelect, a premium content package putting opinion columns behind a paywall. Rosen questions the Times' strategy, arguing that the exclusivity diminishes the value of opinion pieces, particularly for columnists whose influence depends on wide readership. He contrasts this with the success of bloggers who leverage the free web to reach a broader audience and offer a more timely and engaging form of commentary. The core argument challenges the Times' assumptions about the value proposition of exclusive online access to opinion pieces versus the importance of ubiquity and the power of real-time, flood-the-zone reporting.
records.quote: The Times Company’s press release does not seem to realize that “exclusive” opinions are not more valuable than “widely-circulated” ones— and it’s possible they will count for less.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: The Net Knows More Than You: An Open Letter to the People of CBS News
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This open letter from Jay Rosen to the staff of CBS News reflects on the network's handling of the National Guard memos controversy a year prior. Rosen argues that the network's failure to recognize the emerging online criticism, largely from bloggers, demonstrated a disconnect from the evolving media landscape. He praises the launch of CBS News' Public Eye blog as a step towards greater transparency and engagement with online discourse, but critiques the network's continued reliance on opaque reasoning and a lack of self-awareness regarding its relationship with the internet.
records.quote: Transparency will absolutely change you, and it already has. If you don’t change with it, you will lose.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: The Net Knows More Than You:  An Open Letter to the People of CBS News
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Frames CBS News's Public Eye launch and move online as a test of whether the network learned from its National Guard memo failure, arguing that internet-wide scrutiny and meaningful transparency are necessary to rebuild trust.
records.quote: I was asked to be the first guest blogger at Public Eye, the new blog that acts like an ombudsman (sort of) at CBS News.

records.title: PressThink: From Deference to Outrage: Katrina and the Press
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Following Hurricane Katrina, the American media's coverage shifted from deferential to aggressively critical of the Bush administration's response. This piece analyzes various perspectives on this change, examining whether it represents a genuine resurgence of journalistic integrity, a simple shift in power dynamics due to the government's ineffectiveness, or a pre-existing bias manifesting more openly. Rosen argues that the shift in power is best understood as a triangular relationship between the press, the administration, and the public, with the government's failings creating an imbalance that empowered the media.
records.quote: The press gained back some of its missing authority because in this situation public authority was missing.

records.title: From Deference to Outrage: The Road to Katrina
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen traces the shift in press behavior from deference to authority to outrage during Hurricane Katrina coverage, arguing that the disaster revealed what happens when reporters drop their usual stance of studied neutrality.
records.quote: Hurricane Katrina revealed what happens when reporters drop their studied neutrality: the shift from deference to authority to outrage exposed how much the press's usual stance had been a choice, not a given.

records.title: Charging for Columnists: Was TimesSelect Worth It?
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: A critique of the New York Times's TimesSelect paywall experiment, questioning whether charging for access to columnists like Thomas Friedman and Maureen Dowd was worth the trade-off in reduced influence and readership.
records.quote: Charging readers for access to columnists like Friedman and Dowd may have generated subscription revenue, but the Times paid for it in reduced influence — a trade-off TimesSelect never adequately reckoned with.

records.title: PressThink: An Open Thread After a Closed One
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This open thread on PressThink follows a previous post by Austin Bay arguing for a revitalized relationship between the Bush White House and the press. Rosen addresses criticism for closing comments on the previous post and encourages readers to focus on increasing their representation within mainstream media and developing better journalists, rather than dwelling on perceived media bias. He questions the underlying assumption that an objective press is unattainable and proposes a discussion about the necessary role of the institutional press.
records.quote: The bias discourse, however justified you may find it, is making many of you dumber by the day.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Roll Forward: Why the Bush White House Needs the Press to Win the Big One
records.author: Austin Bay
records.summary: This article is a response to Jay Rosen's piece on the Bush administration's 'rollback' strategy towards the press.  Austin Bay argues that Rosen's framing is too simplistic, ignoring the complexities of the global information war against Al Qaeda. He contends that the changing media landscape, driven by technology, has rendered the traditional 'national press' (a NY-DC-LA axis) less powerful, and that the administration's strategy should be viewed in this broader context.  Bay also points to potential biases within the traditional media, stemming from the geographic and political concentration of its editors.
records.quote: The press conflict and US domestic political clashes cannot be isolated from this multi-dimensional war and its harsh historical circumstances.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: "Things I Used to Teach That I No Longer Believe" Was the Title of the Panel...
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen reflects on a panel discussion at the AEJMC convention titled "Things I used to teach that I no longer believe." Panelists, including journalism professors and experienced journalists, shared their disillusionment with the changing landscape of journalism. The decline of a shared sense of mission, the trivialization of news in the 24-hour cycle, and the growing disconnect between journalism educators and students were discussed. Rosen questions the traditional ideals of objectivity and 'making a difference,' arguing that the 'official religion' of journalism has run out of gas and that a new understanding is needed for the profession's future.
records.quote: To learn, when you are ready to pass the torch, that some of the best and the brightest don’t want your torch, because they think it went out a while ago, counts as a sad day for J-schoolers of a certain generation.

records.title: Why Robert Novak Stormed Off the Set
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Analyzes Robert Novak's on-air walkout from CNN's 'Inside Politics' as a collapse of his prior claim that he could not discuss the Plame case while it was under investigation.
records.quote: Thursday afternoon Robert Novak stormed off the set of CNN's "Inside Politics" and got himself suspended.

records.title: PressThink: Why Robert Novak Stormed Off the Set
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Robert Novak's on-air meltdown on CNN's "Inside Politics" is analyzed.  The incident stemmed from Novak's conflicting stances on discussing the Valerie Plame case: initially claiming he couldn't comment due to legal advice, then publishing a column disputing the CIA's account.  His subsequent refusal to answer questions about the case on CNN, culminating in a walk-off, exposed a contradiction in his public behavior and highlighted the breakdown of professional journalistic standards and the complexities of journalistic ethics when dealing with legal constraints and public accountability.
records.quote: Novak was about to be faced with a gigantic contradiction in his public stance, and the Network wanted it.

records.title: BlogHer '05: Notes from the Conference
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen presents observations from the BlogHer '05 conference, focusing on the conversations and concerns among women bloggers. Rosen notes the prevalent discussions surrounding the anxieties and fears associated with online identity, public discourse, and personal attacks, contrasting this with the often-overlooked anxieties experienced by journalists. The piece highlights the unique challenges and opportunities presented by the burgeoning world of women bloggers and their engagement with the public conversation.
records.quote: If blogging is a practice of freedom, it is completely inadequate unless it is a whole practice and to be that it must have women.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: PressThink, Live from the BlogHer Conference
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This is a preview of Jay Rosen's attendance at the BlogHer conference in 2005. He discusses the conference's goals to increase the visibility and networking of women bloggers, notes the notable attendees and speakers, and reflects on the notable absences of prominent conservative women bloggers, prompting discussion about the conference's inclusivity and the nature of online public discourse.
records.quote: I firmly believe that the point of weblogging is not merely to have your own blog, but to participate more fully in the public conversation. This means reading and commenting on other peoples blogs ideally at least as much as you post in your own.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: We Have Been Bull Dozed Aside.
records.author: Orville Schell
records.summary: This article discusses a Carnegie-Knight Initiative, a collaboration between five leading journalism schools and two foundations to revitalize journalism education. Orville Schell, Dean of the UC Berkeley Graduate School of Journalism, details the initiative's three main elements: research and policy, curriculum reform emphasizing interdisciplinary collaboration, and multimedia reporting laboratories. Schell addresses criticisms that the initiative is an elitist 'priesthood,' emphasizing its inclusivity and the urgent need for journalism schools to adapt to the changing media landscape and declining professional standards.
records.quote: What I mean by this is that the chain on which information is vectored to the public and then digested by society and the powers-that-be is broken.

records.title: PressThink: Rollback
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the Bush White House's strategic rollback of the press, arguing that their approach, spearheaded by Karl Rove and others, aimed to diminish the press's influence and control the narrative. This involved non-communication, deliberate misinformation, and leveraging cultural divides to discredit journalists. Rosen contrasts this strategy with the previous, more collaborative model of press relations, highlighting how the Bush administration's actions challenged traditional journalistic norms and the role of the press within a democratic system. Rosen notes the strategy's success until the intervention of Patrick Fitzgerald's investigation, which exposed the White House's actions and brought about the moment described in the opening.
records.quote: The brutalizing of McClellan was no recovery of courage by a suddenly-awakened press. It was the Bush team’s bald assertiveness coming into conflict with truth collection in the criminal justice system, which has exposed a seamy story that journalists themselves would have kept hidden because it involves their confidential sources.

records.title: Rollback
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Describes the Bush White House's 'rollback' strategy toward the press through the confrontation between Scott McClellan and reporters over the Valerie Plame leak.
records.quote: The brutalizing of Scott McClellan at the White House podium on Monday is a development with long roots.

records.title: Time for Robert Novak to Feel Some Chill
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Calls on journalists and news organizations to stop hosting or publishing Robert Novak until he explains his role in the Valerie Plame leak, framing professional solidarity around conscience rather than legal privilege.
records.quote: Wilson never worked for the CIA, but his wife, Valerie Plame, is an Agency operative on weapons of mass destruction.

records.title: PressThink: Time for Robert Novak to Feel Some Chill
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen discusses the controversy surrounding Robert Novak's revelation of Valerie Plame's identity as a CIA operative.  Rosen criticizes Novak for his actions, arguing that he facilitated an act of retribution against a whistleblower, Joseph Wilson.  Rosen calls for a professional consequence for Novak, suggesting a media-wide shunning until he explains his actions, contrasting this with Judith Miller's imprisonment for refusing to reveal her sources.  The piece explores the ethical implications for journalists involved in the case and the larger questions of journalistic ethics, source protection, and the potential chilling effect on whistleblowers.
records.quote: Tell me: how can journalists say with a straight face that they are concerned for future whistle blowers if one of their own, Robert Novak, together with sources made possible an act of retribution against an actual whistle blower?

records.title: PressThink: The Production of Innocence and News of a Vacancy on the Court
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes news coverage of Sandra Day O'Connor's retirement, focusing on the framing of the ensuing political battle as an epic showdown. Rosen critiques the journalistic tendency to present this conflict as a neutral, objective event, highlighting the inherent disconnect between the massive mobilization of activist groups and the actual impact on the Supreme Court nomination process. He argues that this framing serves the “production of innocence,” a journalistic practice that prioritizes appearing neutral over substantive analysis, ultimately obscuring the power dynamics at play and failing to explain how the media campaign is supposed to influence the outcome. Rosen contrasts the large-scale media operations of major news outlets with the smaller-scale, more transparent trust system of his own weblog, PressThink.
records.quote: All the time and money spent on campaigns may have little influence on the outcome, said several senators, because they and their colleagues see a Supreme Court vote as a deeply personal and principled decision.

records.title: The Production of Innocence and News of a Vacancy on the Court
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Critiques press coverage of Sandra Day O'Connor's retirement for describing an impending Supreme Court nomination fight as a national political campaign without explaining how such a campaign could influence senators.
records.quote: Reading the news coverage of Justice Sandra Day O'Connor's retirement, I noticed something strange about one theme in it.

records.title: PressThink: Don't Be a Blogger Manqué, Norman Mailer
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen reflects on Norman Mailer's late-career foray into blogging, juxtaposing his unique journalistic style with the emerging landscape of online writing.  Rosen analyzes Mailer's perspective on journalism, arguing that his approach—characterized by immersive reporting and evocative prose—offers a valuable alternative to conventional news practices. The piece uses Mailer's work as a lens to explore the potential and pitfalls of online journalism, emphasizing the importance of linking, narrative depth, and engaging with the complexities of political events.
records.quote: The thing about journalists is that they learn about a lot of people in a hurry. Less good is that the experience is very rarely existential.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Murray Waas Is the Woodward of Now
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen argues that investigative journalist Murray Waas, through his dogged coverage of the CIA leak case and Bush administration, represents the kind of accountability reporting that Bob Woodward once embodied.
records.quote: Murray Waas represents the accountability journalism that Bob Woodward once embodied — dogged, source-driven reporting on executive power that the press corps had largely abandoned.

records.title: The Downing Street Memo and the Court of Appeal in News Judgment
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Argues that the internet and political blogs have created a 'Court of Appeal' against traditional press news judgment, using the Downing Street Memo as the leading example.
records.quote: The 24-hour audition still happens, and the big winners are still big news.

records.title: PressThink: The Downing Street Memo and the Court of Appeal in News Judgment
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes how the Downing Street Memo story, initially ignored by mainstream media, gained traction through online blogs and activist networks, eventually forcing a reassessment of the initial news judgment.  Rosen argues that the traditional press's authority over what constitutes news is waning, replaced by a 'Court of Appeal' where online discussions and political actors can challenge and overturn initial media decisions. This shift highlights the limitations of traditional news judgment, especially in the face of powerful actors who can shape the narrative and control the flow of information.
records.quote: If the press ruled against you, you just weren’t news.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: One Tribe in Press Nation: PressThink Wins an Award
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This blog post reflects on the PressThink blog winning the Reporters Without Borders Freedom Blog Award.  Rosen uses this as a springboard to discuss the evolving relationship between professional journalists, bloggers, and the concept of a 'press without borders.' He argues for a universal principle of press freedom that transcends national boundaries, recognizing bloggers as legitimate participants in disseminating information and holding power accountable.  Rosen's post touches on the blurring lines between traditional journalism and citizen journalism, the challenges faced by journalists worldwide, and the potential for collaboration and shared identity across these groups.
records.quote: Freedom of the press belongs to those who own one, and blogging means practically anyone can own one.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: "When I’m Reporting, I am a Citizen of the World.”
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Jay Rosen analyzes a discussion between CNN's Bob Franken and a National Review Online blogger regarding patriotism and journalism, sparked by a passage in Alan Feuer's book. Rosen uses this exchange to explore the "newsroom religion" and its limitations, particularly regarding skepticism and national identity, questioning Franken's "citizen of the world" stance and the superficiality of the press's self-understanding as "the skeptics."
records.quote: How can you be a patriot and a journalist? They’re mutually exclusive occupations.

records.title: PressThink: Deep Throat, J-School and Newsroom Religion
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen connects the revelation of W. Mark Felt as Deep Throat with a $6 million initiative to revitalize journalism education.  Rosen argues that journalism operates under a flawed internal 'religion,' perpetuating myths like the Watergate narrative which overemphasizes the role of Woodward and Bernstein while neglecting other factors like the Senate hearings and government agencies. He critiques the ingrained beliefs and practices within journalism education, suggesting that a re-evaluation of its core tenets is necessary.
records.quote: Watergate, by forcing a president to resign, was an exploding supernova in the sky of journalism, blotting out the record of investigative work during Vietnam.

records.title: PressThink: Three Questions for Kevin Drum
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the reaction to Newsweek's controversial article about the Quran and the subsequent media criticism.  It explores the hypocrisy of outrage directed at Newsweek's reporting while ignoring similar practices in other publications, highlighting the use of anonymous sources to create puff pieces and the lack of accountability for this behavior. Rosen questions the lack of a defined professional code of conduct within journalism that would allow for a stronger defense against attacks and explores various perspectives on how journalism should respond to criticism and political pressures.
records.quote: The real crime is not bias or secret sources. It’s fluff. It’s pseudo-sophistication. It’s a lost sense of what good journalism is all about. The real problem with investigative reporting is that it so rarely happens. The solvent for ethics in journalism is entertainment.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Newsweek's Take-Our-Word-For-It World (Follow-up)
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the Newsweek Koran story retraction, focusing on the underlying issues of trust in journalism.  Rosen argues that the incident highlights the declining public trust in the press, exacerbated by politicized attacks and outdated journalistic practices. He criticizes the 'Trust-Me Journalism' approach and advocates for improved reliability measures and updated investigative reporting standards to restore credibility.
records.quote: My point is journalists tend to believe the starting point is given by events themselves (rather than “decided” by them in their conventions) because their professional ideology says there are objective reasons for most everything they do. Even though they know such a thing is impossible, and incorrect as a description of how reporting and news judgment normally work.

records.title: PressThink: Newsweek's Take-Our-Word-For-It World
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes Newsweek's retracted story about the alleged abuse of the Quran at Guantanamo Bay.  Rosen critiques the magazine's reliance on weak, anonymous sources and its prioritization of being first over accuracy and thorough verification. He argues that Newsweek's flawed reporting exemplifies a broader problem in journalism: insufficient standards for reliability in a world where the consequences of misinformation are amplified by instant global communication.  The article highlights the need for increased transparency and stricter sourcing standards within the profession.
records.quote: Under these conditions, it is imperative that journalists in the United States raise their standards for reliability, because the consequences of being wrong—for themselves, for their profession as a whole, and for others far removed—are graver.

records.title: PressThink: In Praise of Daniel Okrent
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the impact of Daniel Okrent's tenure as the New York Times's public editor.  Okrent's influence is seen in four key areas: changing reader representation, establishing an effective public editor's office, actively engaging with critics, and acknowledging the Times's liberal leanings.  His success stemmed from defining his role as a 'reader with access,' directly addressing reader concerns, and holding the Times accountable.  While praised for improving reader engagement and responsiveness, Okrent's approach faced criticism for perceived bias and inadequate handling of certain complaints.
records.quote: He changed the way readers were represented at the Times; this is to my mind his most important and far-reaching accomplishment.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Spokane Mayor Sex Scandal: Would You Give Paper an Award?
records.author: Leonard Witt
records.summary: This interview with Steve Smith, editor of The Spokesman-Review, discusses the ethical implications of using a forensic computer expert posing as a 17-year-old to investigate Mayor Jim West's online activities. Smith defends the methods used, arguing that they were necessary to obtain irrefutable evidence of the mayor's actions, which ultimately led to criminal prosecution. The interview also touches upon the public's and journalists' reactions to the investigation, the resources expended, and the future of investigative journalism in a changing media landscape.
records.quote: But all of our ethics codes, SPJ for example, and even the Poynter’s ethics specialists, allow for exceptions when there is no other way to get the info and the story is important enough.

records.title: Regarding Media Don’t Print the Obit Just Yet: A Response to Tim Rutten
records.author: Leonard Witt (guest blogger)
records.summary: This article responds to Tim Rutten's opinion piece arguing against the demise of print media. The author challenges Rutten's dismissal of civic journalism, arguing that its principles are still relevant and evolving in the context of new media technologies. The author points to the continued success and growth of online spaces dedicated to civic engagement, highlighting the work of several key figures in the field. The piece also criticizes the lack of self-reflection within newsrooms and the resulting ‘censorship by omission’ that marginalizes certain communities.
records.quote: What Rutten fails to realize is that much of the criticism and constructive ideas that grew out of public or civic journalism are still very much alive today, albeit with a slightly more evolved DNA.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Each Nation its Own Press
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Jay Rosen's lecture explores the relationship between nation-states and their respective free presses. He argues that a free press isn't a natural phenomenon but a constructed entity, created and sustained by each nation's laws, institutions, and public rituals. He uses the historical example of the American founding to show how the press was integral to establishing a large republic, facilitating communication across vast territories. Rosen then connects this historical context to the contemporary digital revolution, predicting a time of rupture and reformation for the press as it adapts to the internet and the shift from a one-to-many to a many-to-many communication model. He anticipates questions about the definition of 'journalist' and the role of the press in a changing world.
records.quote: One remarkable fact in the terrible history of famine is no substantial famine has ever occurred in a country with a democratic form government and a relatively free press.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Stop Us Before We're Briefed Again
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen critiques the passive approach of Washington D.C. bureau chiefs in addressing the White House's use of background-only briefings.  Rosen argues that instead of politely requesting change, journalists should unilaterally stop attending these briefings, effectively ending the practice. He contrasts this direct action with the bureau chiefs' strategy of incremental pressure and criticizes media outlets for framing the situation as a negotiation rather than a choice journalists could make independently.
records.quote: The problem is everybody fears missing a big story and thus is afraid to say no when they know a rival will say yes.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: More on the Migration: Developments and Sightings
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This PressThink post from May 2, 2005, discusses the declining circulation of newspapers, the rise of online news platforms like Backfence.com, and the ensuing advertising crisis. The article highlights circulation fraud lawsuits against newspapers, such as the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel, and explores the potential consequences for the industry. It also touches upon the emergence of new digital news models, like Pajamas Media, and draws parallels between the struggles of newspapers, urban schools, and even General Motors.
records.quote: Good-quality readers tend to pay for the newspaper with the intention of reading it.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Don't Be a Blogger Manque
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen reflects on the relationship between traditional literary journalism (exemplified by Norman Mailer) and the new forms of writing emerging through blogs, arguing that bloggers are pushing the boundaries of the form in ways the establishment should recognize.
records.quote: Bloggers are pushing the boundaries of literary journalism in ways the establishment should recognize, doing for the web what Mailer did for print — not lesser versions of the form, but something new emerging within it.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: The Migration
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen discusses the impending digital migration of journalism, exemplified by Infinity Broadcasting's decision to launch KYOURadio, a station broadcasting listener-submitted podcasts.  Rosen reflects on the anxieties and uncertainties within the established media landscape as it grapples with the rise of blogs, podcasts, and citizen journalism.  The piece explores different strategies major newspapers are considering for survival in the new digital environment, contrasting established models with the potential of open-source and citizen-driven media.
records.quote: "Working at a major metropolitan newspaper these days can feel a bit like working for the East German Politburo, circa 1988,” jokes Andrés Martinez, editorial page editor of the Los Angeles Times, in today’s pages. “It’s a good gig with great benefits, and people seek you out at cocktail parties, but you have this sense that your days are numbered.”
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Mood of the Newsroom: Letters from Three Journalists
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen presents a collection of letters and responses regarding Tim Porter's post, "The Mood of the Newsroom."  The letters express anxieties and confusion among journalists about the future of the profession in the face of digital disruption.  A veteran journalist worries about the potential for destructive change, a young journalist feels lost and confused, and a discussion ensues about the Wall Street Journal's low blogosphere presence relative to its circulation, raising questions about the relationship between paid content and online visibility.
records.quote: What frightens me today is that a press corps that once covered wars and battles has now become the battleground on which a different kind of war is being fought.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Tim Porter Lets Out a Roar
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes Tim Porter's blog, First Draft, and his critique of the declining quality of newspaper journalism. Porter, a former top editor, uses his blog to dissect the problems within newsrooms, including formulaic storytelling, lack of online engagement, and a resistance to change. Rosen highlights Porter's self-education journey and the contrast between his blog's insightful analysis and traditional news coverage of the same issues, arguing that Porter's approach demonstrates a path forward for journalism.
records.quote: Newspapers are not the victims of homicide but of suicide.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: The Stand Alone Journalist is Here
records.author: Chris Nolan
records.summary: Chris Nolan introduces the concept of the "stand-alone journalist," enabled by the internet, who operates independently, leveraging blogs and RSS feeds for self-publication and distribution.  This model contrasts with traditional newsrooms, highlighting the changing media landscape and the economic shifts impacting newspapers (particularly concerning classified ads).  Nolan argues that these independent journalists, while not replacing traditional outlets, will supplement them, offering a more personal, interactive, and accessible form of news.
records.quote: The connection between what they do and whether they are trusted is much alive and apparent.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Darn it, that Nick Coleman is Just Good Copy
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen discusses a letter from Nick Coleman, a columnist for the Star-Tribune, criticizing Jay Rosen's perceived lack of defense against right-wing bloggers who attack mainstream media.  Coleman argues that these bloggers exert partisan pressure, leading to biased reporting and a chilling effect.  Rosen analyzes Coleman's letter, comparing his rhetoric to that of David Horowitz, noting similarities in their aggressive and often inflammatory style.  The article further explores the broader implications of right-wing blogs' influence on the media landscape and the potential marginalization of blogging as a whole.
records.quote: The media has elected to make blogs a story long before they really have the capability of covering many themselves with more than a trickle of new information or opinion, fleshed out with a multitude of links to the MSM it, in some cases, purports to so despise.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: All Regimes Are Founded on Opinion: Two Letters to PressThink
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen uses David Hume's maxim that all governments are founded on opinion to argue that institutions like newspapers and churches, built on opinion, are vulnerable when that opinion shifts. Rosen presents letters from readers illustrating this point, focusing on the changing nature of community, the role of bloggers and civic leaders, and the decline of traditional media. The core argument is that loyalty to institutions isn't to the mechanism itself, but to the community and function they serve, leading to shifts in reliance when those needs are met elsewhere.
records.quote: The core function of communicating to and between people is still vital and necessary, but when the mechanism for doing it breaks down, folk will find one that works, no matter what it looks like.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Q & A with Bill Grueskin, Managing Editor, Wall Street Journal Online
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen presents a Q&A with Bill Grueskin, Managing Editor of The Wall Street Journal Online, discussing the Journal's successful paid online model, the debate surrounding free versus paid online news content, and the implications of various media acquisitions. Grueskin argues that the Wall Street Journal's success is tied to its high-quality content and strong brand, justifying its paid model, and that a single answer to the paid vs. free question is fruitless. He also discusses the logic behind recent media acquisitions, attributing them to a pursuit of online advertising revenue and a rethinking of what it means to be a media company in the digital age.
records.quote: Any newspaper web site that limits itself to repurposing content from the paper is in serious trouble.

records.title: PressThink: Are You Ready for a Brand New Beat?
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen critiques the repetitive nature of panels discussing blogs and their impact on journalism, arguing for a shift in focus.  Instead of debating blogs' existence, Rosen advocates for examining how the new news environment functions, particularly hyperlocal blogs.  He highlights examples of successful hyperlocal blogs like Baristanet and H2otown, showcasing their unique approaches to news gathering and community engagement, demonstrating how they create value from previously untapped markets and offer a different perspective from traditional media.
records.quote: The best cure for blog boosterism is to go calling out around the world for people who are doing something different, inventive.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: What’s in Rebecca’s Pocket?
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the emerging landscape of citizen journalism, focusing on three key developments: Al Gore's Current TV network's initiative to pay citizen journalists for video content; Merrill Brown's report, "Abandoning the News," which highlights the crisis facing traditional news media and the need for radical rethinking; and the launch of Dose magazine in Canada, a new media outlet targeting young people but criticized for its lack of genuine engagement with youth perspectives. Rosen questions the viability and impact of these initiatives, examining the challenges and opportunities presented by the integration of citizen journalism into mainstream media.
records.quote: News executives need to quickly mobilize around what are today their secondary platforms, at least measured in terms of where, currently, their largest revenue opportunities exist.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience
