records.title: PressThink: Fourteen New Voices: A Reply to Halley's Comment
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen discusses the response to a challenge by blogger Halley Suitt to promote diverse voices in the blogosphere.  It details Rosen's consideration of options and collaboration with Lisa Stone to identify and highlight ten new bloggers, showcasing a lack of diversity in prominent blogrolls and advocating for a more inclusive and representative online media landscape.
records.quote: The media we consume can only be as good as the media we demand. In Blogworld, the media we demand is the media we’re willing to hunt down and link.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Laying the Newspaper Gently Down to Die
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen discusses the impending death of the newspaper industry and the uncertainty surrounding the future of journalism. While newspapers remain profitable, their business model is unsustainable due to the rise of new technologies and changing consumer habits. Rosen analyzes the industry's response, highlighting complacency, profit-taking over investment in the future, and a failure to adapt to the digital landscape. The piece explores the potential for citizen journalism and new media forms to fill the void, but also notes the skepticism and resistance within the traditional journalistic establishment.
records.quote: “The only way to save journalism is to develop a new model that finds profit in truth, vigilance, and social responsibility.”
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Boston University J-School Faculty Takes a Stand on Video News Releases. Very Intelligent.
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen discusses a unanimous resolution passed by the Boston University Journalism Department Faculty condemning the use of government video news releases (VNRs) without identifying their source, including the use of "phony reporters." The resolution calls for the Bush administration to cease these practices and urges other journalism schools to endorse it. Rosen, Jay Rosen, praises the faculty's action as a rare example of collective activism from journalism schools, highlighting the importance of such collective voices in addressing issues of journalistic integrity and the erosion of the press's influence.
records.quote: “During the civil rights era, and again during the Vietnam war, we found that simple appeals to decency and respect for the rule of law presented by academicians often carried great moral and political impact,” Zelnick wrote to us. “We believe the same may be true with respect to this situation which strikes at the core of journalistic integrity.”

records.title: PressThink: From Meet the Press to Be the Press
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen discusses the Bush administration's efforts to de-certify the press by undermining its credibility and establishing the government as a primary source of information. The administration's use of video news releases (VNRs) without disclosing their origin is highlighted as a key tactic, along with a general shift in power away from traditional media outlets towards smaller providers and the government itself. Rosen argues that this is a fundamental change in the relationship between the government and the press, with the administration actively discrediting traditional journalism to promote its own information as more reliable and unbiased.
records.quote: The traditional notion that the media play a special role in informing people is breaking down.

records.title: Blogging and credibility
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Coverage of Harvard's "Blogging, Journalism, and Credibility" conference, examining the emerging tensions and common ground between professional journalists and bloggers during the early blog era. Published in The Nation.
records.quote: The early blog era forced a reckoning between professional journalists and bloggers over who gets to claim credibility — and the answer was more complicated than either side wanted to admit.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: A Western Civ Course in What's Gone Wrong With the Press
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen explores the rising public anger towards the media, particularly the accusations of liberal bias.  Jay Rosen challenges the common explanations offered, arguing that the root of the problem lies deeper, stemming from a historical conflict between the journalistic pursuit of novelty and revelation and a more conservative worldview that values established truths and distrusts the ever-changing nature of news.  He uses Kenneth Minogue's essay, "Journalism: Power without Responsibility," to support his analysis, tracing the origins of this conflict back to the very nature of journalism's power and its relationship to the public.
records.quote: Journalism is the cultivation of concern for things that are for the most part remote from us.

records.title: PressThink: To Liberate From the White House the White House Press
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen discusses the ineffectiveness of the White House press corps under the George W. Bush administration. Journalists are criticized for engaging in unproductive exchanges with administration officials, focusing on the daily briefings rather than pursuing more effective investigative methods. Rosen and several cited sources suggest abandoning the traditional approach of relying on White House briefings and instead cultivating sources outside the administration, particularly in Congress and among interest groups, to obtain accurate and insightful information. The piece explores alternative strategies to break news and regain influence, drawing parallels to Bob Woodward's methods and emphasizing the importance of creating a definitive narrative.
records.quote: Journalists need to do their jobs regardless of the roadblocks and land mines placed by the White House. And the real reporting doesn’t take place in the briefing room, regardless of who’s accredited, or in the televised news conferences, which have become theater. It takes place behind the scenes, where journalists cultivate sources not just in the administration but on the Hill and among interest groups, to break news the White House doesn’t want broken.

records.title: PressThink: "Digby, if You’re Reading This, Send Me an E-mail." A Book Editor On Why He Loves Weblogs
records.author: Eric Nelson
records.summary: Eric Nelson, a Senior Editor at John Wiley and Sons, discusses the importance of blogs in identifying insightful content and tracking what people are reading. He argues that blogs have changed the media landscape, allowing good content to spread virally, contrasting this with the limitations of traditional media. He also highlights the shift from the 'Information Age' to the 'Age of Insight,' where the best explanations and analyses are most valued.
records.quote: In real estate, it’s location, location, location. In publishing, it’s insight, insight, insight.

records.title: PressThink: Instead of the White House Press, You Envision What?
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen critiques the Washington press corps, arguing that it has failed to evolve with the country and is not a fair representation of the US. Rosen questions the effectiveness of the traditional White House press briefing, suggesting that an alternative, more aggressive and analytical press corps, potentially based online, is needed. The piece also discusses concerns about the encroachment of government regulation on blogging and the need for increased transparency in news-making.
records.quote: The country loses when the President is not regularly and sharply questioned; and a daily session with reporters is part of good government.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: De-Certifying the Press, Continued
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Jay Rosen argues that the Bush administration is actively attempting to 'de-certify' the press, undermining its credibility and role as a check on executive power.  He critiques Howard Kurtz's dismissal of this claim, highlighting the Bush administration's unprecedented efforts to control information flow and limit press access, contrasting this with the actions of previous administrations.  Rosen emphasizes the significance of the press's role as a public interlocutor and the dangers of its delegitimization.
records.quote: If the press loses its credibility, that eliminates agreed-upon facts — the commonly accepted information that is central to public debate.

records.title: PressThink: The Abyss of Observation Alone
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen uses a fictionalized anecdote of a Western journalist embedded with Bosnian Serb snipers to explore the ethical dilemmas faced by journalists in war zones. Rosen questions the neutrality of observation, particularly the concept of 'exposure' as a journalistic principle, and critiques the potential for journalists to become complicit in the events they cover. The piece further examines Robert Kaplan's analysis of CNN's 'cosmopolitan' identity and its implications for journalistic objectivity and the rise of a 'stateless' media authority.
records.quote: You were as responsible for everything you saw as you were for everything you did.

records.title: PressThink: In the Press Room of the White House that is Post Press
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the Bush administration's efforts to undermine the traditional political press. The administration, through actions like excluding print journalists from press events and promoting a fake reporter ('Jeff Gannon'), actively sought to delegitimize mainstream media and its role as a check on power. This was part of a broader strategy to control the narrative and circumvent critical questioning, reflecting a 'post-press' era where the administration viewed journalists as a special interest group rather than representatives of the public.
records.quote: Creating “Jeff Gannon” as a credible White House correspondent, and creating radical doubt about the intentions of mainstream journalists (in order to de-certify the traditional press) are two parts of the same effort, which stretches beyond the Bush team itself to allies in Republican Party politics, and new actors like Sinclair Broadcasting, or FreeRepublic.com, or Hugh Hewitt, or these guys.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Two Letters in Reply to "A Little Detail in the Sale of About.com"
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen presents two letters responding to a previous post about the New York Times' acquisition of About.com. One letter from Scripps-Howard Newspapers discusses the challenges facing local newspapers in the digital age, including stagnant print revenue, the rise of online advertising, and the need to adapt to new pricing models. They debate the effectiveness of permalinking and the need for greater Web-centricity, open-source journalism, and moderation of local civic discourse. The second letter, from the publisher of The Daily Peg, critiques the NYT's acquisition, arguing that they could have built a superior platform more cheaply and quickly. This letter also proposes a hybrid content access model combining free access with limited daily reads and paid subscriptions for enhanced features.
records.quote: The New York Times, if it had really wanted to, and would break free from bureaucracy, could have built something way cooler and more trafficked than About in ninety days.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: A Little Detail in the Sale of About.com to the New York Times
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the New York Times' acquisition of About.com, focusing on the Times' lack of expertise in search engine optimization (SEO) and the implications for journalistic practices and the future of online news.  Rosen argues that the Times' traditional approach to content creation and its expiring URLs hinder its online presence and readership compared to websites like About.com, which prioritize SEO and web permanence.  The acquisition highlights the larger issue of legacy media struggling to adapt to the internet age and compete for online readership and advertising revenue.
records.quote: About.com is a network of about 500 mini-sites where people who know a lot about a subject—they’re called “guides,” but they could also be called bloggers—write columns and offer links and resources about specialty topics from personal finance to parenting to fly-fishing.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: The Local, the Global, and the Journalist In Between: Doug McGill's Local Man Debuts
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen discusses Doug McGill's concept of "glocal journalism" or "worldplace journalism," which involves weaving a global narrative from local threads. McGill's work, exemplified by his coverage of a genocide in Ethiopia from his base in Minnesota, highlights the power of connecting local stories to global issues through the internet. The article also touches upon the cultural context surrounding Eason Jordan's controversy at Davos and the limitations of a strictly "objective" approach to journalism in a globalized world. Finally, it discusses McGill's new blog initiatives focused on glocal journalism and addressing local news gaps.
records.quote: Glocalized journalism is a way of writing the news that describes and explains a community in the widest possible useful context, which is very often—I am tempted to say most often—a global context. Glocal journalism exposes the local effects of global causes, the local reactions to global actions, the local opportunities of global trends, the local threats of global dangers, and the local love of global neighbors.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Closing Thoughts on the Resignation of Eason Jordan
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the resignation of CNN's Eason Jordan following a controversy stemming from comments he made at the World Economic Forum in Davos. Rosen argues that Jordan's resignation was an unjust and troubling outcome, representing a failure of communication and a misunderstanding of the evolving media landscape. He criticizes the “off-the-record” rules of Davos and the subsequent blogosphere reaction, advocating for increased dialogue and transparency in the face of miscommunication rather than immediate dismissal.
records.quote: The solution to miscommunication has to be more communication.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Will Collier E-Mails With a Question
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This PressThink post discusses the reactions to the Eason Jordan controversy, focusing on the online dialogue between conservative bloggers and mainstream media figures.  It explores the nature of the conflict, questioning whether the goal is dialogue or destruction of the mainstream media. Rosen's post highlights the role of bloggers in holding the MSM accountable and the resulting tension and envy between bloggers and established journalists.
records.quote: What I’m interested in is not destruction, but rather disclosure, transparency, reform.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Eason Jordan Resigns
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Eason Jordan, CNN's chief news executive, resigned after a controversy sparked by his remarks at the World Economic Forum in Davos.  Jordan's comments, concerning the deaths of journalists in Iraq, were criticized by bloggers, who accused him of lacking sufficient evidence. The incident highlighted the power of blogs in holding powerful media figures accountable and raised concerns about the relationship between traditional media, bloggers, and the public.  The event also led to discussions about journalistic standards, the role of blogs in the news ecosystem, and the evolving nature of accountability in the media.
records.quote: On any given week the Jeff Gannon saga or the Eason Jordan controversy would have been big news on the blogs, but the fact that they came in the same week—their virtual bloodletting separated by just a few days—marks a much larger sea change. We now entering an age where journalists are so closely scrutinized by thousands of people with almost limitless time and limitless research power that the slightest misstep can end a distinguished career.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Blog Storm Troopers or Pack Journalism at its Best?
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Following up on the Eason Jordan controversy, Rosen surveys a week of blogosphere argument in a numbered set of short takes: whether the World Economic Forum should release the tape of Jordan's remarks, and whether covering the furor amounts to enabling it. He weighs a public disagreement between CJR Daily's Steve Lovelady, who dismisses blogger scrutiny of Jordan as sideline sniping, and Hugh Hewitt, who presses for the tape's release, then untangles competing claims about who actually broke the story, Wall Street Journal columnist Bret Stephens or blogger Rony Abovitz. The piece closes with Rosen's own doubts about running a comments section at all, calling it a ‘tragedy of the commons.’
records.quote: To turn on the comment feature is basically to say, “Okay, I’m going to run a tragedy of the commons case study here at my site.”
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Richard Sambrook of the BBC: What Eason Jordan Said in Davos
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the controversy surrounding CNN chief news executive Eason Jordan's comments at the Davos World Economic Forum regarding the deaths of journalists in Iraq.  Jordan's remarks, interpreted by some as accusing the US military of deliberately targeting journalists, sparked a heated debate among bloggers and media critics. Rosen presents various perspectives on the incident, including Jordan's clarification, responses from other panelists, and the ensuing media coverage, highlighting the role of speed and access in contemporary news reporting and the impact of the blogosphere on traditional media.
records.quote: I’m afraid I believe that bearing witness, first hand reporting from wars, is a fundamental duty of news organisations.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Eason Jordan's Job is the Political Job in TV News
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the role of Eason Jordan, then CNN's chief news executive, arguing that his position necessitates a blend of journalistic integrity and diplomatic skill in navigating complex international relations. Rosen critiques the simplistic framing of Jordan's controversial Davos remarks by bloggers, highlighting the complexities of CNN's global operation and Jordan's multifaceted role as both a news executive and a representative of CNN to world governments. The piece also touches upon the evolving relationship between bloggers, mainstream media, and the public.
records.quote: Eason Jordan is not the President but the Colin Powell of news at CNN, and his skills have to be diplomatic, as well as strategic.

records.title: Weekend Note on Eason Jordan
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This blog post discusses the controversy surrounding CNN chief news executive Eason Jordan's remarks at the World Economic Forum, where he allegedly stated that U.S. troops had deliberately targeted journalists. Rosen, Jay Rosen, expresses a desire to ascertain the facts before commenting on the controversy's outrage level, emphasizing the need to review available accounts and the awaited release of a recording of Jordan's speech.  Rosen's post highlights the varied reactions from different individuals and publications, noting the significant lack of coverage in mainstream media and the largely right-leaning online discussion.
records.quote: Journalist and blogger Joe Gandelman: The allegations he makes are so grave that it seems unlikely this story will die away until either he produces more proof or CNN has to eat political crow and do some damage control.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Publishing News at PressThink
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Jay Rosen announces a book deal with Times Books, a joint venture between Henry Holt and the New York Times Company, for a book tentatively titled *Gatekeepers Without Gates*.  The book will explore the transformation of the press through the internet, focusing on the rise of weblogs and other interactive forms, and the need for media corporations and journalists to regain public trust. Rosen addresses potential conflicts of interest given his criticism of the New York Times and acknowledges the transparency of the publishing arrangement.
records.quote: More is up for grabs than has ever been up for grabs since I started my watch.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: The Befuddling Complexity Defense
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the controversy surrounding a New York Times article by Sarah Boxer about the pro-American Iraqi blog, Iraq The Model. The article is criticized for its lack of journalistic rigor, its presentation of unsubstantiated claims about CIA connections, and its failure to clarify a complex situation. The debate highlights the challenges of reporting on the internet, the difficulties of verifying information online, and the differing expectations of traditional journalism versus online commentary.
records.quote: Good reporting is ordinarily the opposite of that: the situation should be more intelligible, and less opaque, when a Times journalist gets done with it.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: David Akin of CTV in Canada: It's Not the Blog. It's the Net.
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen presents an interview with David Akin, a Canadian journalist who blogs alongside his work for CTV News and The Toronto Globe and Mail. Akin argues that the internet, not blogging itself, is the revolutionary force changing journalism. He views blogging as a valuable tool for newsgathering and community engagement, enhancing his reporting by fostering interaction and providing access to diverse perspectives. While acknowledging the potential of blogs to improve journalistic practice, Akin emphasizes that blogging alone won't solve the broader trust issues facing mainstream media. He believes that increased reporter interaction with sources and improved accuracy are far more critical to building trust than simply adopting blogs.
records.quote: The blog is an increasingly important tool for newsgathering and for maintaining a connection with the community or ecosystem of those that you report on.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: A Jack Shafer Problem
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen responds to Jack Shafer's critique of bloggers' fervent pronouncements about the transformative power of blogging on journalism. Rosen acknowledges the potential for hype but defends the significance of the web's impact as an 'uber distribution channel,' unifying previously disparate media. He highlights the vulnerability of both overselling and underestimating the web's influence on the news business and uses Shafer's own past writings to illustrate the point.
records.quote: What makes the Web so unstoppable is that it’s become the uber distribution channel.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Will the Greensboro Newspaper Open Its Archive?
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen discusses the debate surrounding the opening of newspaper archives to free public access.  Journalists and industry leaders like Simon Waldman, Dan Gillmor, and Alex Jones argue that open archives, with permanent URLs, offer long-term benefits, including increased community engagement, enhanced authority, and potential for new revenue streams through advertising and value-added services.  However, concerns remain about the loss of existing revenue generated from gated archives. The article explores various perspectives, including those from newspaper editors and librarians, highlighting the challenges and potential benefits of transitioning to open-access models, questioning existing business models, and emphasizing the importance of testing this approach practically.
records.quote: Journalism exists, in its golden ideal, to spread truth and give people information that helps their lives. Journalists should advance that cause as far as possible.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Big Wigs From the Blogging & Journalism Conference Say What They Found (Part III)
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen summarizes responses from participants at the Blogging, Journalism and Credibility conference about their experiences and takeaways. The responses cover topics such as the relationship between bloggers and traditional journalists, the potential of wikis, the importance of community, business models for citizen journalism, and the need for editorial processes in blogging. The overall sentiment suggests a growing recognition of the power of online collaboration and citizen media, but also concerns about standards, ethics, and corporate influence.
records.quote: The Wiki, an online structure of networked human interaction that produces a knowledge product more powerful in rhetorical space than the Encyclopedia Britannica, acknowledged knowledge repository of my youth.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Big Wigs Confer, Part Two
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen reflects on Rosen's experience at the Blogging, Journalism & Credibility conference in 2005.  Rosen's perspective shifted significantly regarding the expansive nature of the transition from traditional news production to a more distributed, interactive model.  Key observations include the potential for new business models in the blogosphere, the evolving role of credibility in online spaces, the challenges faced by mainstream media in understanding blogging's value, and the need for collaboration between bloggers and traditional journalists to strengthen free speech and democracy.
records.quote: The challenge for us is how to integrate the best virtues from each side of this currently rather yawning abyss.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Blogging, Journalism & Credibility Conference: Key Moments
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen summarizes key discussions from the Conference on Blogging, Journalism and Credibility. Key takeaways include the impact of public involvement on information consumption, the economic viability of blogging, the fundamental differences between blogging and journalism, the surprising passion for neutrality within the Wikipedia community, the dawn of podcasting's potential, and the crucial need for open news archives.
records.quote: The media is owned. The blogosphere isn’t. We together are building it. The media have to try to get us interested in what they do, but the blogosphere is constructed out of our interests.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Keystone Crisis Management at Ketchum: Check the Home Page
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen critiques Ketchum, a major PR firm, for its mishandling of a crisis involving Armstrong Williams and a Department of Education contract.  Ketchum initially defended itself, then reversed course and apologized, but its website continued to promote a contradictory op-ed piece written by its CEO.  Rosen highlights the irony of a PR firm demonstrating such poor online communication management during a reputational crisis, questioning their competence and highlighting the disconnect between their public statements and their online presence.  Rosen also details unanswered questions sent to Ketchum employees regarding their role in the scandal.
records.quote: There was a lapse of judgment in this situation. We regret that this has occurred.

records.title: PressThink: Bloggers vs. Journalists is Over
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This essay argues that the traditional relationship between journalists and their audience is undergoing a fundamental shift due to the rise of blogs and citizen media.  Rosen contends that professional journalism is no longer sovereign over the information landscape, as blogs and other online platforms are providing alternative sources of news and opinion. This shift is reflected in the declining public trust in traditional media, the changing nature of news consumption, and the emergence of new models of journalism, such as participatory and open-source journalism.  Rosen's essay explores the implications of this changing power dynamic for the future of journalism, emphasizing the need for adaptation and innovation.
records.quote: The media world is not a zero-sum game. Increasingly, in fact, the Internet is turning it into a symbiotic ecosystem — in which the different parts feed off one another and the whole thing grows.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Ketchum and Bloggers: Who Said What?  What Remains?  Lisa Stone Reports.
records.author: Lisa Stone
records.summary: This article examines the muted response of PR bloggers to the revelation that Ketchum, a major PR firm, orchestrated a campaign using taxpayer money to promote Bush administration policies through commentator Armstrong Williams. The author contrasts this lack of response from PR bloggers with the swift condemnation from the National Association of Black Journalists, highlighting the perceived hypocrisy and ethical failures within the PR industry. The article explores the unanswered questions surrounding Ketchum's actions, including potential violations of ethical codes and the implications for the PR-media relationship in the age of blogs.
records.quote: The fact that Ketchum brokered this deal is a clear violation. To pass the buck solely to Williams is the same as letting Charles Manson off scott-free because, after all, it was the rest of the gang who committed the murders; Manson only put them up to it.

records.title: PressThink: Bloggers Are Missing in Action as Ketchum Tests the Conscience of PR
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen critiques the lack of response from PR bloggers to the Ketchum PR firm's involvement in a pay-to-play scandal, where they paid Armstrong Williams to promote the No Child Left Behind Act.  While the scandal was covered by mainstream media, PR bloggers, who are expected to be more attuned to industry ethics, largely ignored it. Rosen contrasts this inaction with the timely and outspoken blog post by Richard Edelman, CEO of a competing PR firm, highlighting the missed opportunity for PR bloggers to hold their industry accountable and investigate the ethical implications of the Ketchum contract.
records.quote: This story challenges the fundamentals of who we are and what we do.

records.title: PressThink: A Short Letter to Dan Rather
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This blog post by Jay Rosen critiques Dan Rather's response to the criticism surrounding the 60 Minutes II report on George W. Bush's National Guard service. Rosen argues that Rather's dismissal of online critics was misguided, as these online sources often provided more accurate information and faster fact-checking than CBS News. He suggests Rather hire a blogger to engage with online discussions and improve the network's responsiveness to criticism and verification efforts. Rosen highlights the value of online feedback and the importance of adapting to the changing media landscape, contrasting CBS's reaction with the potential for positive change and renewal.
records.quote: The fact checking happened online, and the fact free roaming was among your squad at CBS.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: After Trust Me Journalism Comes Openness: Rather Report Released
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the aftermath of the Dan Rather National Guard memo controversy at CBS News.  Rosen critiques CBS's response, arguing that their failure to engage with the online public's scrutiny and lack of transparency exacerbated the crisis. He advocates for increased openness and accountability in journalism, suggesting practices like publishing full interview transcripts online to foster trust and improve journalistic rigor.  The article also touches upon the role of bloggers in uncovering the story and questions the continued employment of CBS News President Andrew Heyward.
records.quote: The public has its own press now, or the least the makings of one. That is new. It is in some way “pressing” for a larger role in the news; and as we have seen lately amateurs are actually capable of doing that.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: The Importance of Being Permanent
records.author: Simon Waldman
records.summary: Simon Waldman, Director of Digital Publishing for The Guardian, argues that the permanence of online content is crucial for news organizations.  Unlike traditional media, the web offers the potential for content to remain accessible indefinitely, building a lasting online presence and establishing authority. Waldman contrasts this with the fleeting nature of much online news, which quickly disappears from search results and active cultural memory. He uses examples like Wikipedia's comprehensive coverage of major events and the long-term impact of Chris Anderson's 'The Long Tail' essay to illustrate the benefits of permanence.  Jay Rosen's commentary emphasizes the contrasting approaches of The Guardian (which prioritizes permanence and linking) and many American newspapers (which often remove content from their free sites, hindering their online presence and impact).
records.quote: Permanence means understanding that when you put something on the Web it should be there for ever: ideally in the same place for perpetuity. It means that if I link to it now, someone else can follow that link in two days, two weeks or two years’ time.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Top Ten Ideas of '04: "What Once Was Good--or Good Enough--No Longer Is."
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen discusses the decline in quality of journalism, particularly in newspapers, due to the changing media landscape and the failure of news organizations to adapt. Rosen highlights the increased competition from blogs and other online platforms, the persistence of an outdated newsroom culture that prioritizes speed over quality, and the missed opportunities for innovation in online presentation. The piece uses examples such as Craigslist's impact on classified ad revenue and the lack of understanding of online linking within a major newspaper to illustrate the need for adaptation and intentional journalism.
records.quote: When what used to be good enough no longer is—because circumstances have changed—the people who had for years been doing “good enough” journalism suddenly have to recognize that demand for their services is growing thin.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Open Source Journalism Comes a Step Closer in Greensboro: A Plan is Shown
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen discusses Lex Alexander's report on citizen journalism for the News & Record, a Greensboro newspaper. The report proposes a shift from repurposing print content online to embracing the internet's culture, including more blog-style journalism, participatory journalism, and a radically different website philosophy emphasizing open standards, transparency, and interaction. The article highlights the newspaper's move towards becoming an 'internet newspaper with a print edition,' contrasting this approach with the legacy 'repurposing' model. Reactions from various individuals, including skeptics and proponents, are presented, alongside discussions on community building online, the role of reputation systems in the blogging era, and the broader implications of this transition for the news industry.
records.quote: It’s taken a long time for daily newspaper people to get there, but it seems to me that Greensboro has arrived at the crossover. It is ready to become an Internet newspaper with a print edition, rather than an old-style newspaper re-purposing its content online.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Top Ten Ideas of '04: "Content Will be More Important than its Container"
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen discusses Tom Curley's assertion that 'content will be more important than its container,' arguing that the focus should shift from the platform (newspaper, broadcast, website) to the quality of the journalism itself. Rosen critiques the resistance of legacy media to adapt to the web, highlighting the reluctance to invest in people and re-educate journalists about the changing media landscape. The rise of RSS and the shift in reader behavior towards content consumption independent of specific websites are presented as key factors driving this change. Rosen also explores the implications for journalism education and the need for a more content-focused curriculum.
records.quote: The franchise is not the newspaper; it’s not the broadcast; it’s not even the Web site. The franchise is the content itself.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: After Miller: Let There Be Light
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen reflects on the Judith Miller case at the New York Times, arguing that the episode should prompt greater transparency and accountability in how major news organizations handle sourcing and editorial judgment.
records.quote: The Judith Miller case should force major news organizations to adopt greater transparency in how they handle sourcing and editorial judgment, rather than treating opacity as a professional virtue.

records.title: News Turns From a Lecture to a Conversation
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen from PressThink discusses the shift in news from a one-way lecture to a two-way conversation, driven by the rise of blogs and the increased power of the audience. Rosen argues that this shift is not merely about correcting errors, but also about democratizing the news process and fostering a more informed public discourse. The increased access to information and tools allows the audience to participate actively in news creation and critique, challenging the traditional authority of mainstream media.
records.quote: The news, as “lecture,” is giving way to the news as a “conversation.”
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: My advice for the News & Record
records.author: Zack Rosen
records.summary: Zack Rosen, nephew of Jay Rosen and a veteran of the Howard Dean campaign's web efforts, offers advice to the Greensboro News & Record on how to effectively integrate blogging and web communities into their online presence. He emphasizes the importance of building a participatory community rather than just a weblog, suggesting the use of advanced platforms like Scoop or Drupal to facilitate this. He points to Daily Kos as an exemplar of successful online community building and cites examples from the Lawrence Journal-World and OhMyNews as models for innovative online journalism.
records.quote: The News & Record, a pretty normal seeming Greensboro North Carolina newspaper, is taking a plunge into the world of blogging and web-community.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Open Source Journalism
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen explores the concept of "open source journalism," arguing that the internet allows for a self-informing public where readers collectively possess more knowledge than individual journalists. It highlights examples like Slashdot's interaction with Jane's Intelligence Review and Josh Marshall's Talking Points Memo, showcasing how citizen participation can enhance reporting through distributed fact-checking and knowledge sharing. Rosen advocates for journalists to embrace this paradigm shift, building "learning machines" that leverage the collective intelligence of their readers to improve reporting and overcome the limitations of traditional journalism.
records.quote: The audience always knew more than the journalist about a great many things, but it didn’t have a network for pulling its scattered self together.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: PressThink's Top Ten Ideas for 2004: Introduction
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes ten key ideas that emerged in the blogosphere and media landscape during 2004.  Rosen focuses on three: the challenges faced by legacy media in adapting to the internet age; the need for journalists to move beyond simplistic "he said, she said" reporting and embrace more assertive judgment; and the transformative impact of the blogging press, analogous to the printing press's effect on the Catholic Church.  The piece highlights the shifting power dynamics in the media, the evolving role of journalists, and the challenges of maintaining credibility and authority in a rapidly changing digital environment.
records.quote: What the printing press did to the Catholic Church the blogging press does to the media church.

records.title: PressThink: Greensboro Newspaper Goes Open Source: A Follow Up
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen discusses the News & Record, a Greensboro newspaper, its initiative to overhaul its website and embrace open-source journalism principles by incorporating public input and becoming more of an online community. The piece highlights the newspaper's collaboration with local bloggers, the innovative approach of its editor John Robinson, and the broader implications for the future of online journalism. It also touches upon the emergence of local aggregators like Greensboro101 and the reactions from other tech bloggers and the broader media landscape.
records.quote: My still-evolving observation is that bloggers and newspapers want basically the same thing: to tell people the news.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: More Undercurrent: Action in Greensboro on Open Source Journalism
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen details the burgeoning blogosphere in Greensboro, North Carolina, and the surprising collaboration between local bloggers and the Greensboro News-Record. The newspaper's editor, John Robinson, is embracing blogging, aiming for a transformative change to its online presence by incorporating reader feedback and creating a more interactive online community. This move is seen as a potential model for other news organizations struggling to adapt to the digital age, showcasing a shift in the relationship between traditional media and its audience.
records.quote: Our editor and M.E. have asked me to figure out how we might change our Web site into more of an online community or public square.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Undercurrent: Nation, Region, Weblog, Home
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen explores the burgeoning global landscape of blogging in 2004, focusing on the emergence of multilingual blogging communities and the implications for journalistic practice and the construction of national and global identities.  Rosen examines how blogs, particularly those written in English, are creating new forms of imagined communities that transcend geographical boundaries and traditional media structures, while also reflecting distinct national and regional perspectives on media and politics. The piece highlights initiatives like Global Voices Online and the creation of blogging tools in Arabic as examples of this global development and raises questions about the nature of this emerging 'citizens' media' and its impact on the relationship between journalism, community, and nationhood.
records.quote: “In fact, all communities larger than promordial villages of face-to-face contact are imagined,” says Benedict Anderson in his great study of modern nationalism (Imagined Communities, Verso, 1983.) They differ, he adds, “by the style in which they are imagined.”
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Kind of a Drag: A Short History of Spin Alley and the Press
records.author: Lisa Stone
records.summary: This article traces the history of "Spin Alley" in American politics, from its origins in the 1984 Reagan-Mondale debates to its critique by Jon Stewart in 2004.  The author identifies three phases: an initial fascination with spin as a political tactic, a subsequent disillusionment with its inherent dishonesty, and finally, a movement to transcend spin through fact-checking and a renewed focus on journalistic integrity. The article highlights the evolving relationship between journalists and political spin, showing how journalists initially accepted spin as part of the game, then grew critical of its manipulative nature, ultimately advocating for a more ethical approach to political reporting.
records.quote: The public confronted the same issues of deception and media spin that we see as characteristic of modern politics, Knights wrote, bridging the 400-year gap between politics in Stuart England and Jon Stewarts visit to Crossfire.

records.title: PressThink: The Big Listen Option for CBS News After Rather
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This blog post discusses the departure of Dan Rather from CBS Evening News and proposes that CBS undertake a nationwide public listening tour to understand American views on broadcast news before making decisions about the future of the program and its anchor.  Rosen's post also touches on related news, including Dan Gillmor's move to citizen journalism and discussions around the "Memo-gate" scandal at CBS.
records.quote: Something powerful is happening, it’s in the early stages and I have a chance to help figure this out.

records.title: PressThink: What is the Internet Doing to Political Journalism and its Public?
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen previews Jay Rosen's participation in a Berkman Center conference on the internet's impact on politics.  The conference explores how the internet has changed political journalism and the public's engagement with it, questioning whether it has genuinely improved political discourse or simply altered the flow of information, introducing new competitors, and stimulating writerly invention.  Rosen highlights the interactive, less formal nature of his session, emphasizing a skeptical approach to assessing the internet's actual influence on politics.
records.quote: The Internet changes the flow in political journalism by giving users way more of it.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Notes and Comment on The Media Company I Want to Work For
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen discusses the reactions to Mark Glaser's essay, "The Media Company I Want to Work For."  The responses reveal a growing sense of readiness among journalists and others to create new media ventures that are faster-moving and more responsive to community needs than established media.  The article highlights examples like Backfence.com, a hyperlocal news aggregator focused on user-generated content, and Pegasus News, illustrating a shift toward citizen journalism and de-professionalization of news, driven by the internet and new technologies.
records.quote: People care most about news and information about the places, people and things closest to them, but this desire for intensely local (neighborhood-level) information is all but unmet by traditional media.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: The Media Company I Want to Work For
records.author: Mark Glaser
records.summary: Mark Glaser, an online journalist, expresses his frustration with the slow pace of change in established media companies and outlines his vision for a new kind of media company that embraces the internet, interactivity, citizen journalism, and community involvement.  This new model would utilize a multi-platform approach, including web, print, audio, and video, with revenue generated through targeted advertising, paid content, and syndication.  The company would prioritize reader engagement and community participation, potentially even using a community-based payment system for contributors.
records.quote: This is my hope for the future of journalism, because the old way is in tatters and rotting by the side of the road. It’s time for the readers and enlightened journalists to take back their power, to set the media’s agenda, to rip out the reins from the graying media barons who have their blinders on.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Writer Says Media is Election's Big Loser: 21 Times
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen compiles 21 examples from various sources (blogs, newspapers, opinion journals) expressing the sentiment that the mainstream media were the biggest losers in the 2004 US presidential election.  Rosen presents these examples to analyze the underlying criticisms of the media's performance and its relationship with politics,  leaving the interpretation largely to the readers.
records.quote: The problem for Old Media is that it no longer has the kind of monopoly control over political news that it enjoyed a quarter-century ago. And its efforts to help John Kerry proved counterproductive.

records.title: Reaching for Moral Values in the Post Election Debris
records.author: Weldon Berger
records.summary: Weldon Berger critiques the press's post-election focus on 'moral values' as a key factor in the 2004 election outcome. He argues that the media overreacted to exit poll data and created a misleading narrative, neglecting other important issues and misinterpreting the role of values in voters' decisions. He suggests that the press's confession of missing the 'moral values' story might be a cover for deeper issues with their understanding of the American public and basic journalistic principles.
records.quote: Moral values, like religion, is a frame whereby issues are evaluted, not a specific issue in and of itself.

records.title: PressThink: Dan Rather: Park Avenue Ordinary
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes Dan Rather's departure from the CBS Evening News anchor position in March 2005, following controversy surrounding a 60 Minutes story about George W. Bush's National Guard service.  Rosen discusses the factors contributing to Rather's departure, including his unconventional style and the investigation into the story's questionable sourcing. He contrasts Rather's personality with the prevailing 'smooth' style of television news and reflects on the significance of Rather's career and legacy in the changing media landscape.
records.quote: Bringing devastating memos into a campaign’s final sprint is like bringing pistols on stage. You better know what you are doing at that point in the script.

records.title: A Reply to David Shaw: Are We Headed for an Opposition Press?
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This is a response to David Shaw's critique of Jay Rosen's proposal for a more openly liberal news network as a counterpoint to Fox News. Rosen defends his idea as a provocation meant to challenge the prevailing journalistic norms, particularly the concept of 'objectivity' as a neutral stance. He argues against the idea that striving for neutrality prevents truth-telling and suggests that alternative approaches to journalism are needed in a changing media landscape.  The core of Rosen's argument challenges the established 'Contraption' – the standard routines and principles of mainstream journalism – arguing that it inhibits truth-telling and fails to address the evolving political and media environment.
records.quote: Journalism isn’t a profession, but an activity. And it’s an activity that technology is putting within the reach of many more Americans. That’s bad news if you’re Dan Rather, but it’s good news for the rest of us.

records.title: PressThink: Off the Charts: Sinclair Broadcast Group's Political Vision
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes Sinclair Broadcasting's controversial decision to air an anti-Kerry documentary, 'Stolen Honor,' on its stations before the 2004 election. It argues that Sinclair's actions deviated from established broadcast practices and business logic, driven by a political agenda to become a conservative broadcast network. The piece examines Sinclair's previous controversial decisions, like refusing to air a Nightline episode reading the names of soldiers killed in Iraq, and discusses the implications of Sinclair's expanding media ownership and the role of its corporate affairs VP, Mark Hyman, as an on-air commentator.
records.quote: Sinclair got here by flying under the radar, the preferred method of winning regulatory relief. But that phase is clearly over.

records.title: PressThink: How Do You Blog Ideas into Events? PressThink Tries to Find Out
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This blog post recounts Jay Rosen's experience at the Online News Association (ONA) conference in Hollywood, 2004. He discusses the emerging phenomenon of event blogging, highlighting its various forms and its role in disseminating information and shaping the narrative around the conference. Rosen uses the conference as a platform to further his argument about the breakdown of the traditional mainstream media model ('the contraption'), emphasizing the need for a stronger two-way connection between journalists and their audience and the uncertain future of who 'owns' journalism in the age of digital platforms like Google News and Yahoo News.
records.quote: I said that human editors are good to have, a smart algorithm is also good, but what will ultimately spell the difference in quality is the strength of the relationship or two-way connection between the filterers (editors) and the users for whom the filtering (editing) is done.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: NYT committee to study ways to improve paper’s credibility
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes a New York Times memo announcing a committee to improve the paper's credibility. The memo focuses on issues such as the overuse of anonymous sources, background briefings, and the role of public criticism. Rosen critiques the memo's approach, arguing for more proactive measures, greater engagement with readers, and the utilization of game theory to understand the dynamics of sourcing. He suggests the NYT should adopt a more public and transparent approach to address these concerns.
records.quote: The number one way to improve your accountability is to go outside the paper and to the readers, however that might be construed.

records.title: PressThink: Matt Welch on Shifting Terms of Authority in the Newspaper Press
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen discusses Matt Welch's suggestions for newspapers to adapt to a changing media landscape characterized by declining public trust and the rise of blogs.  Welch proposes increased transparency within newsrooms, including publicly sharing staff political affiliations and creating detailed online profiles for reporters. He also advocates for editors to be more publicly engaged and less defensive in responding to criticism. Rosen reflects on the anxieties of some journalists regarding the limitations of traditional journalistic methods and their openness to new approaches in the face of criticism and the rise of the internet.
records.quote: The idea is not to advertise your bias, but on the contrary, to be as upfront and transparent as you demand of others. You’ll also be knee-capping the bias-hunters, and figuring out whether your news organization has some ideological blind spots worth addressing.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Not Up to It
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen, written in 2004, reflects on the impact of 9/11 and the 2004 US Presidential election on journalism. Rosen argues that the traditional, impartial model of journalism is inadequate for covering the current political climate, particularly in the context of the War on Terror. He highlights the changing relationship between the press and the public, suggesting that the media's identity has been redefined by external forces and that journalists must grapple with their role in relation to the war on terror and the broader struggle against threats to open society.
records.quote: There is a war being conducted against the open society. Journalists are combatants in that one. They cannot afford to lose it, and they cannot afford to prosecute it with broken equipment.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: BloggerCon III: Notes and Observations on the People of Moore's Law
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen reflects on the third BloggerCon conference, held at Stanford Law School. Rosen observes a clash of interpretations between those viewing it as a tech conference and those seeing it as a forum for democratic participation and media production. Rosen highlights the tech community's acceptance of rapid platform changes, contrasting it with the inertia of mainstream journalism. He emphasizes the shift from a consumer-driven media landscape to a producer-driven one, exemplified by bloggers who create and share information, effectively becoming 'vendors to the public square.' The article explores the implications of this producer democracy for journalism, medicine, and politics, suggesting a changing relationship between authority and knowledge.
records.quote: A pizza-stained paper plate sat between Moulitsas and Atrios. Together, they have more readers than The Philadelphia Inquirer.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: PressThink is Looking for a Second Author (Maybe) and a Donor (Definitely)
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Jay Rosen, author of the PressThink blog, seeks a contributor to assist with writing and website maintenance, a donor to support the blog's expansion, and guest writers to contribute to discussions about the press's predicament following the 2004 election. He outlines the desired skills and contributions for the contributor role, highlighting the lack of monetary compensation but offering exposure and opportunities for professional development.
records.quote: I can get the right person many thousands of readers—including working journalists—some blog visibility, your name in Google, a chance to have voice in debates about the future of the press, and to plunge into Web publishing, build a brand.

records.title: Are We Headed for an Opposition Press?
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Following George W. Bush's 2004 re-election, this article questions whether the American press will evolve into an 'opposition press,' openly aligning with political viewpoints, mirroring European models.  Rosen analyzes Rosen's post-election media landscape, noting the impact of partisan blogs and the need for a re-evaluation of journalistic practices.  Concerns are raised about the intimidation of the press and the potential for further polarization given the Bush administration's perceived antagonism toward the media.
records.quote: “The press has been pretending for too long that its old operating system will last forever,” argues NYU’s Rosen. “It won’t.”

records.title: PressThink: People, Nation, Republic: Reflections for Election Night
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen reflects on the nature of political fictions, using the upcoming election as a context. It draws upon the works of Edmund S. Morgan, Benedict Anderson, and James W. Carey to explore how concepts like 'the sovereignty of the people' and 'the press' function as powerful, imagined communities that shape our understanding of democracy and national identity. Rosen emphasizes the role of media in fostering public conversation and warns against the press becoming a detached observer rather than a participant in that conversation.
records.quote: Political fictions work by challenging “the governing few” to reform the facts of our existence to fit the aspirations the fiction had earlier fed. And in this way it becomes fact.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: No Longer Do the Newsies Decide
records.author: Daniel Weintraub
records.summary: This article discusses the changing landscape of political journalism in the early 2000s, marked by the rise of blogs and cable news. Daniel Weintraub, a journalist who embraced blogging early on, reflects on the loss of control and influence experienced by traditional journalists due to increased accessibility of information and reader feedback. He argues that while this shift is initially unnerving, it presents opportunities for improvement, suggesting a move towards more compelling storytelling, greater reader engagement, and collaborative journalism. He acknowledges the challenges but ultimately expresses a relatively optimistic view of the future, emphasizing the importance of adapting to the changing media environment.
records.quote: If our world is changing, we simply have to change with it. We have to engage more with our readers, become more a part of the conversation and less of a lecturer.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: The Coming Apart of An Ordered World: Bloggers Notebook, Election Eve
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This 2004 post reflects on the US presidential election, contrasting the traditional press's coverage with the burgeoning influence of blogs and the changing relationship between the press, the public, and political power. Rosen critiques the horse-race journalism of major outlets, highlighting the disconnect between their reporting and the public's experience. He analyzes the Bush administration's strategic attempts to undermine the press's credibility and influence, noting the increased intensity of attacks on journalists perceived as biased. Rosen emphasizes the rise of alternative media and questions the future relevance of traditional journalism's role in political coverage.
records.quote: We’re an empire now, and when we act, we create our own reality.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: The Fading Mystique of an Objective Press
records.author: Doug McGill
records.summary: Doug McGill's essay critiques the journalistic practice of objectivity, arguing that its pursuit often leads to a superficial 'he said/she said' approach that masks deeper truths and fails to serve the public interest. He contends that the ideal of objectivity is often used to rationalize newsroom failures and proposes a more rigorous approach that prioritizes pattern recognition and a deeper understanding of the issues being reported, even if it deviates from traditional notions of neutrality.
records.quote: The untold story in the media is most often a story not that the public wants to know, but ought to know.

records.title: PressThink: Too Much Reality: Is There Such a Thing?
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This PressThink blog post reflects on Rosen's experience during a BBC interview about the rapidly changing political and media landscape in 2004. Rosen grapples with the overwhelming amount of information and interconnected events, struggling to articulate a coherent narrative. Rosen's post then presents a list of related phenomena and invites readers to connect them, sparking a discussion in the comments section with various perspectives on the changing media environment and the loss of control over information.
records.quote: Technological change has always had profound social consequences, but few inventions in history have caused more political and cultural change than movable type printing.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Sinclair Goes to Air Friday Night: Notes and Comment on "A POW Story"
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes Sinclair Broadcast Group's handling of the documentary "Stolen Honor," focusing on their decision to air a related special program instead of the documentary itself.  Rosen critiques Sinclair's shifting justifications and mendacious behavior, highlighting the ideological pressure exerted on news producers by CEO David Smith and Vice President Mark Hyman.  The article details the controversy surrounding the documentary, Sinclair's attempts to influence the narrative, and the firing of Jon Leiberman, a Washington bureau chief who spoke out against the company's actions. Rosen ultimately portrays Sinclair as an ideologically driven group operating in a paranoid style, manipulating news for political purposes.
records.quote: Sinclair is always innocent.

records.title: PressThink: "Call it Commentary, Call it Editorial, Call it Programming, but Don't Call it News." Sinclair Fires Jonathan Leiberman
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen details the controversy surrounding Sinclair Broadcasting Group's decision to air the anti-Kerry documentary "Stolen Honor" on its 60 stations. Rosen focuses on the firing of Jon Leiberman, Sinclair's Washington bureau chief, for publicly criticizing the decision. The event is analyzed as a deliberate act by Sinclair to politicize its news coverage, consolidate its power, and purge dissenting voices, demonstrating a strategy of right-wing influence within the media landscape through acquisitions and control of newsrooms.
records.quote: “For me, it’s not about right or left — it’s about what’s right or wrong in news coverage this close to an election.”
concepts: Not the odds but the stakes

records.title: PressThink: Sinclair Broadcast Group: What Are They Doing in the Middle of Our Election?
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This blog post analyzes the Sinclair Broadcast Group's offer to Senator John Kerry to appear on their stations to respond to a documentary critical of his Vietnam War record.  Rosen argues that Kerry should accept the offer, framing it as a potential opportunity to address the criticisms directly and gain a significant advantage in the election.  Rosen's post explores the reactions of various commentators, including those who believe Kerry should reject the offer due to the potential for legitimizing the documentary's claims, and those who support Rosen's position.
records.quote: Sinclair thought it could finally expose a pretender to the throne who almost took the prize. That’s a deed of service to the throne. It’s also a sign to others: we’re here. Instantly you’re a force in the Republican Party.

records.title: Agnew with TV Stations: Sinclair Broadcasting Takes On John Kerry and The Liberal Media
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes Sinclair Broadcast Group's decision to air the documentary "Stolen Honor" shortly before the 2004 election. Rosen argues that this move, along with Sinclair's broader strategy of centralizing news production and promoting a conservative viewpoint, represents a new kind of political force in broadcasting—a media empire with a clear political agenda, unlike traditional media companies. He draws parallels to Silvio Berlusconi's media empire in Italy, highlighting the blurring of lines between media ownership and political influence and the potential threat to journalistic objectivity and the fairness of elections.
records.quote: In a commercial empire it makes no sense to invite a storm like that. But what if a company were built for that sort of storm? A lot depends on how we define Sinclair Broadcast Group: as a media company with a political agenda, or a political actor that’s gotten hold of a media company and is re-shaping it for bigger battles ahead.

records.title: PressThink: John Kerry Should Accept Sinclair Broadcasting's Offer
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This series of blog posts from Jay Rosen's PressThink analyzes Sinclair Broadcast Group's decision to air an anti-Kerry film days before the 2004 election. Rosen discusses the ethical implications of Sinclair's actions, particularly their attempt to frame the film as a news program to circumvent equal-time rules. He also considers the strategic implications for Kerry, suggesting he should accept Sinclair's offer of a response segment to create a powerful, unmediated confrontation with the right.  The posts also touch upon the broader issue of the conservative assault on journalistic objectivity and the use of media bias accusations as a political tactic.
records.quote: I can’t think of a precedent of holding up programming to show a political documentary at a point where it would have the maximum effect on the vote.

records.title: The Best Approximation of Accuracy Possible in a Given Moment
records.author: Chris Satullo
records.summary: Chris Satullo responds to criticism of his article criticizing sloppy thinking in media bias discussions. He argues that journalists strive for accuracy under immense time constraints and imperfect information, acknowledging unintentional biases. He criticizes ideological critics who wrongly assume journalists share their biases, highlighting examples of overly partisan attacks from both left and right-wing groups. Satullo defends his concept of 'public life going well,' clarifying its non-partisan nature and emphasizing its focus on facilitating productive public discourse and democratic participation.
records.quote: Public life goes well when elections are about the issues most on the mind of the electorate, when the voters voice helps frame the choices and the debate, and the candidates are required to respond to that voice.

records.title: PressThink: Authorized Knower: Farnaz Fassihi's Accidental Baghdad Dispatch
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the unexpected public dissemination of a private email written by Wall Street Journal reporter Farnaz Fassihi detailing her experiences in Baghdad. The email, initially intended for friends, became a widely circulated online document, sparking a debate about the boundaries between a journalist's private opinions and their public reporting. Rosen discusses the implications of this incident for the relationship between journalists, their sources, and the public, particularly in the context of the war in Iraq and the growing power of the internet.
records.quote: The unvarnished e-mail is not just a better read than so much conventional copy — it gives people a behind-the-curtains feeling that they love.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Political Jihad and the American Blog: Chris Satullo Raises the Stakes
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the reaction of mainstream journalists to the rise of blogs, particularly in the context of the Dan Rather/CBS memo controversy. Mainstream journalists, exemplified by Nick Coleman and Tom Brokaw, viewed the bloggers' criticism as an attack on the media, failing to recognize the potential benefits of this new form of citizen journalism. Chris Satullo's article in the Philadelphia Inquirer is highlighted as a counterpoint, arguing that journalists should embrace the increased public engagement and scrutiny provided by bloggers, while also cautioning against the manipulation of the 'bias' narrative by those with ulterior motives. Satullo distinguishes between legitimate criticism seeking improvements in journalism and those seeking to destroy it through propaganda.
records.quote: What matters is that journalism survive, that the craft of speaking truth to power with factual care not be snuffed out.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Nick Coleman's Blogged Down in Web Fantasy
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes Nick Coleman's op-ed criticizing bloggers, highlighting its rhetorical style and Rosen's seeming satisfaction in provoking a negative reaction.  Rosen contrasts Coleman's dismissive view of bloggers with the emerging recognition of blogs' significance within journalism, citing NPR's ombudsman Jeffrey Dvorkin.  The piece underscores the changing media landscape and the mainstream media's struggle to adapt to the rise of online voices and the changing understanding of journalistic credibility.
records.quote: “Bloggers are hobby hacks, the Internet version of the sad loners who used to listen to police radios in their bachelor apartments and think they were involved in the world.”
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: You Watched. Tell Me What You Saw in Jim Lehrer's Performance.
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen presents a post-mortem analysis of Jim Lehrer's moderation of a 2004 presidential debate between George W. Bush and John Kerry. It compiles reader comments and critiques of Lehrer's performance, focusing on his question selection, perceived biases (or lack thereof), and overall effectiveness in facilitating a substantive exchange between the candidates. The discussion touches upon the role of a debate moderator in shaping public understanding of the candidates and the issues, with some arguing that Lehrer successfully steered the debate towards key policy matters while others criticized his question choices and style.
records.quote: His skill turned what promised to be nothing but a presentation of spin and sound bites into something more nearly debate like. In this he did citizens a great favor.
concepts: Not the odds but the stakes
The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Nagourney's Challenge: Quit Spin Alley
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen discusses Adam Nagourney's decision to forgo Rosen's post-debate spin room at the 2004 presidential debate, choosing instead to write his story from Washington D.C. based solely on what the candidates said.  Rosen praises this as an act of dissent against the pervasive influence of spin in political journalism, highlighting its potential to encourage other journalists to prioritize substance over manufactured narratives. The article also explores the role of bloggers in fact-checking and holding both the press and candidates accountable.
records.quote: “What’s important to me is what the candidates say. I don’t care about anyone else,” he told the Miami Herald.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Every Four Years Journalism
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen critiques the 'Every Four Years Journalism' approach to election coverage, arguing that the standard model of campaign reporting—focused on horse-race dynamics, candidate profiles, and issue positions—is outdated and fails to address the changing media landscape. Rosen points to the rise of partisan sources like Fox News, the increased influence of blogs, and the growing public distrust of traditional media as reasons for a need for innovation in election coverage. He contrasts the complacent attitude of many established journalists, exemplified by Rick Berke of the New York Times, with the more critical and engaging approach of commentators like Jon Stewart, who are better able to connect with audiences in the age of media fragmentation and spin.
records.quote: Jon Stewart, who is in every sense a professional, is part of this plurality. He delivers a take on the news that is more truthful than the news for a good hunk of the audience. And so Stewart is cited by Campaign Desk for some of the most original work of the year. Often, he’s more believable than both the candidates or the press.

records.title: PressThink: Does CBS News Have a Political Future in This State?
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the political and journalistic fallout from the CBS 60 Minutes II report on President Bush's National Guard service.  Rosen critiques CBS's response to the controversy, particularly the composition and charge of its internal review committee, arguing that the network's attempts to separate itself from politics undermined its credibility and hampered a thorough investigation. The article highlights the tension between journalistic objectivity and the inherent political nature of the situation, emphasizing the need for transparent and comprehensive inquiry to restore public trust.
records.quote: The challenge for professional journalists today is to understand how their role has changed.

records.title: Philip Gourevitch: Campaign Reporting as Foreign Beat
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Philip Gourevitch's experience covering the 2004 presidential campaign is analyzed as a case study of the limitations and complicity within the embedded press corps.  Gourevitch highlights the self-imposed constraints of the travelling press, their fear of losing access, and their complicity in accepting the candidates' controlled narratives. He argues that the press's focus on the 'horse race' and 'electability' overshadows substantive policy discussions and contributes to a 'pretend' debate. The article emphasizes the need for a more adversarial and independent press capable of challenging power.
records.quote: Freedom doesn’t lie in access. It means having an adversarial press, an independent press, a political press that can challenge power.

records.title: PressThink: Did the President of CBS News Have Anyone in Charge of Reading the Internet and Sending Alerts?
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes CBS News's handling of the controversy surrounding Dan Rather's report on President Bush's National Guard service.  Rosen criticizes CBS's initially hostile response to online criticism questioning the authenticity of the documents used in the report, highlighting a failure of leadership and verification processes.  Rosen contrasts CBS's reaction with the more self-correcting practices of other news organizations, lamenting the network's loss of credibility and the wider implications for the relationship between legacy media and the public in the age of the internet.
records.quote: CBS News, having now admitted that documents it relied on were inauthentic, will have troubles graver than a retraction of Dan Rather’s account and an official apology to President Bush, to CBS viewers and to the American public.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Rather's Satisfaction: Mystifying Troubles at CBS
records.author: Jay Rosen
