However, he also expresses concern about the potential for the project to devolve into hateful attacks on journalists, highlighting the existing climate of anti-media sentiment and the need for responsible criticism.
records.quote: Adopting a campaign reporter, and writing a weblog about the work that reporter does, is involving yourself in the press.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Special to PressThink: Interview With Herbert Gans, America's Senior Sociologist of News
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This interview with Herbert Gans discusses his critique of journalistic objectivity and his advocacy for a "multiperspectival" approach to news. Gans argues that traditional objectivity, by prioritizing limited perspectives and sources (often those in power), fails to adequately represent the political and social diversity of society. He contends that a multiperspectival approach, encompassing viewpoints from various social strata and incorporating a wider range of ideas, would better serve democracy. While acknowledging the practical constraints faced by journalists, Gans emphasizes the principle's validity and encourages journalists to strive for greater inclusivity in their reporting.
records.quote: Journalists cannot be objective in their choice of topics or sources, or of what they define as facts. However, they must report these sources and facts objectively or at least with detachment from their own personal values and biases.

records.title: PressThink: Adopt a Campaign Journalist in 2004: The Drift of a Suggestion
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This PressThink article documents the emergence of the "Adopt-a-Journalist" movement in the early 2000s blogosphere. Bloggers, spurred by perceived biases in mainstream media coverage of the 2004 presidential campaign, began closely monitoring and critiquing the work of specific journalists. This initiative, exemplified by blogs like the Wilgoren Watch, sparked debate about the role of citizen journalism, media accountability, and the relationship between bloggers and traditional journalists. The article captures the excitement and controversy surrounding this early form of online media criticism, showcasing diverse viewpoints from both participating bloggers and established journalists.
records.quote: Bloggers adopting journalists could be the best thing that happens to journalism, because it creates a class of people who elevate the perceived importance of journalism.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Journalism Is Itself a Religion: Special Essay on Launch of The Revealer
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This essay, written on the launch of Rosen's new online journal, *The Revealer*, explores the parallels between journalism and religion. Rosen argues that journalism operates with its own internal belief system, including a priesthood (elite journalists), a creed (the Journalist's Creed), and sacred objects (the public, the First Amendment). He uses the example of Columbia Journalism School to illustrate how journalism education functions as a form of theological training, instilling values and a sense of purpose in aspiring journalists. Rosen's essay also touches upon the ethical responsibilities of journalists and their role in shaping public perception.
records.quote: The ultimate justification for journalism and the First Amendment is that together they constitute us as a civil society and set us in conversation with one another.

records.title: Horse Race Now! Horse Race Tomorrow! Horse Race Forever!
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen critiques the "horse race" style of political journalism, exemplified by articles in the New York Times and Washington Post that omit the internet's influence on the 2004 presidential campaign.  Rosen draws a parallel between this approach and Bill James's concept of "inside baseball" in sportswriting, arguing that both prioritize insider perspectives and clichés over a broader, more informed analysis.  He contrasts this "inside baseball" approach with an "outside baseball" perspective that utilizes publicly available information for a deeper understanding of the subject, advocating for a more comprehensive and less reliant approach to political reporting.
records.quote: Inside baseball is both a knowledge system and a belief system.

records.title: Why Do Paul Krugman's New Year's Resolutions Lack Resolve?
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This text is not a single article but a curated list of Jay Rosen's work and recommended resources related to journalism, blogging, and the internet's impact on the news media. It highlights various interviews, presentations, and blog posts covering topics like the transformation of journalism by the web, the rise of citizen journalism, and the changing dynamics of authority in the press. The text also includes a commentary section analyzing Paul Krugman's advice to journalists on covering the 2004 election campaign and the role of partisan voices in the press.
records.quote: Krugman’s great advantage as a journalist is that he is not a journalist.

records.title: PressThink: Thoughts on the Killing of a Young Correspondent
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This memorial speech, delivered at the service for Sander Thoenes, a young journalist killed in East Timor in 1999, explores four key aspects of Thoenes' life and work: his global citizenship, his connection to the university tradition, the impact of Dutch colonialism, and the relationship between media and journalism. Rosen argues that Thoenes' commitment to truth-telling and his ability to connect with people from diverse backgrounds made him an exceptional journalist, and his death highlights the importance of press freedom and ethical journalism.
records.quote: Sander was doing his job, but the point to remember is how he defined his job: citizen of the world tries to tell the world what goes on in the struggle for an open society.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Politically Significant Cluelessness
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Frank Rich sent a "get a clue" letter to colleagues, members of a tone deaf political class. They don't get Dean. Or the Net.

concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Interesting Theory. But Journalists Don't Do Theory. Do They?
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This blog post analyzes the coverage of the 2004 Dean presidential campaign, questioning the journalistic practice of avoiding theoretical frameworks in favor of a purportedly objective 'reporting' approach. Rosen critiques commentators like Jeff Jarvis and John Dvorak for employing rhetorical strategies that inflate claims to subsequently debunk them, highlighting the lack of engagement with actual evidence. He contrasts this with Everett Ehrlich's three-sided analysis of the campaign, arguing that a theoretical lens can lead to more accurate and insightful coverage. Rosen's post also explores the inherent resistance within journalism to theoretical engagement, citing comments from newspaper editors who view theory as irrelevant to the practice of news reporting.
records.quote: This notion, if accepted, affects everything an editor and a team of correspondents would do with the “more time, talent and money” they need to cover the 2004 campaign.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Nine Story Lines in a New Campaign Narrative
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes the Howard Dean 2004 presidential campaign, highlighting its innovative use of the internet and its departure from traditional campaign strategies.  Rosen identifies nine key storylines emerging from Dean's approach, focusing on themes of decentralized control, distributed ownership, citizen engagement, and the evolving relationship between campaigns, technology, and the public. He argues that these changes represent a significant shift in the political landscape, offering new opportunities for storytelling and political participation.
records.quote: The campaign system has been de-centered in the open style pioneered by Howard Dean.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Tough Guy Journalism More in Vogue in LA
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This PressThink post analyzes Tim Rutten's critique of Daniel Okrent's inaugural column as the New York Times' public editor. Rutten criticizes Okrent's self-disclosure of political views, viewing it as a surrender to 'bias talk' and a sign of weakness. Rosen counters this, arguing that Okrent's transparency is a positive step towards building credibility with a more discerning audience who values human perspective over the unattainable 'view from nowhere'. Rosen contrasts Rutten's 'tough guy' approach with a more nuanced understanding of audience engagement in the digital age.
records.quote: Journalists think good information leads to opinion and argument.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Private Life, Public Happiness and the Howard Dean Connection
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This text analyzes Samantha Shapiro's New York Times Magazine article on Howard Dean's 2004 presidential campaign. Rosen critiques the traditional campaign coverage model, highlighting Dean's unconventional, decentralized approach leveraging the internet. He contrasts this with the established 'hub-and-spoke' system, arguing that Dean's campaign challenged the established media's understanding of political participation and reporting. Rosen uses Shapiro's article, particularly its focus on the personal lives of Dean's online organizers, to illustrate the challenges of covering a digitally-driven campaign that defies traditional journalistic frameworks.
records.quote: Maybe what’s missing in people’s private lives is not only girlfriends and boyfriends, but something larger, “public happiness”— the opportunity to participate in a meaningful way and show the system a thing or two.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Special to PressThink: Interview With Rodney Benson on Journalism, French and American Style
records.author: Jay Rosen, Rodney Benson
records.summary: This PressThink interview with Rodney Benson compares the French and American press systems. Benson highlights key differences, such as the French press's more overt opinionated style, inclusion of contextual information, and eclectic mix of genres, fostering a more robust national public debate. Conversely, the American press, striving for objectivity, often presents a more segmented and less opinionated approach. The discussion explores how these differences reflect the distinct political cultures, media systems, and societal values of France and the United States.
records.quote: Okrent wasn’t confessing to bias in describing himself a social liberal, a free-trader, and a centrist Democrat in foreign policy. Nor was he falling in love with his reflection in the New York Times. He was treating readers like adults.

records.title: Governing Incorporates the Press and Vice Versa: The President's Secret Flight to Baghdad
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen analyzes President Bush's secret Thanksgiving 2003 flight to Baghdad as a case study in the politics of publicity. Reporters on the trip had their phones confiscated and were sworn to secrecy. Rosen identifies two inadequate frameworks for discussing such events — the cynical dismissal ('PR stunt') and the savvy admiration ('political masterstroke') — and traces the roots of the modern publicity state to the 1919 Versailles peace talks, when mass media first made public opinion a real-time factor in diplomacy.
records.quote: The American political language does not include a grown-up vocabulary for such events, which are co-equal with the publicity they generate and could not exist without that publicity.

records.title: A Public Editor for an Internet Public
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This text is not a complete article but a bibliography/listing of Jay Rosen's work and recommended readings related to the changing media landscape, particularly the rise of the internet and blogs. It highlights Rosen's commentary on the evolving authority of journalism, the impact of weblogs, and the relationship between online and print media, including the New York Times' experiment with a public editor.
records.quote: Okrent is the kind of test case Len Apcar was seeking: a Times-person already licensed to give his views and draw conclusions.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Raze Spin Alley, That Strange Creation of the Press

records.quote: Spin Alley is journalists helping to stage an event defined beforehand by its absence of information.

records.title: PressThink: Important if True: Online and Offline Meet Up to Change Politics

This will scramble the mind of the press if the press retains its master narrative: winning. Ed Cone— journalist, weblogger, tech thinker, biz writer—has done what is so far the definitive piece on What’s Different About Dean and why it matters.
records.quote: Not since the televised Nixon-Kennedy debates has there been a comparable shift in the art and science of running a campaign.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: A Politics that is Dumber Than Spam
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This text is a bibliography of Jay Rosen's work and a list of recommended blogs and online news sources active around the early 2000s. It reflects Rosen's engagement with the rise of the internet and its impact on journalism, particularly focusing on the emergence of blogs as a new form of news and commentary. The excerpt details Rosen's disillusionment with the 2000 presidential campaign, highlighting its focus on numbers and strategic targeting rather than substantive engagement with the public.
records.quote: It cannot be the case that 95 percent of the country must be ignored so that campaign rationality can prevail.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Exit, Voice and Loyalty at the Los Angeles Times
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This text is not a complete article but rather a collection of links and excerpts showcasing Jay Rosen's work and commentary on journalism, particularly the impact of the internet and blogs on the news industry. It highlights the changing dynamics of authority in journalism, the evolving relationship between the press and the public, and the challenges faced by traditional media in the digital age. The included excerpt discusses the Los Angeles Times' decision to publish a story about Arnold Schwarzenegger shortly before a recall election and the subsequent backlash, illustrating the complexities of journalistic decision-making and the evolving public response to the press.
records.quote: Hirschman said that when customers are dissatisfied with a firm, or constituents are angry with any organization, they have three basic options: exit, voice and loyalty.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: We Just Don't Think About It: The Strange Press Mind of Leonard Downie
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Columnist Matthew Miller tried to ask Len Downie about the latent politics of news judgment. But the editor of the Washington Post won't go there: "We are not allowing ourselves to think politically." The current issue of the Columbia Journalism Review offers a treat for fans of the minimalist style in press thought.
records.quote: Miller: But how do you decide which issues get front page treatment?

records.title: PressThink: Politics in a Different Key
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This text is not a single article but a curated list of Jay Rosen's work and recommended links to other blogs and online resources related to journalism, the internet, and politics, circa early to mid 2000s. It highlights the changing media landscape, the rise of weblogs, and the emergence of new forms of political engagement and journalism enabled by the internet. Rosen emphasizes the shift in power dynamics within the media and the challenge to traditional journalistic authority.
records.quote: The game is called Get Elected. All parties play (all who usually get elected.) It is overseen by a class of professionals who are supposed to know: how do you actually get elected in this country?
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: The Reagans and CBS
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Analysis of the controversy surrounding CBS's planned miniseries about Ronald and Nancy Reagan, and what the network's decision to pull the program revealed about the relationship between media, politics, and conservative criticism.
records.quote: CBS's decision to pull its Reagan miniseries revealed how media institutions can capitulate to organized political pressure, exposing the fragile boundary between editorial independence and conservative criticism.

records.title: PressThink: Opinion Bad, Reporting Good and Nothing Else Do You Need to Know
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: How dumb should an ombudsman assume Americans to be? NPR's Jeffrey Dvorkin forces us to ask that. His answer: very dumb indeed. “Whenever an NPR journalist opines in public about issues in the news, the consequences are fraught, in my opinion.” So says NPR ombudsman Jeffrey A.
records.quote: Bad punditry is bad not because it’s got those evil opinion thingies in it. It’s bad because it comes from people who don’t know very much about the dangerously wide range of topics on which they are expected to vent.

records.title: PressThink: The Other Bias at Fox News: Volume
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Another former Fox News grunt has spoken up, but it's a different tale. The "bias" is to get people screaming at their television sets-- liberals included. Matt Gross, now an assistant editor at New York magazine, used to work at Fox, but on the website, not in the field.
records.quote: It wasn’t that they were toeing some political line… it was that the facts of a story just didn’t matter at all. The idea was to get those viewers out of their seats, screaming at the TV, the politicians, the liberals — whoever — simply by running a provocative story.

records.title: PressThink: The Fox News Daily Memo: Is the Fix In?
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: According to a former news producer there, The Memo is the daily bible at Fox News, and it tells how stories are to be played. It's management. It's politics.
records.quote: The roots of FNC’s day-to-day on-air bias are actual and direct. They come in the form of an executive memo distributed electronically each morning, addressing what stories will be covered and, often, suggesting how they should be covered. To the newsroom personnel responsible for the channel’s daytime programming, The Memo is the bible.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: PressThink: Has Media Bias Has Become a Dumb Debate? A Man of the Left Responds to PressThink's Questions
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: "Any leftist who stops to think about the matter would probably agree: the media are too liberal, indeed!" And that means a genuine left perspective is left out. Brian Dominick takes bias apart, from his side of the table. A reader writes: My name is Brian Dominick, and I’m an online news editor who has mostly been involved with explicitly Leftist media projects over the years, including ZNet.
records.quote: The problem with bias, instead, is that it is not stated. News media should be up front about their bias, but they almost never are.

And that's rare. (Note: for the case of the missing link, now closed, go here.) records.title: PressThink: Special to PressThink: Interview With Jeff Jarvis, Part Two

Rosen contends that "the press" embodies a historical struggle for press liberty and public service ideals, which are essential components of a functioning democracy. He uses the example of Disney's acquisition and subsequent sale of newspapers to illustrate how the commercialization of media threatens these values and the unique role of the press in upholding them. records.quote: A newspaper is not just a record of community life but can serve as a catalyst for the civic dialogue that sustains it.

records.title: Book example of how media miss real issues
records.author: Lincoln Journal Star
records.summary: Book review discussing 'The Choice' and how media coverage misses real political issues, focusing on consultants rather than substance. Jay Rosen is mentioned as someone who studies media coverage.
records.quote: Media coverage of presidential campaigns focuses on consultants and strategy rather than substantive issues, missing what actually matters to voters.

records.title: MEDIA from A21 Skepticism is considered a key quality of journalism
records.author: Star Tribune
records.summary: The article discusses the role of skepticism in journalism and how journalists cover newsworthy events.
records.quote: Skepticism is treated as a foundational professional value in journalism, shaping how reporters approach and frame newsworthy events.

records.title: 'Choice' pays too little attention to issues
records.author: Syracuse Herald-Journal
records.summary: A review of Bob Woodward's book 'The Choice' discusses the book's focus on campaign strategy rather than issues. Jay Rosen is quoted as a public journalism leader criticizing the book's premise and focus on political consultants.
records.quote: I find it interesting that he assumes the mystery of politics that needs investigating is how these professional consultants work. Of all the things Americans need to investigate about their politics these days, that doesn't seem high on the list.

records.title: Inside again: The choice was ... theirs
records.author: The Boston Globe
records.summary: Review of Bob Woodward's book 'The Choice' which covers the 1996 presidential election. The review mentions that the book gives little evidence of the 'public journalism' movement, with Jay Rosen identified as its evangelist.
records.quote: The public journalism movement, which holds that reporting should begin and end with the needs of citizens rather than the agendas of officials, found little reflection in Woodward's access-driven account of the 1996 presidential race.

records.title: Work in progress: Can public journalism save a troubled profession?
records.author: The Ottawa Citizen
records.summary: A book review discussing public journalism and its potential to revitalize the troubled journalism profession. The review mentions Jay Rosen, described as a former New York University journalism professor, as a key figure in the public journalism movement.
records.quote: Public journalism, with figures like Rosen at its center, offered a vision for revitalizing a profession struggling to reconnect with its public purpose.

records.title: Getting the Connections Right: Public Journalism and the Troubles in the Press (Perspectives on the News)
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: At the same time, the profession itself is facing economic decline, as well as challenges from new information and communication technologies that threaten to eclipse traditional journalism. What is a journalist to do?Jay Rosen makes the case that journalists can avoid succumbing to these worrisome trends by practicing what is increasingly being called "public journalism." What is needed is a new connection between public and press, one in which the press recognizes its influence in public life and helps citizens to participate, and be fully informed and engaged.
records.quote: Journalists can avoid succumbing to economic decline and technological disruption by practicing 'public journalism'—building a new connection between press and public in which the press recognizes its influence in civic life and actively helps citizens participate and stay informed.
concepts: Not the odds but the stakes

records.title: "Public journalism" - just another way of doing what we've always done
records.author: News and Record
records.summary: Article discusses the concept of public journalism and its various forms. Jay Rosen is mentioned as someone who has written extensively about and analyzed public journalism, with reference to reviewing the literature on the subject.
records.quote: Public journalism, its critics argue, is simply a repackaging of what good journalists have always done — engaging communities and serving the public interest — dressed up in new language without fundamentally changing the practice.

records.title: Newspaper 'public journalism' effort to revitalize public life triggers debate
records.author: The Morning Call
records.summary: An article discussing the public journalism movement and the debate it has sparked within the newspaper industry. The article identifies Jay Rosen as the person who coined the term 'public journalism' and serves as director of the Project on Public Life and the Press at New York University.
records.quote: Jay Rosen, who coined the term 'public journalism' and directs the Project on Public Life and the Press at NYU, has sparked an industry-wide debate about whether journalism should actively work to revitalize public life.

records.title: Public Journalism A Case for Public Scholarship
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Jay Rosen argues for "public journalism," a movement reforming the American press. He critiques the existing disconnect between journalism practice and academic theory, advocating for collaborative, participatory approaches that prioritize civic engagement and a deliberative public sphere. Rosen highlights examples of newspapers implementing these new practices, emphasizing the need for journalists to actively support public life and engage in a mutually beneficial relationship with scholars.
records.quote: Public journalism, then, is a way of studying the press in common with journalists, where they are not the objects of inquiry, or targets of an academic critique, but co-producers of a form of understanding that could not exist without them.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Newspapers need to give citizens a voice, critics say
records.author: Asbury Park Press
records.summary: Coverage of a conference about newspapers giving citizens a voice. Jay Rosen is quoted defining public journalism as a self-conscious examination of professional newspaper culture.
records.quote: Jay Rosen defined public journalism as a self-conscious examination of professional newspaper culture, arguing that papers must give citizens a genuine voice rather than treating them as passive readers.

records.title: 'Public journalism' gets an ethical going-over
records.author: The Central New Jersey Home News
records.pub: The Central New Jersey Home News
records.summary: A panel yesterday discussed the advantages and potential irritants of newspaper writing that begins and ends with an audience in mind - 'public journalism,' termed by The Home News for its innovative reporting approach before an auditorium filled with students at the Busch Campus Center.
records.quote: Public journalism is newspaper writing that begins and ends with an audience in mind — asking citizens what's worth covering rather than deciding for them.

records.title: NEGATIVE NEWS misses the point
records.author: Calgary Herald
records.summary: By Ross, a journalism professor at New York University and director of the Project on Public Life and the Press, and reporting on negativity, 'We're still missing the entire sale of negativity, not for the sake of negativity, but for the sale of political drama.'
records.quote: Negativity in journalism is not the problem itself — the problem is negativity deployed as political drama, missing the deeper failures of civic life that journalism should expose.

records.title: Journalism
records.author: The Day
records.summary: A column on public journalism cites Jay Rosen's contrast between journalism's traditional concern with professional separation and public journalism's effort to repair connections with citizens.
records.quote: The challenge is how to get the connections right, because the connections are what’s faltering.

records.title: Every day a Saturday: Newspapers and community
records.author: Maria Henson
records.summary: Column by Maria Henson about community connections and the role of newspapers in civic life. In the 'Newspapers and community' section, Henson describes attending a conference on public journalism where NYU professor Jay Rosen invited Wendy Orange, a former psychologist and freelance writer, to listen to the proceedings, and discusses the connections between newspapers and public life.
records.quote: The leading advocate for the public journalism movement, New York University professor Jay Rosen, ultimately wants public life to go better.

records.title: What role do you play as citizen?
records.author: The Wichita Eagle
records.summary: A major editorial/opinion piece by Davis Merritt Jr. explaining the public journalism movement as a cultural change in how newspapers relate to their communities. The article includes multiple references to Jay Rosen's work and writings on public journalism, including quotes from his papers for the Kettering Foundation.
records.quote: Public judgment occurs when something is taken to heart in light of the importance of the good things we want in order to make a new and better choice, one that is collectively important.

records.title: Media advocacy to push causes steps over line
records.author: The Fresno Bee
records.summary: This article discusses media advocacy and whether it oversteps journalistic boundaries. It cites Roger Tatarian's views on "public journalism" and advocacy journalism.
records.quote: Advocacy journalism risks crossing a line that separates reporting from cause-pushing — a line public journalism proponents have not yet clearly defined.

records.title: Publishers, editors told future lies in 'public journalism'
records.author: The Coeur d'Alene Press
records.summary: Article reports on remarks to Pacific Northwest newspaper publishers and editors about the future of newspapers lying in 'public journalism,' which draws people in and asks them what's worth doing. The article notes declining readership and rising cynicism as motivations for the public journalism movement.
records.quote: The future of newspapers lies in public journalism, which draws people in and asks them what's worth doing — a response to declining readership and rising public cynicism about the press.

records.title: Journalists urged to try reaching out
records.author: The Olympian
records.summary: A brief article reporting on a conference where Jay Rosen spoke to Pacific Northwest journalists about public journalism and community engagement. Rosen urged newspapers to use their unique ability to help rebuild community.
records.quote: Rosen urged newspapers to use their unique position to help rebuild community through public journalism and greater civic engagement.

records.title: Newspapers must reconnect citizens with issues, execs told
records.author: The Spokesman-Review
records.summary: Jay Rosen tells Northwest newspaper executives that alienation from politics and media is driving people out of public life, and argues that public journalism should reconnect citizens with civic affairs.
records.quote: Increasingly [journalists] are seen as insiders themselves — part of a discredited political class.

records.title: What is R/UDAT? And what am I doing with it?
records.author: The Island Packet
records.summary: First-person article by a journalist describing involvement in an R/UDAT community assessment. The author discusses the rise of 'public journalism' and how journalists can get involved in community problem-solving, mentioning a group at New York University's journalism program.
records.quote: Public journalism asks whether journalists can move beyond detached observation to actively participate in community problem-solving — a question a group at NYU's journalism program is taking seriously.

records.title: Journalists should champion free speech, not fee speech
records.author: Lee Krenis More
records.summary: Media column discussing paid speaking fees and public trust in journalists. It ends with New York University journalism professor Jay Rosen predicting that journalists would become subjects of character stories.
records.quote: You're going to start having character stories about journalists. It's inevitable.

records.title: Public access, not excess, is media problem
records.author: Richard Harwood
records.summary: Richard Harwood column quoting New York University journalism professor Jay Rosen on an “everywhere culture” loosening the ground on which newspapers stand and on newspaper reading as participation in a world where politics and public affairs matter.
records.quote: To pick up a newspaper and scan the front page is to feel yourself a member of a world in which politics and public affairs matter.

records.title: Elite Press Reporting On Elite Government
records.author: Valley News
records.summary: An opinion piece by Washington Post media critic Richard Harwood discussing changes in the journalism landscape and the relationship between elite press and elite government. The article references Jay Rosen's writing about how newspaper journalists have been replaced at networks and magazines.
records.quote: Elite newspapers and elite government have developed a mutually reinforcing relationship, with journalists increasingly serving as interpreters for one powerful class to another rather than as a voice for the broader public.

records.title: Mixed message
records.author: The Vancouver Sun
records.summary: A letter to the editor criticizing a statement by Jay Rosen about objectivity in journalism. The letter writer takes issue with Rosen's claim that objectivity should be used to frame problems to enable societal discussion, arguing this suggests journalists manipulate how stories are presented.
records.quote: The real purpose of objectivity is to frame problems in ways that enable society to talk about them.

records.title: Open phones; A new role for journalism
records.author: Alex S. Jones; John Dinges; Davis Merritt Jr.; Jay Rosen
records.summary: An early On The Media broadcast featuring a panel discussion on new roles for journalism. Rosen appears alongside John Dinges and Davis Merritt Jr. -- a key figure in the public journalism movement -- to discuss how journalism might evolve to better serve democratic life. This is one of Rosen's earliest known broadcast appearances, predating PressThink and his major written works.
records.quote: One of Rosen's earliest broadcast appearances finds him arguing that journalism must evolve beyond its traditional role to more actively serve democratic life.

records.title: A reluctant editor takes the plunge into participation
records.author: Tallahassee Democrat
records.summary: A Tallahassee Democrat editor describes reconsidering journalistic detachment after joining a community relations council and quotes Jay Rosen criticizing Washington Post editor Leonard Downie's refusal to vote.
records.quote: Downie invests too much in his professional identity and too little in his standing as a citizen.

records.title: President meets the press
records.author: The Flint Journal
records.summary: Editorial discussing the relationship between President Clinton and the White House press corps, arguing for more civility and sense. The piece mentions Jay Rosen as being correct in chastising the press corps to exercise more sense and civility.
records.quote: The White House press corps would benefit from more civility and sense in its relationship with the president, and critics like Jay Rosen are right to say so.

records.title: Journalism professor barks at press, but the culprit escapes
records.author: The Arizona Republic
records.summary: An Arizona Republic editorial challenges Jay Rosen's Tikkun argument that repetitive coverage of minor controversies was damaging Bill Clinton's presidency, saying the press was neglecting more serious policy failures.
records.quote: The withdrawal of another White House nomination, the ‘Travelgate’ mess, the pricey haircut — these themes are recycled to death.

records.title: I Am Not Optimistic But I Do Have Hope: The Future of Journalism in A Media Age
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: This 1993 lecture distinguishes between 'journalism' and 'The Media,' arguing that journalism's purpose is to foster a public, not merely an audience.  Rosen critiques the prevailing view of news as merely 'part of our world' and challenges the notion of journalistic objectivity as espoused by Leonard Downie Jr. He contrasts two visions of American democracy—Hamilton's emphasis on private gain and Jefferson's focus on public participation—and asserts that journalism should align with the latter, advocating for a reinvention of journalism to prevent its absorption into the media industry.
records.quote: Journalism’s mission is to contribute to public happiness. That is the “part of our world” that journalists must understand and convey.
concepts: The People Formerly Known as the Audience

records.title: Study of network TV is out of touch
records.author: R.G.
records.summary: A Globe and Mail review says a documentary about U.S. network television relies on analysis from Jay Rosen and Todd Gitlin, but faults the film for overlooking cable television and changing viewer choices.
records.quote: “The big lie,” says Gitlin, is the cherished notion that TV “can show you the world,” that everything worth knowing and feeling “is televisable, picturable.”

records.title: Who should the newspaper be published for?
records.author: Journal of the San Juan Islands
records.pub: Journal of the San Juan Islands
records.summary: Article discusses the purpose of newspapers and references Jay Rosen's essay about media trends. Rosen's analysis of the tension between grabbing attention versus serving the community is quoted.

records.summary: Coverage of a conference on Gulf War press restrictions. Jay Rosen says public support for the military and hostility to reporters strengthened the government's bond with the audience.

records.summary: Analysis of suburban voters as key to the 1992 presidential election. Jay Rosen is mentioned as a New York University professor who called suburbanization 'one of the most important stories in American politics.'

records.title: Political power has moved to the suburbs

records.title: The Impossible Press: American Journalism and the Decline of Public Life
records.author: Jay Rosen
records.summary: Rosen's doctoral dissertation traces the history of the idea that the function of the press is to inform the public. It argues that the rise of the mass circulation newspaper, while creating a technical ability to reach everyone, actually undermined the conditions necessary for a "universal town meeting." Drawing heavily on Walter Lippmann and John Dewey, it suggests that the professionalization of journalism ("objectivity") was a retreat from the problem of creating a genuine public life in a complex society. It contrasts news as "symptom" vs. news as "symbol" and explores how the press creates a "pseudo-environment" of public opinion.
records.quote: An impossible press was born, one which sought to solve the whole problem of public life simply by controlling the conduct of journalists.
